GENUS ADELON

Pages 243-243

Lesson. No <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>; no <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TUBERCLES">tubercles</a> on the palate; no whalebone; body fusiform; forehead prominent; jaw in a continuous line with the forehead. *A. Dalei*, Lesson; *Delphinus Dalei*, Blainv., F. Cuv.; *D. edentulus*, Schreber, Desm. 783; *Delphinorhyncus micropterus*, Cuv. (See Plate XVII., <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> 6.) Body fusiform; some appearance of a neck; forehead prominent; spiracle curved forwards; jaws prolonged in form of a subcylindrical beak, and in the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> with the facial line, the upper somewhat shorter than the lower; no teeth, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> only rudimentary; no rugosities on the palate; pectorals and dorsal very small; tail <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> shining-grey, dark above, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> beneath; vertebrae <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a>, and from fifteen to twenty more; ribs nine; maxillary and intermaxillary <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-BONES">bones</a> rising <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> above the frontal. This beautiful animal stranded itself near <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAVRE">Havre</a>; its resorts, habits, &c., are wholly unknown. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> was originally founded on the *Bottlehead* of Dale, and designated as *B. edentulus* by Schreber, Blainville, and Desmarest. The name was applied afresh to a specimen stranded near Havre in 1825, and examined by Drs Suriray and Blainville. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> Hunter was <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> in saying that his *Bidentatus* was the same as Dale's, then the authors last quoted were incorrect in associating that name with the Havre specimen. This was Cuvier's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, who says (in *Reg. An.*) that the name was "très imprécise." Nevertheless we retain it, as we believe the species has been accurately described under that designation. The **GENUS Ziphias** being fossil, we omit. Cuvier states that their craniums ally them to the Cachalots, and still more to the Hyperoodons. He has distinguished three species, all of which appear to be destitute of teeth. **SUBDIVISION III. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">GREAT</a>-HEADED WHALES.** We now advance to the last subdivision of the ordinary whales, which is distinguished from the others by having the head much larger than the usual proportions, amounting to one-fourth, or even to one-third of the whole bulk. Though this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECTION">section</a> includes by far the most important animals of the order, yet the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> it contains is small, extending to but three genera, and about twice as many ascertained species. All of these, from their extraordinary magnitude, and the majority from their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> value, have from <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> immemorial engaged the liveliest and most general <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>; and hence, notwithstanding their gigantic size, their structure is better known, and their habits and disposition better ascertained, than those of most others of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RACE">race</a>.

GENUS CACHALOT

Pages 243-246

Bon. Desm. Cuv. *Physeter*, Linn. Head nearly one-third of the whole size; blow-hole single; no baleen; no <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> only rudimentary, in the upper jaw; lower jaw narrow, elongated, received into a furrow in the upper one, armed on each side with a range of strong teeth. Produces the spermaceti and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMBERGRIS">ambergris</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>. *C. macrocephalus*, Cuv. Bon. Lacép. *Physeter catodon*, Linn. The *Spermaceti Whale*. (See Plate XVII., fig. 11.) One or more humps on the back; lower jaw having from 20 to 23 teeth on each side; a few rudimentary ones hid under the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUMS">gums</a> in the upper jaw; length 80 feet; <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> greenish-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">black</a> above, whitish beneath. Vertebrae, 7, 14, 38, = 59. Some of our readers may perhaps be surprised, that under the generic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TERM">term</a> Cachalot we introduce to their notice only a single <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. This we do, not because we deny the existence of others, but because these have not hitherto been accurately described or established. Desmarest some years ago admitted three sub-genera and eight species; and Lacépède has three genera and eight species, including his cachalots, physalus, and physeter. Every one who, pre- --- 1 Journal de Physique, 1789. 2 Phil. Trans. 1787. 3 Lesson, 130. Though this is clearly asserted by Lesson, we do not find the mistake in the Encycl. Method. It is very apparent in Lacépède's Cetacea, p. 320. 4 See Ooz. Foss. t. v. 325. Less. 120. Fr. Cuv. 244. 5 From Cachou, a tooth, in the Basque tongue. 6 We shall here exhibit the older classification by copying that of Lacépède. I. Genus Cachalot. Having blow-hole at the extremity of the snout. 1. Subgenus. Those which have a hump or bumps on their back. 1st sp. C. macrocephalus. 2nd sp. C. catodon. 2. Subgenus. 4th sp. C. albus. II. Genus Physeter. Having blow-hole on the head, not at the extremity of the snout. 5th sp. P. cylindricus. Having a bump on the back. III. Genus Physeter. A <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-FIN">fin</a> on the back. 6th sp. P. Macroptera. 7th, P. Orthonoë. 8th, P. Mular. Cetacea, vious to our own days, had attempted to reconcile the many contradictory accounts which have been given of this extraordinary animal, seems in his turn to have been foiled; and it was reserved for Cuvier to cut at all events, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not to unravel, the entangled knot. He remarks: "The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of this animal is so perplexed, so many beings have been confounded with it, and the species have been so wantonly multiplied, that to obtain more precision on the subject, I have been obliged to review, chronologically, everything that naturalists have written concerning it." And after making this review, he concludes, "<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">Will</a> it now be regarded as <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> temerity in me, after having produced the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of so many learned men, to maintain that up to the present <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a>, there is no ground to suppose that there is more than a single species of Cachalot?" We take our <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> very much from that supplied by Cuvier. It is one of the largest Cetacea, attaining the length of 70 and 80 feet; its head is very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> in all its dimensions, and the length of that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> does not appear to have been much exaggerated when stated to be about a third of the whole body; the snout is very obtuse, and apparently truncated; the lower jaw, very narrow, is received between the upper lips as in a furrow, the teeth entering, when the mouth is shut, into cavities on the edge of the palate. The blow-hole, 12 inches <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a>, in the form of an f, is on the anterior extremity of the head, in the centre of a round protuberance, formed of thick fibres, which <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACT">act</a> as a sphincter. The pectorals are small and obtuse; there is a small dorsal protuberance only, far <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the back, and sometimes two or three smaller ones; the tail is very large. The colour above is a blackish and somewhat greenish-grey; below it is whitish, as also round the eyes. The immense cavity at the upper part of the head, covered only by a tendinous but very resisting integument, is divided interiorly into compartments, also tendinous, which communicate with one another, and into great cells filled with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, which is fluid when the animal is alive, but after <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> assumes the concrete form with which we are familiar under the name of spermaceti. This substance was long absurdly regarded as the brain, which, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, occupies a very small space in the interior of the cranium. The ambergris again, is found in the intestinal canal, but in what precise part, and under what exact circumstances, has not yet been ascertained. From the popular and highly interesting statement of Mr Beale, we learn that the blubber on the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> of a large whale is about 14 inches thick, and on most other parts of the body from 8 to 11. This covering the southern whalers call the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLANKET">blanket</a>; it is of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> colour, and when melted down yields the sperm oil. He states, that the opening of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a> is of sufficient size to admit a small quill. The throat is capacious enough to give passage to the body of a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a>, in this respect presenting a strong <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a> to the contracted gullet of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GREENLAND">Greenland</a> whale. According to Mr Beale, the peculiarity of the sperm-whale which strikes every beholder, is the unwieldy bulk of the head; but this, instead of being an impediment, is conducive to its agility, for the greatest part of it containing oil, the head receives a tendency to rise so far above the surface, as to elevate the blow-hole for the purposes of respiration; and should the animal wish to increase its speed to the utmost, the narrow lower portion of the head, which bears some resemblance to the cut-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a> of a ship, is the only part exposed to the resistance of the water, and it is thus enabled to press its ponderous way, with the greatest ease, along the ocean. "<a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>, how manifold are thy works! in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> thou hast made them all." "They that go down to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> in ships, that do business in the great waters; these see the works of the Lord, and his wonders in the deep." Mr Beale's observations on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a> of this whale are curious. He states that, when undisturbed, it passes tranquilly along, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUST">just</a> below the surface of the water, at the rate of about three or four miles an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, its progress being effected by a gentle oblique <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the tail from side to side. When proceeding at this rate, the body lies horizontally; the water, somewhat disturbed by its progress, is known by the whalemen under the name of "<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-WHITE">white</a>-water," and from its appearance, an experienced eye can, from a distance of several miles, judge of the rate at which the whale is advancing. In this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of swimming, it is able to attain a velocity of about <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> miles an hour. When it swims at a more rapid rate, the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the tail is altered, the water is struck directly upwards and downwards, and each time the blow is made with the lower surface, the head sinks down eight or ten feet; and when the blow is reversed, it rises out of the water, presenting to it only the sharp cut-water portion. This mode of swimming is what is called going-head-out, and in this way the whale can attain a speed of 10 or 12 miles an hour, which is probably its greatest velocity. The sperm-whale is remarkably distinguished from its congeners by its blowing. If the water is smooth, the first part observed is the hump, projecting two or three feet above the surface; at very regular intervals of time, the spout emerges, at the distance of forty or fifty feet; from the extremity of the spout the jet is thrown up, and when seen from a distance, appears thick, low, bushy, and of a white colour. It is formed, according to Mr Beale, by the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AIR">air</a> expelled forcibly through the spiracle, acquiring its white colour from minute particles of water previously lodged in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> fissure. It is projected at an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of 45°, in a slow and continuous manner, for about three seconds, and may be discovered at the distance of 4 or 5 miles. This leviathan is, like the mysticetus, remarkably timid, and is readily alarmed by the approach of any unlooked-for object. When frightened it is said by the sailors to be "galled," probably galled; and in this state it performs many actions in a manner very different from the usual mode. One of these is what is called "sweeping," which consists in moving the tail slowly from side to side on the surface of the water, as if feeling for any object that might be near. This whale has also an extraordinary fashion of rolling over and over on the surface, especially when harpooned; in which <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CASE">case</a> it will occasionally coil an amazing length of rope around it. But one of its most surprising feats—as it is of those of all the larger genera—is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAPING">leaping</a> completely out of the water, or "breaching," as it is called—a practice which, from its dangerous results to those around, is regarded by mariners as far "more honoured in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> than the observance." The mode in which this appears to be done is by descending to a certain depth, and then making several powerful strokes with its tail, thus imparting great velocity to the body before it reaches the surface, when it darts completely out of the water. It seldom breaches more than twice or thrice at a time, and in quick succession; the performance may be seen at the distance of six miles from the mast head. We once witnessed a Scotch whale performing a similar feat in Loch-fyne, between the loved shores of Minard and Castle Lachlan. The sperm-whale seems now to have nearly vanished from the northern hemisphere, though it is frequent in numerous places in the southern. In the year 1791, seventy- --- 1 Ona Fossil. t. v. p. 339. 2 For a somewhat minute and valuable account of the anatomy of a sperm-whale, which was <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> ashore on the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> in April 1825, see a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> by James Alderson, Esq. in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> vol. of the Trans. of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a> Phil. Soc. 3 Observations on the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> History of the Sperm-Whale. Lond. 1833. five vessels belonging to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> were engaged in the trade, whilst in 1830 only thirty-one ships were sent out, all from the port of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, with an aggregate burden of 11,000 tons, and 937 men. On its introduction into commerce spermaceti was chiefly employed in medicine, in which its <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> is still <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>; and it is also freely used in the cosmetic art. Its largest and most valuable application, however, has long been in the manufacture of candles, in which it maintains a rivalry with wax, as cheaper and not less elegant. Ambergris, according to its <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, is a peculiarly valuable product of the sperm-whale. The majority of sperm-whales, however, do not yield it. Sometimes it sells in London at about £1 an ounce, but frequently two or three voyages are accomplished, and successfully too, without any ambergris being obtained. It is seldom or never found in young fish, but only in those of full size, or rather of great <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>. It is generally considered the result of some diseased <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> in the intestinal canal; the quantity obtained, therefore, is very various. Sometimes 50 lb. have been extracted from a single individual. Ambergris is frequently found in considerable quantities on the sea-shore, especially in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> seas. It is highly esteemed by the orientalists. With us its use is confined almost wholly to the perfumer. C. sulcatus? <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABEL">Abel</a> Rémusat. Lacépéde. Reported to have a furrow below the lower jaw, and to frequent the Chinese seas. Aggadachyk? Tschiduk? Tschumtschugagah? Pallas and Chamisso. These are alleged Kamtschatkan varieties. See Less. and Fr. Cuv. Genus <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BALENA">BALENA</a>, Lacép. Cuv. Less. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>-whale of northern fishers. No teeth; blow-holes <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a>; no dorsal fin; long whalebone or baleen in the upper jaw; blubber thick and highly productive of oil. B. mysticetus, Linn. Desm. (No. 798.) True whale, Bon. Lacép. Greenland whale of Fab. and of fishers. B. borealis, Klein. (See Plate XVII., <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> 12.) Length about 60 feet; body of vast circumference; fanons more than 300 on each side of upper jaw, extending from 10 to 15 feet in length; colour black above, and partly white beneath. Vertebrae 7, 13—2. In former times there was much exaggeration as to the dimensions of this whale, 80 and 100 feet being assigned as a frequent size, and 150 and 200 feet as not uncommon. Some of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> stated, that it attained even a much greater length. From the researches, however, of Dr Scoresby, it seems irrefragably established, that the mysticetus never exceeds nor has exceeded 65 or 70 feet. That excellent observer was personally concerned in the capture of 322 whales, not one of which exceeded 60 feet. It is thickest a little behind the fins, whence it gradually tapers in a conical form towards the tail, and slightly towards the head. The head is remarkably large, forming nearly one-third of the whole bulk. Its under part is flat, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> from 16 to 20 feet in length, and from 10 to 12 in breadth. When the mouth is open it presents a cavity as large as a small apartment, and capable of containing a ship's jolly-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> full of men. The mysticetus has no dorsal fin, the pectoral fins are about <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> feet long and five <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. The tail is semilunar, indented in the middle. On the most elevated part of the head, about sixteen feet from the extremity of the jaw, are situated the blow-holes, consisting of two longitudinal apertures, similar to the holes in the body of a violin, from eight to twelve inches in length. The mouth, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of teeth, contains two extensive rows of baleen, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called whalebone, suspended from the upper jaw and sides of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> bone. The plates are generally curved longitudi- nally, and give to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> of the mouth the form of an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>. They inclose the tongue between their lower extremities, and are themselves covered by the lower lip. There are upwards of 300 of these plates on each side of the jaw; they are longest in the middle, whence they gradually diminish away to nothing both in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRONT">front</a> and behind. The tongue is incapable of protrusion; and the throat is remarkably narrow,—according to Sir C. Giesecke, not exceeding an inch and a half in width. The colour of the true whale is mostly velvet-black, with white in some parts underneath, and a tinge of yellow. The blubber, constituting the most valuable part of the animal, forms a complete wrapper round the whole body from eight to twenty inches thick. Being somewhat <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> than the medium in which it swims, the Greenland whale can remain on the surface with its spiracles above water, without any effort or motion; and it is thus sometimes found asleep upon the waves. Though bulky and clumsy, it is capable of making great exertion. A whale extended motionless on the surface can sink, in the space of five or six seconds, beyond the reach of its <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> enemies. Dr Scoresby has observed a whale descending, after it had been harpooned, to the depth of a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MILE">mile</a>, with the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> velocity of seven or eight miles an hour. The usual rate, however, at which they swim when on their passage from one station to another, seldom exceeds four miles an hour. Sometimes they <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LEAP">leap</a> entirely out of the water, and sometimes they throw themselves into a perpendicular position, with their heads downwards, and waving their tremendous tails on <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> in the air, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> the water with awful violence,—the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> reverberating to the distance of two or three miles. This feat is denominated "lob-tailing." They usually remain at the surface to breathe, about two minutes—seldom longer; and during this time they blow eight or nine times, and then descend for an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> usually of five or ten minutes, although sometimes, when feeding, of fifteen or twenty. When harpooned or apprehending danger, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> is greatly prolonged. The food of these animals, so vast and strong, is too remarkable not to claim a moment's <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. They have no teeth, and hence we at once perceive that they cannot prey either on the smaller of their own kind or on fishes; and their throat is so narrow that they could scarcely dispose of such a morsel as might be swallowed by an ox. Their well provided pasture grounds, however, exhibit to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a> of the curious one of the most wonderful manifestations of beneficence and power. Vast portions of those spaces in which the whale is found, consist of what is called green-water; as there is yellow and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-RED">red</a> water, in other parts of the ocean. This was examined by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Scoresby in 1816, and to his astonishment he found that it obtained its colour from the presence of countless millions of animalculæ, most of them invisible without the aid of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a>, and of which the greater <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> consisted of a species of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEDUSA">medusa</a>. These minute creatures are not the immediate food of the whale; they form, however, the prey of the various shrimps, small <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRUSTACEA">crustacea</a>, cuttle-fish, &c. upon which the monster of the deep is supported. When this whale feeds it swims with considerable velocity below the surface, with its jaws widely extended. A stream of water consequently enters its mouth, and along with it large quantities of minute crustaceans and molluscous animals; the water flows out again at the sides, but the food is entangled by the baleen or whalebone, which, from its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> arrangement, and thick internal covering of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, does not allow a particle to escape, even of the size of the smallest grain. The mysticetus, though often found in great numbers, can scarcely be said to be gregarious; --- 1 See Mem. du <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MUSEUM">Museum</a>, t. iv. 2 Giesecke. 3 Edin. Phil. Journ. vol. i. for it generally occurs either solitary or in pairs, except when attracted to the same spot by an abundance of palatable food, or a choice situation among polar icebergs. B. Nordoeper, Anderson, Bon., Lacép., Desm. (No. 799.) B. glacialis, Klein. We reject this species, as established by mistake on insufficient grounds. B. antarctica, Delalande, Cuv., Desmoul., Lacép., Fr. Cuv. Usually from forty to fifty feet long; colour wholly black; line of the forehead more depressed than in the mysticetus; pectorals longer and more pointed. Vertebrae 7, cervical, all ankylosed, 15 dorsal, others 37, in all 59. This species, nearly up to the present period, has been confounded with the preceding; and probably we might have been still ignorant of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, had not M. Delalande, during his residence at the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> of Good Hope, prepared one of these animals, and transmitted its skeleton to France, where Cuvier soon detected its specific <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>. The whale of the Southern Seas is decidedly smaller than that of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, measuring only from thirty-five to forty-five feet, though sometimes extending to fifty. Its baleen, owing to the great curve of the upper jaw, appears to be relatively longer, usually reaching to about nine feet in a fish of forty feet. Whilst the pectoral fins appear longer and more pointed, the lobes of the tail are less marked than in the preceding species. This whale is found in the bays of Terra del <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FUEGO">Fuego</a>, and on the western coast of South <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>; it also occurs around <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-NEW_HOLLAND">New <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, as well as along the African shore. It visits the Cape of Good principally in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a>. Its capture is more easily achieved than that of the great Greenland species. The ensuing quotations seem to us to indicate the existence of other still undetermined species in the Arctic Regions. "The whales," says Dr Scoresby, "seen in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> in lat. 80° N., which are usually full grown animals, disappear generally by the end of April. Those in 78° are of a mixed size; such as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> to fields in May and June are generally young animals. Those seen in 76° are almost always of a very large kind. In some the head measures four-tenths of the whole length, in others scarcely three-tenths; in some the circumference is upwards of seven-tenths of the length, in others less than six-tenths. It is probable the difference in the appearance of the heads, and the difference of proportion existing between the heads and bodies of some mysticetes, are characteristic of different species or subspecies. Those inhabiting lower latitudes have commonly long heads and bodies compared to their circumference, moderately thick blubber and long whalebone; those of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> latitudes, that is 78° or 79°, have more commonly short broad heads, compared with the size of the body." It is certain, observes M. Frémenville, "that the fishers confound many species which are still unknown. On my expedition towards the North Pole, in 1806, I remarked there were great differences in the shape of the tails of the whales which were taken, and which, without doubt, belonged to species not yet accurately ascertained." It is also more than probable that another occurs in the southern seas. "I am certain," says Baron Cuvier, "that at least a third species exists at the Cape of Good Hope, seeing we have satisfactory knowledge of vertebrae, which, with the characters of the subgenus (without dorsal-fin), present also distinct specific characters." We cannot dismiss these slight notices of this important species, without referring the reader to Dr Scoresby's elaborate treatise on the Arctic Regions, which contains a most interesting history and description of the northern whale-fishery. Consult also the first volume of the Editor's Cabinet Library, entitled Narrative of Discovery and Adventure in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLAR_SEAS">Polar Seas</a> and Regions. Fourth Edition, 1835. We may further add, that the first tolerable figure of B. Mysticetus ever published was the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> one of Scoresby. Genus Robqualus, Cuvier., Less., F. Cuv. (See Plate XVII, figure 13.) No teeth; a dorsal-fin; folds under the throat and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHEST">chest</a>; famous in upper jaw, but short;

GENUS CANIS

Pages 171-177

Linn. Cuv.** | Incisives | Canines | Molars | |-----------|---------|--------| | 6 | 1—1 | 6—6 | The incisive <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> are all placed on the same line, and are usually trilobate, before being worn by <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. The upper molars consist of three small single-lobed false molars, one bicuspidate carnivorous cheek-tooth, and two small tuberculous teeth with flattened crowns. The inferior molars consist of four false molars, one carnivorous cheek-tooth, and two tuberculous grinders. The tongue is smooth. The anterior extremities are furnished with five toes, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POSTERIOR">posterior</a> with four. This genus, of such <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> importance as containing the numerous and various breeds of our <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> dog, is in one <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> other of its forms most widely spread over almost all the regions of the habitable globe. We shall not here attempt to give the peculiar <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CANIS">Canis</a> familiaris, by which general specific <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TERM">term</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we may be allowed the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, naturalists are in use to distinguish the domesticated races from the wolves, jackals, and foxes, because their characters are so extremely variable in their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and admit of such an extended range of modification, that the exceptions to any presupposed peculiarity are almost as numerous as its confirmations. The more curved form of the tail probably distinguishes all domestic dogs from wolves, while the rounded outline of the pupil serves to separate them from the foxes, in which that organ, when exposed to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, assumes a lenticular shape. We shall proceed to a few general observations on the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of these animals, without attempting even an enumeration of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> domestic kinds. The real origin of our domestic breeds whether from a single or complex source, may be said to be now entirely unknown, as a subject either of history or <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>. It is lost in the usual obscurity of a remote antiquity, and can now only be ascertained (if at all) by the investigations of the naturalist. So infinitely varied is the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> aspect of these invaluable creatures, and so much does it seem to depend, not only on the physical conditions of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> under which they exist, but on the moral and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> state of the particular nations by whom they are held in subjection, that in numerous instances all traces of resemblance to the supposed original, or indeed to any known <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of wild animal, have disappeared; and after the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAPSE">lapse</a> of ages, we are in fact at last presented with what may be termed <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> creatures, incapable of subsisting without the aid and companionship of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and of which assuredly no natural <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TYPE">type</a> ever existed in any <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> or country. It is clear from what we know of the harmonious laws by which Divine <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> regulates the economy of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ANIMAL_KINGDOM">animal <a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, that no such creature as a pug dog could ever have existed as an independent being in a state of nature, or formed one of those "<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> links" by which <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> is so softly blended. It would have marred the immaculate <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of the primeval world. Many varieties, however, of the domestic dog, though originally produced by what may be termed accidents, have now become permanent subspecies, if we may use the term, each of which is signalised by some characteristic peculiarity of either a physical or instinctive nature, and differs from an ordinary variety (as exhibited among unreclaimed animals), in the power which it possesses of reproducing individuals exactly similar to itself. Several of these varieties from their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> value to mankind, have been so encouraged and preserved in purity, as to have become impressed with characters not only distinctive, but of so uniform and permanent a nature as to exhibit in certain instances the aspect of a total <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in kind. Making due allowance, however, for the influence of all extraneous or accidental causes, we yet deem it impossible to doubt that the origin of the dog tribe, as it now exists under the extended dominion of mankind, has been rather complex than simple. We do not <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> to maintain that every strongly marked variety has had each its own original source, or that even when nature "Wanted's as in her prime, and play'd at <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> Her virgin fancies," there ever existed wild greyhounds, unreclaimed pug dogs, or native pointers and poodles, all alike independent of each other, and of their now acknowledged <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LORD">lord</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, because the question in that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CASE">case</a> would, from their multiplicity, be specially set at rest by the occurrence of one or other of these animals in its original and unsubdued condition. But we think it improper to refer the various breeds to one and the same origin, the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> seeming to ourselves more natural which supposes that the characteristic kinds, or great leading varieties of each country or continent, have either directly descended from, or been crossed and remodelled by a union with, such of the native (canine) animals of the same natural genus, as we still find to occur in such country or continent. For example, although we may admit with Guldentraadt, that the Kalmar and some other eastern dogs, may have derived their origin from the jackal, the same cannot be said of those of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-NEW_HOLLAND">New <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, or of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">North</a> and South <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, where the jackal is unknown; and several of our own northern varieties are evidently descended so much more immediately from the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WOLF">wolf</a>, as to render the ancestral aid of the "lion's provider" altogether superfluous. We also know that in America and New Holland, at the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of (and consequently <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to) the discovery of these countries by Europeans, there existed both wild and domesticated dogs, the former of which were evidently indigenous, and in all <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> the origin of the latter. We believe that Pallas was among the first to give currency to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that the dog was to be regarded in a great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> as an adventitious animal, that is to say, as a creature produced by the fortuitous and diversified alliances of several natural species. Both the shepherd's dog and the wolf dog, in his opinion, derive their origin from the jackal, while the mastiff is regarded as more nearly related to the hyena, and the smaller tribes of terriers, &c., to the fox. His <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>, though somewhat fanciful, merit the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of the naturalist. We object, however, to the hyena, which (though classed with the dogs by Linnaeus) is not in fact a canine animal, but belongs to a distinct and well-defined genus, characterized by having five toes on each foot, and five molar teeth on either side of both jaws; whereas the truly canine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RACE">race</a>, such as dogs, wolves, and jackals, have only four toes on the hinder extremities, with six molar teeth on each side of the upper jaw, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> on each side of the under. The general proportions of the hyena, too, are very different, the fore-legs being longer than the hind ones, which has the effect of raising the shoulders and anterior portion of the body; whereas in the other species <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUST">just</a> named, the hind legs are longer than the fore ones, a character which probably obtains among all swift-footed animals. The immediate relationship of the fox is likewise doubtful. His <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> would be useful as giving the earthly propensities of the terrier tribes, but we cannot overlook the peculiar shape of the pupil, which is what naturalists call nocturnal, that is <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a>, and narrowing under the influence of light; whereas in dogs and other canine species, though it decreases in size under that influence, it retains its circular form. The difference in the habitual character and instinctive habits of the fox must also be borne in mind. It is scarcely necessary to say that it is a wary, silent, nocturnal animal, of sly and solitary habits, never congregating, or hunting its prey in packs, but preferring a gradual and unperceived approach, and the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of an insidious cunning, to the more open warfare declared by its congeners. This distinction is in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of greater importance than may at first appear, for we consider the social or gregarious sentiment in animals as --- 1 We have given a more extended view of the origin and natural history of domestic dogs in the 5th and 6th numbers of the Quarterly Journal of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a>, and in the first volume of our Illustrations of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, genus Canis. The reader will find a valuable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> (by another <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAND">hand</a>) on sporting dogs, under the term Hounds, of this Encyclopedia. See volume xi. p. 782. 2 For Humboldt's opinion of the indigenous dogs of South America, see Personal Narrative, vol. ii. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> 2. the true basis of a thorough domestication. A solitary species may, indeed, be tamed, so far as the individual is concerned, but if the social <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INSTINCT">instinct</a> is wanting, its descendants will be only half reclaimed, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> must be again resorted to. But the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, which we call the social instinct, and which is so strongly possessed by sheep, oxen, and other domestic kinds, when once properly directed towards himself by the skill of man, renders these animals forever both attached and subservient to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> race. Another strong objection, though of a more <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a> kind, to the theories of Pallas and Guldenstaedt, is founded on their slight consideration, if not entire <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXCLUSION">exclusion</a>, of the wolf as the most probable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARENT">parent</a>, especially in northern countries, of a numerous and important tribe of our domestic dogs. In reference to the point at issue, we indeed regard this animal, as of all others, the most entitled to our strong attention. Many well-known varieties of the dog exhibit so wolfish an aspect, that their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> from that species, at a more or less remote period, can scarcely be doubted; and we incline the more to this opinion, when we consider that the jackal is not a northern animal, that the wolf is eminently so; and that the remotest tribes of the human race, inhabiting the highest northern latitudes, have never been found unaccompanied by a domesticated breed of dogs, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> a greater resemblance to the wolf than to the jackal. All the principal and regulating facts in the natural history of the wolf and dog are identical. The rutting season commences at the same <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and continues for an equal period in each; and both carry their young for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> weeks. —Gillibert's opinion that the period of the wolf's gestation extended to three months and a half having since been proved to be erroneous. Then the jackal is a puny and powerless creature, compared with many of its alleged descendants, while the wolf is one of the strongest of European carnivorous animals. Though those of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> are not gigantic, the wolves of Lithuania are extremely <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>, frequently measuring five feet in length from the muzzle to the insertion of the tail; and the same, or even increased dimensions are maintained by those of still more northern climes. Both their coat and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> vary in accordance with the climate. In high northern latitudes they become <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-WHITE">white</a> in winter, and a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">black</a> variety occurs in Spain. This natural <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VARIATION">variation</a> of the colour of the wolf is a circumstance of some importance in relation to the present inquiry, because the tendency to become white at one extremity of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a>, or range of colours, and black at the other, combined with what may be called the central or representative hue of the animal, which is <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>, supplies in fact the three elementary colours of the whole tribe of dogs, and thus in a great measure accounts for the variety of markings by which our domestic races are distinguished. In a state of domestication the wolf is capable of assuming and retaining all the docility and gentleness of the dog, and the productive union of the two, though at one time doubted by Buffon, was at an after period ascertained and demonstrated by that brilliant historian of the brute creation, and has since been frequently confirmed in recent times. We shall here rest satisfied with a single citation: "Those naturalists," says <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Sabine, "who believe that no animal, in a perfectly natural and wild state, will connect itself with one of a different species, will consider the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> agitated question of the specific identity of the wolf and dog, as determined by a circumstance of frequent occurrence at Melville <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">Island</a>. In <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>, which are the months in which wolves are in season, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> paid almost daily visits to the neighbourhood of the ships, and remained till she was joined by a setter-dog belonging to one of the officers. They were usually together from two to three hours; and as they did not go far away, unless an endeavour was made to approach them, repeated <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> was obtained of the purpose for which they were thus associated." Now the only reasonable objection which, as it appears to us, remained to the experiments of Buffon and the younger Cuvier, was deducible from the fact of these having been made upon animals in confinement, and which were consequently existing under constrained and artificial circumstances. But here such objection ceases. We witness the voluntary cohabiting of two creatures brought up under entirely different circumstances,—the one with as much of wildness as the most forlorn region of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> could induce upon an originally <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> nature, the other so altered in its form and aspect by the immemorial subjection of itself and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> to the dominion of man, as to have lost almost all outward resemblance to the stock from whence it sprung; and yet, notwithstanding this disparity of manners, and the different conditions of the social state, they mutually recognise and acknowledge each other, and the immediate representative of the natural and unaltered species, "like the wild envoy of a barbarous clan," seeks and obtains the affection of the enslaved descendant. Unless all our established notions regarding the legitimate distinctions of species are essentially false, what more do we require to prove the identity of the animals in question? It is also of importance to bear in mind the existence of wild dogs of the domestic breed, which live in a fierce and emancipated state in the plains and forests of many different countries, because this fact demonstrates that no changes, either physical or artificial, on the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-EARTH_S">earth's</a> surface, whether produced by the agency of man or otherwise, can have extinguished the original source, when its descendants, after regaining their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, are thus found to breed and prosper in a state of nature. We insist the more upon this observation, because we think it cuts deeply at the base of a theory, or rather <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>, maintained by certain naturalists, who, unable in any way to disencumber the subject, give it the slip by asserting that we must now for ever seek in vain for the original type of our domestic races, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of its extinction, either by universal servitude, or actual extermination. Now, it would certainly be surprising if the original source of the plurality of our domestic dogs had ceased to exist in an independent state, when we see the wild species of so many of our other domestic animals still flourishing in their original positions, notwithstanding their more confined limits, the smaller <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of their young, and their comparatively defenceless nature. Those troops of wild (emancipated) dogs which we know to exist in the midst of European colonies, in spite of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> efforts to destroy them, prove that in the infancy and early progress of human society, a naturally wild species could neither be entirely subdued, nor utterly exterminated. Nor is there any evidence whatever from history, tradition, or the geological phenomena of nature, of the extinction of any wild animal of the dog kind; and, as <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers mention all the actual species of that tribe in the countries where they still exist, it may more reasonably be concluded that one or more of these wild species are the actual source of our various domestic breeds, than that the source itself has been extirpated. It is proper, while endeavouring to trace the origin of what Baron Cuvier has called "the completest, the most singular, and the most useful conquest ever made by man," more especially when we know how ancient that conquest must have been, to refer to the native species of the country usually regarded as the cradle of the human race. From the earliest periods of which we have any detailed records... <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the more minutely authenticated histories of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times, there has never been any indication given of the existence, in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR"><a class="</a>xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>, of more than four wild animals of the dog tribe, viz. the hyena, the wolf, the fox, and the jackal. The first of these species, we have already stated, is not now regarded by naturalists as pertaining to the canine race, and we have also referred to certain strongly marked distinctive peculiarities of the fox; so that we consider the wolf and jackal as alone entitled to our particular regard in relation to the present inquiry. We have already said enough to shew the strong claims of the wolf, so far as the northern races are concerned; but the multiplicity of size, form, and locality of our domestic dogs, seems to indicate a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> origin, and it cannot be denied that many of the southern dogs present so marked and peculiar a character, that their descent from the jackal is obvious. It is not our <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> to enter in this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> into anatomical details, but we may state generally, that an attentive <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> scarcely exhibits any sensible difference between the internal structure of the jackal and that of the shepherd's dog. This is the opinion espoused by Pallas and Guldenstaedt, the former of whom maintains that the dogs of the Kalmuks are in truth neither more nor less than jackals. This animal has always abounded in Asia Minor, where all the theologians of the west have placed the paradisiacal cradle of the human race, and where it must have been easily accessible to the first families of mankind. We willingly coincide in this view, with the reservations before mentioned regarding the great northern dogs, and those of the still remoter countries of the New World, where the jackal is unknown, but where its place is amply filled by gaunt and grizzly wolves. It is, indeed, by no means likely that the dogs mentioned by Pietro <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARTYR">Martyr</a> and Oviedo, as living with the inhabitants of the little Antilles and the Caribs of Terra Firma, were derived from species foreign to America; because the authors first named (both of whom were contemporaneous with and witnesses to the discovery and conquest of America) describe these dogs as being of various colours and kinds of coat, from which we may infer that they had been, even then, for a long period reduced to servitude. They were all <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MUTE">mute</a>; that is to say, they never barked; but that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> seems, in truth, to be neither natural nor innate, but rather acquired by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, as domestic dogs run wild have no other cry than a sharp or prolonged howl; and the silent species of barbarous nations, when introduced into civilized society, speedily acquire the bark of our domestic kinds. It may, moreover, be borne in mind, that there are at least two kinds of jackal,—the better known species, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> Jackal (Canis aureus, Linn.), and that from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SENEGAL">Senegal</a>, described by Frederick Cuvier under the name of Canis <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ANTHUS">anthus</a>. These animals, though regarded as specifically distinct, have bred together in the Garden of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLANTS">Plants</a>. This is a fact of considerable importance, as shewing the facility with which a mixed breed from the jackal might be procured; and as it was previously known that the wolf manifested the same instinctive inclination towards different varieties of the dog, we thus obtain a more extended knowledge of a feature in the character of the canine race, which throws considerable light upon our inquiries. When we see that both the wolf and jackal thus breed with other species, and that all our domesticated dogs breed with each other, although some are scarcely distinguishable from the wolf, while others seem identical with the jackal, we can scarcely doubt that all such domesticated varieties have in fact arisen primarily from these two animals,—the southern from the jackal, the northern from the wolf; and that the intermediate varieties have sprung from an intermixture of the jackal-dogs on the one hand, and of the wolf-dogs on the other, afterwards crossed and commingled in various conceivable ways, both by accident and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>. We confess that the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> variations are still surprising, if not unaccountable; such as the difference between a lofty limbed and almost gigantic stag-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HOUND">hound</a> of the ancient Irish breed, and the low-legged waddling turnspit, or terrier of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SKYE">Skye</a>; but that domestication for many thousand years, and the altered habits of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> which ensue from it, have been strongly influential in moulding the form and character of the canine race, is evident from this, that the dogs of all wild and secluded nations, whose domestic animals may be supposed to exist most nearly in a state of nature, are all more strongly allied either to the wolf or the jackal, than those that partake the fortunes of civilized men, who dwell in large cities, or in thickly peopled countries; and this approximation to the aspect of the wild animal in the one case, and departure from it in the other, is in truth the surest <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">index</a> to the primitive types which it is possible to obtain. Thus from two or three original sources or distinct kinds, have been derived about ten times the number of mixed races,—many of which, and chiefly those which <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> the most artificial or altered modes of life, have now lost all traces of resemblance to the stock from which they sprung. The length of the preceding observations will prevent our entering into any detailed account of the infinitely varied dogs of the domestic kind. The subject is, indeed, far too extensive for our present limits, for there is scarcely a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATION">nation</a> of the earth, savage or civilized, that does not benefit by their friendly assistance, or derive delight from their affectionate companionship. We doubt not that many tribes of mankind would cease to exist if their dogs were withdrawn from them, and we know of scarcely any which would not suffer severely from such deprivation. Their strength, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>, and courage,—their intelligence, perseverance, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a>,—their exquisite <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of smell,—their finely accommodating instincts, and, in many <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, their extreme beauty and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a>,—have deservedly rendered the canine tribe the objects of the most unfeigned wonder and admiration to all observers and narrators, whether of ancient or modern days, from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HIPPOCRATES">Hippocrates</a> to the Etrick Shepherd.¹ Having figured, as an illustration of the present genus, the Hare Indian, or Mackenzie River dog (Canis familiaris, var. lagopus of Richardson, see Plate V., <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> 4), we shall here conclude with a few <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> in explanation of its history and habits. This variety, as far as yet known, is cultivated only by the Hare Indians and other tribes that frequent the borders of the Great Bear Lake, and the banks of the Mackenzie River. It is too small to be used as a beast of burden, and is therefore employed solely in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHASE">chase</a>. It has a mild and demure countenance, a small head, slender muzzle, erect thickish ears, somewhat oblique eyes, rather slender legs, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> hairy feet, and a bushy tail. Though it is covered with long <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, intermingled at the roots with a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, it differs from the American foxes, and agrees with the wolves, in always having callous protuberances, even during winter, on the soles of the feet and at the roots of the toes. Its size is inferior to that of the prairie wolf, but rather greater than that of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-RED">red</a> fox of America. Its resemblance, however, to the former is so great, that, on comparing live specimens, Dr Richard- ¹ The reader who desires a knowledge, or at least a notion of domestic dogs of various kinds, will consult with advantage (in addition, of course, to the various sporting Animals of our own country), Mr Griffith's valuable English edition (with additions) of the Régne Animal—the Menageries (vol. i.) of the Library of Entertaining Knowledge—our <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-ESSAY">essay</a> "On the Origin and Natural History of Dogs" in the Quarterly Journal of Agriculture (4th and 6th Nos.)—and Captain Brown's Compendium entitled Anecdotes of Dogs. son could detect no decided difference in form (except the smallness of the cranium), nor in the fineness of the fur, nor even in the arrangement of the spots of colour. It bears, in fact, the same relation to the prairie wolf that the Esquimaux dog does to the great grey wolf of the northern parts of the New World, a fact which affords an interesting <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONFIRMATION">confirmation</a> of the general views contained in the preceding paragraphs. The Hare Indian dog is very playful and affectionate, and easily attached by kindness. It is, however, not very docile beyond the range of its immediate instincts, and has a great dislike to confinement. Its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, when injured or afraid, is that of a wolf; but when merely excited or surprised, it makes an attempt to bark, usually ending, however, in a kind of howl. For its size, it is extremely swift and strong. A young one purchased by Dr Richardson from the Hare Indians, became greatly attached to its master, and when not more than seven months old, ran by the side of his sledge upon the snow, for 900 miles, without fatigue. During this long journey, it often carried, of its own <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ACCORD">accord</a>, a glove in its mouth for a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MILE">mile</a> or two; but though gentle in its manners, it exhibited but a limited love of learning, and made no progress in fetching and carrying comparable to that of the Newfoundland dog, or many other kinds. It was at last unfortunately killed and eaten by an Indian on the banks of the Saskatchewan, who pretended that he mistook it for a fox,—a reason which, according to our European notions, would not so much have led to as deterred from such a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>. We shall now say a few words regarding wolves. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> wolf (Canis lupus, Linn.) is the fiercest and most carnivorous of the wild animals yet indigenous to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. It resembles a large lank-faced, ill-conditioned dog, with a straight tail, a coat of a greyish-fawn colour, and in the adult state, a blackish streak upon the anterior legs. It varies, however, considerably, both in size and colour, according to the nature of the different localities in which it occurs, being larger and fiercer in more northern and unpeopled countries,—feebler and of smaller size when surrounded by enemies, and living in a state of continual fear and precaution. He wanders about in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> during the morning and evening twilight in search of food, which in a sufficing <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> he seldom finds. Frogs, field-mice, and the putrid remains of larger animals, are not despised. The rutting season of the female is in January. She is then followed by numerous males, the strongest or boldest of which having driven away the others, becomes her <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a>, and seldom quits her till the young have completed their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>. When about to bring forth, she prepares her den in some sheltered and secluded spot, which she furnishes with leaves, dried grass, and a portion of wool or hair from her own body. The number of her litter varies from five or six to nine, and the young are born with their eyes closed. For several days the mother never quits them, she herself being carefully fed by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a>. She suckles for two months, but about the end of the fifth or sixth <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEEK">week</a> she disgorges half-digested food, and soon after accustoms them to kill and feed upon small animals which she has previously captured. It has been observed that, during this period, the young are never left alone, but are always guarded by one or other of the parents. In about two months they lead them from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COVERT">covert</a>, and initiate them in the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol12.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> of the chase. In November or December they begin to wander forth by themselves, but they usually remain more or less united in one family, till the parents are obliged to prepare for another brood. The wolf in a wild state is a cowardly though cruel animal. He has sometimes been observed so stupified by sudden fear as to be killed or secured alive without danger or difficulty. At the same time, when pressed by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a>, and assembled in troops during the winter season, they become formidable both to man and beast. We know from the ancient chroniclers, and from various legal enactments and feudal tenures, how greatly <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, especially <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, was infested by wolves during the days of our Saxon ancestors; and that in the reign of Athelstan it was found necessary to erect a kind of retreat at a place called Flixton, for the protection of passing travellers. Wolves, however, appear to have become almost extinct in England as far back as the termination of the thirteenth century, at least we do not find them recorded as a nuisance after the year 1281. "It is none of the least blessings," observes Hollinshed, "wherewith God hath indited this island, that it is void of noisome beasts, as lions, bears, tigers, pards, wolfs, and such like, by means whereof our countrymen may traffyle in safetie, and our herds and flocks remain for the most part abroad in the field without any herdsman or keeper. This is chiefly spoken of the south and south-west parts of the island." For whereas we that dwell on this side of the Tweed, may safetie boast of our securitie in this behalfe: yet cannot the Scots do the like in everie point within their kingdome, sith they have grievous wolfs and cruel foxes, besides some other of like disposition continuallie conversant among them, to the general hindrance of their husbandmen, and no small damage unto the inhabitants of those <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>." According to the same authority, the extirpation of wolves from England was imposed as a tribute by <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KING">king</a> Edgar upon the conquered Welsh. Ludwal, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>, paid yearly a tribute of 300 wolves, so that in four years none were left. The last seen in Scotland was killed by Sir Ewen Cameron in the year 1680. In <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> the species was not totally extirpated till about thirty years after that period. In a state of domestication the wolf can be regarded as nothing more than a dog of a somewhat anomalous and unusual aspect. M. F. Cuvier has more than once rendered them so tame and docile, that but for their unextinguishable love of live <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a>, they might have been allowed to wander where they chose. They associated freely and fondly with common dogs, and speedily acquired from them the habit of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BARKING">barking</a>. In general, however, and when left free to manifest their natural instinct, dogs exhibit a great aversion to wolves; and the latter, according to Hearne, frequently slay and devour the train dogs of the Esquimaux. Captain Lyon, who describes the wolves of Melville <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENINSULA">Peninsula</a> as comparatively fearless, states, that one afternoon a fine dog having strayed a short way <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AHEAD">ahead</a> of its master, five wolves made a sudden and unexpected rush upon it, and devoured it in so incredibly short a time, that before the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> who witnessed the attack could reach the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, the dog had totally disappeared with the exception of the lower part of one leg. In those forlorn regions they frequently came alongside the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FROST">frost</a>-bound ship, and one night broke into a snow-hut, and carried away a brace of Esquimaux dogs, which appeared to have made a vigorous though unavailing resistance, the ceiling being all besprinkled with blood and hair. So strong, as well as ferocious are these blood-thirsty creatures, in spite of what one might suppose the subduing influence of intense <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, that when the alarm was given, and an armed party proceeded to attempt a rescue, one of the wolves above alluded to was observed, when fired at, to take up a dead dog in his mouth, and to set off with it at an easy canter, although the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of the victim was supposed to be equal to his own. These and similar facts, apparently of a na- --- 1 For an excellent account of this, as well as of the other dogs of North America, see Fauna Boreali-Americana, part i. p. 79. 2 Chronicles, vol. i. p. 378 3 Private Journal, pp. 151, 339, &c. ture contradictory to the theory of an identity of species which we have previously propounded, is, in truth, in proper accordance with what we know takes place among many other animals, when wild and tame individuals chance to encounter. A strongly marked jealousy, if not positive enmity, seems to exist between the unsubdued members of the same species and such as have passed beneath the yoke. It may be supposed to result, not unnaturally, from that perception of "similitude in dissimilitude" which, according to circumstances, leads alike to the extremes of love or hatred. We have already alluded to the strong instinctive affection which in due season has been seen to exist between them, and we certainly do not conceive that, from a few chance murders rendered almost imperative by the pressure of the times, an argument of any value can be deduced against the natural identity of the wolf and dog. The black wolf of Europe (Canis lycaon, Linn. le loup noir, Buff.) differs very slightly from the common brown species except in colour. Its ferocity, however, is said to be greater. It occurs accidentally in France,—more frequently in Spain and the Pyrenean range. There were two of these black wolves some years ago in the menagerie of the King's Garden in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, which every season brought forth young as fierce and mistrustful as themselves, but not like their parents in their colour and external markings. From this circumstance we would hesitate to regard the black wolf as more than an accidental variety. Indeed it has been regarded by some as a mixed race, originally sprung from the common wolf and a black dog run wild among the woods or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. The American Indians do not regard the black wolves as distinct from the others, although they abound on the banks of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MISSOURI">Missouri</a>, and they report that one or more of that colour are occasionally found in the litter of the common kind. In regard to the wolves of the New World in general, naturalists do not quite accord in their enumeration of the species. A brown wolf, described as possessing all the characters of the European kind, is said to exist within the limits of the United States; but the more northern American species, though they may possibly approximate those of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a> and of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAPLAND">Lapland</a>, certainly differ greatly in their general physiognomy from the natives of France and the Pyrenees. They are of a more robust and larger form, their hair is longer, finer, and more woolly, their muzzle thicker and blunter, their head larger and rounder, with a sensible <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEPRESSION">depression</a> at the union of the nose and forehead. Except in their superior size and strength, the North American wolves so greatly resembled the sledge dogs of the natives, that our arctic travellers more than once mistook a band of these predaceous animals for the domestic troop of an Indian party. The howl of each is precisely the same. When the deep and long enduring snows of winter have entombed the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACE">face</a> of nature in their silent shroud, these creatures often suffer dreadfully from famine, and were they not for the most part as fearful as rapacious, they would assuredly prove most unpleasant neighbours. But the simple expedient of tying an inflated bladder to a branch, so as to admit of its waving in the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, is sufficient to keep a whole herd at a distance. At times, however, they become more venturous; and at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUSE">House</a>, in 1820, a wolf which had been seen prowling around the fort, and was <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> at and severely wounded by a musket-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BALL">ball</a>, returned again in the dark, streaming with blood, and carried off a dog among fifty others,—the latter howling piteously, but unable to summon courage to attack the gigantic intruder. Sir J. Richardson was even told of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> Carnivora. Indian woman having been strangled by a wolf, while her husband, who <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the onset of the animal, was hastening to her assistance; but their destruction of human life is most extremely rare.
