Illiger. Incisives 6 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> 4, canines 1—1, molars 6—6; = 40 or 38. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of this genus resemble hedgehogs in the prickles which are intermingled with their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, but their <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> are very different. They are nocturnal animals, and inhabitants of the torrid zone (occurring in Madagascar and the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of France), and are said to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> several months of the year in a lethargic state. This is a singular circumstance in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of any intertropical species; and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TERM">term</a> hibernation, usually bestowed upon the torpid condition (in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of its constant connection with the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLD">cold</a> of winter), cannot be used in the present instance, be- --- 1 The student who finds a discrepancy in our statement of the above dentition (or in that of other insectivorous groups), when compared with the descriptions of other authors, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> bear in mind that this arises chiefly from a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in nomenclature. In the present instance we follow M. Desmarest. Baron Cuvier seems to think that in Condylura there are only two <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of incisive teeth in the upper jaw; what we have considered as the third pair, being regarded by him as the canines. We presume the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of their insertion in relation to the maxillary bone would determine the point; but we have ourselves no access to a cranium of any species of the genus. 2 Bartram and other writers who have asserted the existence of moles in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, are supposed by later writers to have mistaken the shrew-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOLE">mole</a> (sceloporus). Sir J. Richardson, however, informs us that there are several true moles in the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MUSEUM">Museum</a> of the Zoological <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, which were brought from America. They differ from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> European species in being smaller in size, with a thicker and shorter snout. The fur is brownish-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">black</a>. Dr Harlan supposes the mole of the United States <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a> with T. europae of Linn. It was named T. americana in Dr Bartram's MS. 3 Memorie Scientifiche, decima prima. Consult also C. L. Bonaparte's Iconografia della Fauna <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ITALICA">Italica</a>. cause, according to the relation of Bruguiere, it most frequently occurs during the greatest heats. About three species of the genus are known to naturalists. As an example, we have figured the radiated Tanree (Centene semi-spinosus), which is no larger than a mole (See Plate III., <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> 10.) The tanrees are known to Europeans under the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of pig-porcupines. They utter a grunting cry, are generally very fat, and are used as food by the natives of Madagascar. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIVISION">DIVISION</a> III.—CARNIVORA. The genera of this division are characterized by possessing six incisors in each jaw. Their molars are usually of a trenchant or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> character, sometimes tuberculous, but never beset with the jagged <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POINTS">points</a> which we so often meet with in the preceding division. Their canines are extremely strong. Although the epithet carnivorous, as Baron Cuvier has remarked, applies, in a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, to all ungulate <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a> which possess the three different kinds of teeth, since the whole are more or less dependent on animal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> for their support, yet it is among the various groups of our present division that we meet with the really sanguinary kinds. They are more or less exclusively carnivorous, according as their teeth are more or less of a cutting character, and their regimen might almost be calculated from the relative proportion between the tubercular and the cutting surface of their grinders. The bear tribe, which is the best adapted (of carnivorous creatures) for subsisting on a vegetable diet, has almost all the teeth tubercular. Hence the accordance of its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOVE">love</a> for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> and berries. The anterior molars of this division are usually the sharpest on their edges; then follows a molar larger than the others, and usually furnished with a tubercular heel. Behind that molar we find one or two small teeth nearly flat upon the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. It is with these latter that dogs chew the grass which they so frequently swallow. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> molar <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUST">just</a> alluded to, and the corresponding tooth of the upper jaw, are what we designate as the carnivorous cheek-teeth (les carnassiers of F. Cuvier); the anterior pointed ones are the false molars, and the flattened <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POSTERIOR">posterior</a> ones, the tubercular grinders. The amount of these teeth differs slightly in some of the genera. Thus, for example, in the feline <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RACE">race</a>, or cats, there is no separate tubercular tooth in the lower jaw; but its <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FUNCTION">function</a> is performed by the inner projecting lobe of the under carnivorous cheek-tooth, the rounded point of which, when the jaws are closed, is applied to the flat surface of the upper tubercular grinder. It will be readily conceived that such species as possess the fewest false molars, and the shortest jaws, have the greatest power in biting, and are likely to prove the most carnivorous. We subdivide the Carnivora, in the first place, into three <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> tribes, in accordance chiefly with certain distinctive peculiarities in the form of the hinder feet. These tribes are named Plantigrada, Digitigrada, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PIN">Pin</a>-nipedia. Tribe I.—Plantigrada. Entire sole of the foot placed upon the ground in walking. Five toes to both the fore and hind extremities. No circum. Genus <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-URSUS">Ursus</a>. Linn. Incisors 6; canine 1—1; molar 6—6; = 42. Tail short. Of the six molars on each side of the upper jaw of this genus there are three which we would denominate false molars; another corresponds to the carnivorous cheek-tooth, and the remaining two are tuberculated grinders. In the under jaw there is generally an additional molar on each side. It must be remembered, however, that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of teeth in the bears is very variable even in the same species, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of the individual. The false molars especially vary greatly,—for in young animals they have not become apparent,—in aged ones they have disappeared. Among carnivorous quadrupeds, as we have already hinted, we find many different degrees of ferocity, from the all-subduing and blood-thirsty disposition of the tiger, which so savagely rejoices to imbue its horrid jaws in the palpitating <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of a living victim, to the more omnivorous propensities of the Plantigrada, such as the bear, raccoon, or coati-mundi,—species which, though addicted to prey on other animals, are at the same <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> endowed with a much greater capacity to adapt their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> to a miscellaneous diet. This accommodating <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INSTINCT">instinct</a> no doubt corresponds with, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it does not proceed from, the less determinate formation of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIGESTIVE">digestive</a> and prehensile organs; such as the stomach, teeth, and claws. The unequalled strength and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> of the tiger,—its sharp retractile talons, the great development of the canine teeth, and the compressed and cutting character of the molars, combined with the simplicity of the stomach, and the shortness of the intestinal canal, render it, as it were, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TYPE">type</a> of carnivorous animals. It exhibits no tendency in any of its forms to the herbivorous structure, but is strictly and characteristically a flesh-eating animal, “a most beautiful and cruel beast of prey.” It is otherwise with our present genus containing the race of bears. Their <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> forms are massy and inactive, their claws are unretractile, their muzzles more elongated, their jaws consequently weaker, and their teeth, though sufficiently formidable, manifest a decided relation to the herbivorous structure in the breadth of the molars, and their bluntly tuberculated crowns. In accordance with these conditions of their organization, we find that even the polar bear (Ursus maritimus), one of the most carnivorous of its kind, may be sustained for a length of time in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>, on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> alone. It is known that several species, in the wild state, are remarkably fond of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONEY">honey</a> (a substance which, though in one <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> an animal secretion, is, in another and more essential one, a vegetable product), and have been observed climbing trees to obtain it. Others feed on fruits, reptiles, insects, particularly ants; and Sir <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STAMFORD">Stamford</a> Raffles possessed a tame Malay bear (U. Malayanus), which gave <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of its refined appetite, by refusing to eat any thing but mango-stews, or to drink any other wine than champagne.¹ Here, then, as among every other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GROUP">group</a> which can occupy the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of the naturalist, we find the most beautiful and harmonious uniformity to prevail between the special end in view, and the means of its attainment. Of all carnivorous animals, bears are the least qualified either to pursue in open warfare, or to secure by ambuscade, a living prey. Their plantigrade position renders their movements comparatively slow, and the nearly equal length of their fore and hind legs deprives them of the power of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAPING">leaping</a>. Had, therefore, their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> love of flesh and blood been as insatiable as that of the tiger, and their means of obtaining it so much more restricted, their lives must have passed in misery, and the species would ere <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> have become extinct.² But He who “tempers the <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> to the shorn lamb,” has drawn strength from this very weakness, and ordained that, with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DETERIORATION">deterioration</a> of those <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> which are essential to the well-being of a strictly carniv- ¹ Linn. Trans. vol. xii. ² Wilson’s Illustrations of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, vol. i. Genus Ursus. rous animal, should arise a capacity of deriving nourishment from a wider and more miscellaneous range of materials—and thus the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a> is beautifully maintained between the instinctive propensity and the subduing power. The geographical distribution of the genus Ursus, though formerly believed to be confined to northern countries, is now known to be very extensive. We are acquainted with eight or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> species, several of which occur in the warmer regions of Continental <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">Islands</a>. We cannot here, however, afford room for more than the briefest summary. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-WHITE">white</a> or polar bear (U. maritimus), which does not occur among the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ANTARCTIC">antarctic</a> icebergs, is common to the northern shores of Asia and America. This gigantic prowler among <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FROST">frost</a>-bound regions, attains to a higher latitude than any other known quadruped, and seems indeed to dwell by preference "In thrilling regions of thick-ribbed <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-ICE">ice</a>." Its southern limit seems to be somewhere about the 55th <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a>. It is a truly ice-haunting and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> species, occurring along a vast <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of shore, but never entering into wooded countries, except by inadvertence, or during the prevalence of great mists, nor shewing itself, unless accidentally, at any considerable distance from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. It might naturally be supposed, that animals of almost gigantic size, of great strength, and considerable ferocity, would be too formidable and dangerous to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> race, to remain long unknown in any of their distinguishing characteristics. Yet the specific differences, it must be admitted, of the black and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> bears, both of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> and America, are still insufficiently illustrated. Both continents produce a black bear and a brown one; the white or polar species, just mentioned, is common to the northern latitudes of each, while America alone is inhabited by the grizzly bear, Ursus ferox. This is undoubtedly the most formidable animal of the northern parts of the New World. When full grown it equals in size the great polar species, and is not only of more <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> habits, but of a fiercer and more vindictive disposition. Its strength is so enormous, that it will drag away the carcass of a buffalo weighing a thousand pounds. Dr Richardson informs us, that a party of voyagers, who had been occupied all <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> in tracking a canoe up the Saskatchewan, were seated around a fire enjoying the repose of the evening twilight, and partly occupied in the agreeable task of preparing their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a>. Suddenly a huge grizzly bear sprung over the canoe, which they had tilted behind them, and seizing one of the party by the shoulder, carried him off. The remainder were scattered in terror, with the sole exception of a metif named Bourraso, who, grasping his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-GUN">gun</a>, followed the bear, whom he <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SAW">saw</a> deliberately retreating with his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> in his mouth. He called out to his unfortunate comrade that he was afraid to fire lest he should <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HIT">hit</a> him instead of the bear, but he was answered to fire instantly, as the monster was squeezing him to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. On this he took steady aim, and lodged his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BALL">ball</a> in the body of the brute, which immediately dropped its original prey, and turned round to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> itself upon the brave Bourraso. He, however, contrived to effect his escape, and the bear, probably feeling itself severely wounded, disappeared into a neighbouring thicket. The rescued <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a> eventually recovered, although one of his arms was fractured, and he was otherwise severely bitten. Another individual, still living in the neighbourhood of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EDMONTON">Edmonton</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUSE">House</a>, was attacked by a bear of this species, which suddenly sprung out of a thicket, and scalped him by a single scratch of its tremendous claws, laying bare the skull, and pulling <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the skin of the forehead quite over the eyes. Assistance being at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, he was rescued from the bear without farther injury, but he was left in a painful and unfortunate predicament, for the scalp not being properly replaced in time, he lost the power of vision (although his eyes remained uninjured), owing to the hardening of that skinny and tenacious vein. The grizzly bear inhabits the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROCKY_MOUNTAINS">Rocky <a class=</a>"xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">Mountains</a>, and their eastern plains, at least as far <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> as latitude 61°, and its southern range, according to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">Lieutenant</a> Pike, extends to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>. Another and much smaller species of the New World is the black bear of North America (U. Americanus, see Plate IV., figure 3). It is esteemed as food. The only South American species with which we are acquainted, is the Ursus orasatus of Frederick Cuvier (Ibid. figs. 4 and 4 a). It is black, with the throat and muzzle white, and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> fulvous spot upon the brows. The European bears are generally supposed to be two in number, the brown or common bear (U. arctos, Linn.), and the black bear (U. <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NIGER">niger</a>). The latter, however, is by some considered only as a variety. There are at least three bears in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>. The long-lipped bear (U. labiatus) is met with occasionally in menageries in this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, under the name of Ursine Sloth (first bestowed upon an individual accidentally deficient in the canine teeth). It dwells in holes and caverns, which it sometimes excavates with its long claws, and feeds on fruit, insects, and honey. It is rather a docile and intelligent animal, and is taught various tricks by the jugglers of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>, who frequently exhibit it for the amusement of the people. The Malay bear (U. Malayanus, Raffles), before alluded to, occurs likewise in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMATRA">Sumatra</a>, where it is said to cause great damage by climbing to the summit of the cocoa trees to drink the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MILK">milk</a>, after devouring the tops of the plant. A third Indian species is the bear of Thibet (U. Tibetanus, Cuv.), a species intermediate between the two preceding, but more ferocious than either. Its claws are weaker than usual, and some suppose that it cannot climb trees. It was found by Dr Wallich among the mountains of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NEPAUL">Nepaul</a>, and by M. A. Duvauzel in those of Silhet. We may conclude by observing, that bears have never been found in any <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times, although those of Lybia are mentioned by <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> and other <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>: | Acetes | |--------| | Herridus in jaculis et pelle Libyidis urse. |

The only <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> distinctly ascertained to belong to our present genus, is the *C. capensis* (*Talpa asiatica*, Gmelin), <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOLE">Mole</a>, an animal somewhat less than the mole of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, of a brownish <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, but remarkable for exhibiting (especially when moistened) beautiful metallic reflections of a green and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> colour. This burnished aspect is extremely rare among the mammiferous tribes. The species in question inhabits the Cape of Good Hope (not <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>, as erroneously indicated by Scha), where it is found to be troublesome in gardens. It is subterranean and insectivorous, and differs from the true talpe in having only three claws to the fore-feet. Its eyes are almost obsolete. This animal was <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> ashore near Brodie-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUSE">House</a>, Elginshire. Its ordinary habitat and habits are wholly unknown. *D. Desmarestii*, Risso. Less. Fr. Cuv. Upper jaw short and without teeth, lower much longer, convex, and having near its extremity two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> conical teeth, three inches long, one <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; eye small; pectorals short; dorsal fin over the vent; tall large and festooned; upper portion of the body of the colour of polished <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-STEEL">steel</a>, with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of white streaks arranged without regularity; belly white; inside of the mouth bluish-black. Risso's specimen was fifteen feet long. According to the naturalist of Nice, who alone has described and drawn this animal, it affects the deep waters of the Mediterranean, and comes towards the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> in the months of May and September. It very much resembles the preceding.

False teeth in the upper jaw, and, allowing these have no existence, still the name has been affixed by Cuvier to a genus which undoubtedly exists, and which possesses marked peculiarities in the prominence of the forehead, and the shortness and flatness of the beak, produced by the maxillary crest.
