Vertebrae 7, 9, 26, in all 42 (<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a>); ribs 9 <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a>. Two strong teeth at the extremity of the lower jaw. This genus was admitted upon the authority of M. Bausard, an officer of marine, who examined two individuals, mother and cub, which were stranded near <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONFLEUR">Honfleur</a>, and who, with landable zeal, published an account of them in the year 1789. The circumstance on which rested the claim of these specimens to be considered generic was the total want of teeth in either jaw, and their having the upper jaw and palate furnished with small unequal and hard <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, which were about half an inch long in the cub, and somewhat larger in the mother. Bausard's memoir appeared two years later than Mr Hunter's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of his *B. bidentatus*, which was admitted as distinct by Bonnaterre, Lacépède, &c. Hunter says nothing of false teeth in the palate, and mentions that two strong and robust teeth existed at the extremity of the lower jaw. These, then, were long regarded as two <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. Bonnaterre, in describing Bausard's specimens, very unaccountably assigned to them two teeth in the lower jaw, and thus very naturally misled Lacépède, Illiger, and for a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> even Baron Cuvier. It was probably when holding this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that Cuvier, in visiting Mr Hunter's <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a>, and examining the head of his *Bidentatus*, came to the conclusion that Bausard's and Hunter's specimens were one and the same species, belonging, however, to a genus distinct from all others. He attached the title of *Hyperoodon* to both.

GENUS LUTRA

Pages 171-171

Ray. Mustela, Linn.** | Incisives | Canines | Molars | |-----------|---------|--------| | 6 | 1—1 | 5—5 | Head flat. Body <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> and low. Tail strong and depressed at the base. We here <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> those amphibious fish-eating animals <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called otters, of which there are many <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. The character and aspect of our European kind (Lutra vulgaris, Erxleben, Mustela lutra, Linn.) are well known. It occurs over all <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> and a considerable portion of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>. It is a fierce creature, tenacious of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and very injurious to fresh-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FISHERIES">fisheries</a>, from its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of preying very exclusively on the upper parts only of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TROUT">trout</a> and salmon, leaving a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> portion of the caudal extremity unconsumed. What can be the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of its objection to this despised portion? In Scotland we find the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OTTER">otter</a> frequently inhabiting the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-shore as well as the interior, and seeking its food both in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALT">salt</a> and fresh water. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> brings forth her young, usually four <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> five in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, during <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>. The fur is valuable, and forms an article of export from our northern isles. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CANADA">Canada</a> otter (L. Canadensis, Sabine), resembles the European species, both in food and habits, but it is a much larger animal, with a shorter tail, and is distinguished by the fur of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a> being of the same shining <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> as that of the back. It is found across the whole of the northern parts of North <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, where, during the winter season, it haunts the falls and rapids for the sake of open water, and when these are frozen over in one district, it <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> travel a long way in search of others, which may have resisted the power of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FROST">frost</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> pursued by the hunters during these peregrinations, it will throw itself forward on its belly, and slide through the snow for several yards, leaving behind it a deep furrow, and repeating this peculiar movement with such rapidity, that the swiftest runner on snow-shoes with difficulty overtakes it. It also doubles on its track very cunningly, dives occasionally beneath the snow, and at last, when too closely pressed to render flight available, it will turn and defend itself with courageous obstinacy. During the spring season, on the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Bear Lake, this species frequently robbed the nets of Sir John Franklin's first expedition, usually carrying off the heads of the fish, and leaving the bodies sticking in the meshes. It brings forth, in April, from one to three at a birth. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">Seven</a> or eight thousand skins are annually imported into England. Another well known American species is the sea otter (Lutra marina, Steller), which Dr Fleming, on the supposition that it possesses only four incisives in the lower jaw, desires to constitute a separate genus called Enhydra. It is mentioned, however, in the narrative of Cook's (third) voyage, that a young sea otter had six of these <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> as usual in the lower jaw, and it may therefore be inferred that two drop out before the attainment of the adult state. The species inhabits the northern parts of the Pacific from <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KAMTSCHATKA">Kamtschatka</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-YELLOW_SEA"><a class="</a>xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-YELLOW">Yellow</a> Sea on the Asiatic shores, and from Alaska to <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CALIFORNIA">California</a> on those of America. It seems to have more of the manners of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> than of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a> otter, and is sometimes met with out at sea, at a vast distance from the shore; Pennant says even as far as a hundred leagues. The fur is very handsome, and was much esteemed by the Chinese, who gave extraordinary prices for it in former days. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CANTON">Canton</a> market, however, has long been overstocked, and the influx has of course reduced the value. It varies in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> and condition of the animal, and the season of the year. Those obtained in winter are of a finer <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, and otherwise more perfect than at any other <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, and, according to Meares, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> is much more beautiful than the female. Those in highest estimation have the belly and throat interspersed with brilliant silver hairs, while the other parts consist of a thick black coat, with a silky gloss of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> fineness. Besides these northern otters we have a Brazilian species, and one (supposed to be distinct) from Carolina, while several Asiatic kinds have been described by Sir <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STAMFORD">Stamford</a> Raffles, Dr Horsfield, and MM. Diard and Leschenault. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> otter (Lutra inunguis, F. Cuv.), is alleged to be destitute of claws, and on the supposition of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a> character, has been formed into a separate genus called Aonyx by M. Lesson. He bestows on the sole species the name of Delalandii, as it was first brought from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the Hottentots, by the French naturalist of that name. It <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> about three feet in length exclusive of the tail, which is ten inches. The fur is soft and thick, of a chestnut-brown colour, paler on the flanks, with a mixture of grey about the head. It inhabits the salt pools along the marine shores of the Cape, and preys on fish and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRUSTACEA">crustacea</a>. **2D SUBDIVISION.** Two tuberculous teeth behind the carnivorous cheek tooth of the upper jaw. Body proportionally shorter than in the preceding subdivision, and the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a> longer. Our present <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GROUP">group</a> is mainly constituted by the genera <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CANIS">Canis</a> and Viverra of Linnaeus, including the dogs, wolves, and foxes, the civets and ichneumons, besides a few <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> genera of recent introduction.

GENUS MELES

Pages 167-170

STORR.** | Incisors | Canine | |----------|--------| | 6 | 1—1 | Molars | 5—5 | |------| Tail very short. Two pectoral and four ventral mammae. An anal pouch. Here naturalists <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the badgers, a small genus, widely distributed over <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and occurring both in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. At the same <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> we have no precise knowledge of more than two <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. Our <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> badger (*Meles vulgaris*, *<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-URSUS">Ursus</a> metér*, Linn.) is greyish-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> above, beneath <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, with a longitudinal black band on each side of the head, passing round the eye and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a>. The tuberculous molars at the bottom of each jaw, especially those of the upper, are distinguished by their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, of which the effect is to limit that of the carnivorous <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, and consequently to diminish the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> appetite for <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a>, at all events, the power of exercising it. The tuberculous molar of the upper jaw, occupies a space equal to that of the carnivorous cheek tooth, and of the two false molars, by which it is preceded, and the lower half of the under carnivorous tooth is enlarged, so as to be properly opposed to the larger tuberculous tooth above. It is thus half tuberculous and half carnivorous. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> incisives of each side of the lower jaw are not inserted on the same line as the others, but farther in. Although the badger is undoubtedly a carnivorous animal, it is much less so than many others of the ferine order, and even in a state of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> feeds freely on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> and roots. We have known it enter a garden to devour strawberries. When domesticated it is omnivorous, like the cat and dog. Its subterranean <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and woodland habits, are well known. The American badger (*Meles Labradoria* of Richardson and others), or *cervus* of Buffon, is of a mottled or hoary grey <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> above, whitish on the under surface. The fur is very soft and fine. This species inhabits the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> plains or prairies which skirt the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROCKY_MOUNTAINS">Rocky <a class=</a>"xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">Mountains</a> as far <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a> as the banks of the Peace River. It abounds in the plains of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MISSOURI">Missouri</a>, although its southern range has not been hitherto defined. The holes which it perforates in the prairies, in the vicinity of Carlton-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, are often annoying to horsemen, especially when the ground is covered with snow. The greater <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of these burrows, however, are not dug by the badger itself, but are merely enlargements of the subterranean dwellings of marmots (*Arctomys Hoodii* and *Richardsonii*), which it at the same time most ungenerously digs up and devours. It appears indeed to be fully more carnivorous than the European species,—a specimen which Sir J. Richardson killed, having had a small marmot nearly entire, and several field mice, in its interior. But it had also been feeding on some vegetable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. It passes the winter, from November to April, in a torpid state. Although the badgers approach the marten tribe in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of their dentition, they are far from resembling those finely formed, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, and lively creatures in other particulars; their bodies, though strong and muscular, being rather heavily formed, and their movements by no means <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>. Their physiognomy, it has been observed, announces neither quickness of intelligence, nor vivacity of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>. They <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> a retired, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not a solitary life. Badgers, though frequently mentioned by Latin writers under the names of *taxus* and *meles*, seem to have passed unnoticed by the Greeks. Yet we know that the European species occurs in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a>. --- 1 See *Lion. Trans.* vol. xv. p. 161. 2 The species have even been commingled by several recent systematic writers with the genus *Perodurus*. 3 *Annales des Sciences Nat.*, t. iv. 4 *Fauna Boreali-Americana*, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">Part</a> i. p. 39. The Glutton of the north of Europe (Gulo arcticus, Ursus gulo, Linn.) may be mentioned as an example of our present genus. It is common in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>, especially in the neighbourhood of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DRONTHEIM">Drontheim</a>, and is remarkable for its fierceness and voracity. It is said to climb trees, that it may the more readily pounce upon deer and other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> animals which it could not otherwise obtain. It fastens on their necks with teeth and claws, till its astounded prey rolls upon the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> from loss of blood, or terror at such an unexpected and insidious foe. In a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> state it has been known to eat thirteen pounds of flesh in a single <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. It is not larger than a badger. The glutton does not become torpid in the winter season. The Wolverine of North America (Gulo luscus, Sabine), though regarded by Baron Cuvier as nothing more than a variety of the preceding, is by others considered as a well distinguished species. Its habits are characteristically described by Sir J. Richardson: "The Wolverine is a carnivorous animal, which feeds chiefly upon the carcasses of beasts that have been killed by accident. It has <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> strength, and annoys the natives by destroying their hoards of provision, and demolishing their marten traps. It is so suspicious, that it <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> rarely enter a trap itself, but, beginning behind, pulls it to pieces, scatters the logs of which it is built, and then carries off the bait. It feeds also on <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MEADOW">meadow</a>-mice, marmots, and other rodentia, and occasionally on disabled <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a> of a larger size. I have seen one chasing an American hare, which was at the same time harassed by a snowy owl. It resembles the bear in its gait, and is not fleet; but it is very industrious, and no doubt feeds well, as it is generally fat. It is much abroad in the winter, and the track of its journey in a single night may be often traced for many miles. From the shortness of its legs, its makes its way through loose snow with difficulty, but when it falls upon the beaten track of a marten trapper, it will pursue it for a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> way. Mr Graham observes, 'that the Wolverines are extremely mischievous, and do more damage to the small fur trade, than all the other rapacious animals conjointly.' They will follow the marten hunter's path round a line of traps extending forty, fifty, or sixty miles, and render the whole unseervicable, merely to come at the baits, which are generally the head of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARTRIDGE">partridge</a>, or a bit of dried venison. They are not fond of the martens themselves, but never fail of tearing them in pieces, or of burying them in the snow by the side of the path, at a considerable distance from the trap. Drifts of snow often conceal the repositories thus made of the martens from the hunter, in which <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CASE">case</a> they furnish a regale to the hungry fox, whose sagacious nostril guides him unerringly to the spot. Two or three foxes are often seen following a wolverine for this purpose."1 The wolverine is said to be a great destroyer of beavers, but it must be only in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, when those industrious animals are at <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a>, that it can surprise them. An attempt to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BREAK">break</a> open their house in the winter, even supposing it possible for the claws of a wolverine to penetrate the thick mud walls when frozen as hard as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, would only have the effect of driving the beavers into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a> to seek for shelter in their vaults on the borders of the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DAM">dam</a>.2 Next to the polar bear, the wolverine is one of the most northern of known quadrupeds. Its <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-BONES">bones</a> were found in Melville <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">Island</a>, nearly in latitude 75°. A third species of this genus is the Grison, or banded glutton (G. vittatus), an inhabitant of a warmer clime. It is very common in Paraguay. A fourth is the Taira (G. barbatius.—Mustela barbatius, Linn.), described by Azara Carnivora, under the name of le <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> furet. It is likewise a native of South America. The Ratel, or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CAPE">cape</a> glutton (G. mellivorus.—Viverra mellivora and capensis, Gmelin), differs from the preceding in having one false molar less in each jaw, and in the upper tubercular teeth being slightly developed, as in cats; but in its <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> aspect it resembles the grison and badger. It is described by Sparmann as being about the size of the latter,—the fur greyish above, and black below, with an intermediate line of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-WHITE">white</a>. It inhabits the Cape of Good Hope, where, with its long claws, it disinters the nests of wild bees, and feeds upon their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>. Though long regarded as exclusively of African origin, it now appears, on the testimony of General Hardwick, to occur in several parts of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, along the courses of the Ganges and the Jumna. Its manners, however, do not at all correspond with those assigned to the African variety. It inhabits the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> banks of the great <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, and seldom issues abroad during the day. At night it prowls about the Mahomedan habitations, and will sometimes even scratch up recently interred <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> bodies, unless the graves be protected by a covering of thorny <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>. So rapid indeed are its subterranean operations, that it will work its way beneath the surface in the course of ten minutes. Its favourite food consists of birds and small quadrupeds. There is a specimen of this animal in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a> Zoological Gardens, remarkable for its playfulness and good humour. It solicits <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> by a great variety of postures, and tumbles head over heels as soon as it has succeeded in attracting the notice of a visitor.3 Tribe II.—Digitigrada. The groups of this tribe derive their name from their peculiar <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of locomotion. The heel does not touch the ground, and the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACT">act</a> of walking is performed, as it were, upon the toes. We may name as familiar examples the pole-cats, martens, dogs, hyenas, and the whole of the feline <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RACE">race</a>. Like most of our attempts, however, at a general arrangement, founded on any single <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a>, we find this principle imperfect, or at least admitting of exceptions in relation to the character prescribed, in as far as several species might be added, which truly agree with their digitigrade congeners in their prevailing character, but approach the plantigrades in their mode of locomotion. The genuine Digitigrades, however, such as cats, are among the most agile of their tribe, and as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> is an almost indispensable adjunct in the habits of a carnivorous creature, we find that these light-footed kinds are also the most exclusively flesh-eating of all the feline order. Indeed all the genera of our present tribe may be said to be more strictly carnivorous than those of the preceding. 1st Subdivision. A single tuberculous tooth behind the carnivorous cheek-tooth of the upper jaw. Body much elongated. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LIMBS">Limbs</a> short. This subdivision corresponds to the old genus Mustella of Linnaeus, and includes all those small and slender bodied animals which, in our own <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, are usually designated as <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VERMIN">vermin</a>, such as weasels, polecats, &c., the Verminium genus of Ray. They are very blood-thirsty, and extremely destructive for their size, destroying great quantities of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAME">game</a>, both in woods, fields, and moorish mountains, and... committing ravages in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a>-yards, and other enclosures, Carnivora, especially of remote country dwellings. They are wary, nocturnal, and insidious, and, from their worm-like form, can penetrate minute openings—thus gaining access to places where their presence was little expected, and less desired. The general dentition may be stated as: incisives \(6\), canines \(1-1\), molars \(4-4\) or \(5-5\); \(=34\) or \(38\). We shall now proceed to give a short sketch of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> genera (increased in number though restricted in extent), into which the musteline <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GROUP">group</a> of Linnaeus has been subdivided in recent times. The polecats (subgenus *Putorius*, Cuv.) are among the most sanguinary. Their lower carnivorous cheek-tooth has no interior tubercle, their upper tubercular tooth is broader than long, and they have only two false molars above and three below, on each side. They exhale a strong and disagreeable odour. The species are extremely numerous, and widely spread. We have three well known British kinds—the foumart, or common polecat (*M. putorius*, Linn.), of which the ferret (*M. furo*) is regarded simply as a variety by some,—the weasel (*M. vulgaris*, Linn.), and the ermine or stoat (*M. erminea*, Linn.). Another species, remarkable for its amphibious habits, and known under the name of *Mink* (*Mustela lutreola*, Pallas), is very common in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FINLAND">Finland</a>, and in other parts of the north and east of Europe, from the Icy to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK_SEA">Black <a </a>class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>. Erxleben, however, is in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-ERROR">error</a> when he supposes it to be a North American species. The animal of the New World is the vison (*M. vison*, Gmelin) or minx <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OTTER">otter</a> of Pennant. Both species prey much on fish, reptiles, and aquatic insects, and the latter is easily tamed. "One," says Sir J. Richardson, "which I <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SAW">saw</a> in the possession of a Canadian woman, passed the day in her pocket, looking out occasionally, when its attention was roused by any unusual noise." Other species inhabit the warmer countries of the earth, such as <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> (*P. africanus*, Desm.), Madagascar (*P. striatus*, F. Cuvier), and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JAVA">Java</a> (*P. nudipes*, Id.). The last-named animal, of a yellowish fawn-colour, with the head and termination of the tail white, is figured in this work, Plate V., <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> 1. There is a Cape species (*Pierroa zorilla*, Gmelin) which, in its general aspect, resembles the polecats; yet the form of its fore-claws is somewhat peculiar, and seems to indicate subterranean habits of life, and a propensity to dig. It has, on this account, been formed by some authors into a separate subgenus under the name of *Zorilla*—perhaps an inappropriate <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, and apt to mislead the student, in as far as it was first applied by Spanish writers to one of the mephitic species of America. The Martens properly so called (*Mustela* of Cuvier, but to which the generic name of *Martes* would be more appropriately applied), have a small interior tubercle on the lower carnivorous cheek-tooth, and (compared with the preceding) an additional false molar both above and below. Each of these characters is supposed to indicate some diminution of the purely carnivorous propensity. We have two British species, the common or beech marten (*M. fagorum*, Ray, *M. martes*, var. *fagorum*, Linn.), of which the throat and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BREAST">breast</a> are white, and the pine marten (*M. abietum*, Ray, *M. martes*, var. *abietum*, Linn.), of which the throat and breast are dingy <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>. The former is the more common in England, and the southern and central parts of Scotland,—the latter prevails in the north. Though the specific names are derived from their supposed propensities towards particular kinds of forests, it appears Carnivora, that their habits, like those of most other species, are of an accommodating kind. Both sorts, and more especially the first named, are often found in districts "rocky, bare, sublime;" of which the most hopeless attribute is that of forest scenery. The common marten more frequently approaches <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FARM">farm</a>-houses than the other, and was probably, for that reason, distinguished by the name of *domestica* by the old writers, such as Gesner and Aldrovandus. The pine marten is extremely common over the northern parts of America, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and is particularly abundant where the trees have remained standing after being killed by fire. Its fur is fine, and has long formed an important article of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, upwards of a hundred thousand skins being collected annually in the districts devoted to the trade. It is well known that it also formed a lucrative subject of export from Scotland before the Union. Dr Fleming says it builds its nest on the tops of trees. According to Sir J. Richardson, its habits in America are rather subterraneous. We have seen its young winding their worm-like way amid the treeless *corries* of the Highland mountains, where not even a sapling wild-ash waved its leaves in the grey solitude. One of the most famous of the foreign martens is the zibelline or sable (*M. Zibellina*, Linn.), so noted for the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of its fur. It is very like our martens both in size and proportions, and is usually of a rich lustrous brown colour, somewhat paler in summer, and marked during that season with grey upon the throat, and whitish on the ears and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACE">face</a>. It is spread over a wide extent of northern Asia, where it is held in the highest estimation of all the fur-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> animals; and its pursuit among the frozen wastes of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KAMTSCHATKA">Kamtschatka</a> is probably the most painful as well as perilous of those sacrifices which the human race, either by force or free will, have ever made to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RICHES">riches</a>. The winter robe is by much the most esteemed, being then fuller, darker, softer, and more <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a> and lustrous than at any other season. In this state it is equally coveted by Chinese mandarins, Tartarian chiefs, and the noblesse of Europe, and is justly regarded as one of the most precious and magnificent of all the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> adornments of the human frame. A single skin of the richest <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> is worth from twelve to fourteen pounds, and in its attempted acquisition many hardy hunters perish miserably of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and famine. The Russian dealers, however, are so skilful in the perfect <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of these furs, that they often succeed in selling the summer skins for those of winter. We may add, that to the pursuit of the sable we owe the discovery of the eastern countries of Siberia. The pekan or fisher (*M. canadensis*, Linn.) is a well known species of North America. Its habits resemble those of the pine marten, but it is nearly twice the size, and its fur is coarser, and less valuable. **Genus Mephitis**, Cuv. Incisives \(6\), canines \(1-1\), molars \(4-4\) or \(5-5\); \(=34\). As in the polecats, there are two false molars above and three below, but the upper tubercular tooth is very large, and as long as <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>; the lower carnivorous cheek tooth has two <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TUBERCLES">tubercles</a> on its inner side, a character in which the species approach the badgers. They resemble the latter also in the lengthened claws of --- 1 Baron Cuvier has applied the generic name *Putorius* to the group which contains the polecats and the weasel, and he bestows that of *Mustela* on the martens. We think the latter should have been given to whatever group contained the true weasel (*M. vulgaris*, Linn.), as it is otherwise apt to carry false associations. Some recent writers adopt the genus *Putorius*, as assigned by Cuvier, but give the title of *Martes* to the martens properly so called. This is very well in its way, but then we lose the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TERM">term</a> *mustela* altogether as a generic appellation. Now we think, that whenever a Linnaean genus is raised to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of a family, the original generic title should still be retained, as indicative of one of the restricted groups. 2 Arctic <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, vol. I. p. 67; and Fauna Boreali-Americana, Part I. p. 48. 3 Ibid. p. 49. the fore feet, and the almost plantigrade form of the hinder extremities. The animals of this genus are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called skunks or mephitic weasels, and are remarkable for their intense and ineradicable odour. Although several species are described by naturalists, it does not clearly appear that more exists than one, the skunk weasel of Pennant (Mephitis Americana, Rich., Viverra putorius, Gmelin), which is spread over a great extent of territory in the New World, and varies in different localities. Its size is that of a domestic cat; its fur, though rather coarse, is very ample, of a black colour, marked by longitudinal bands of white, and the tail, which is long and bushy, has generally two broad longitudinal white stripes above upon a black ground. The skunk, as described by Sir J. Richardson, inhabits rocky and woody regions, spending the winter in a hole, and seldom stirring abroad during the colder seasons. It preys on mice, and in summer feeds much on frogs. Its gait is slow, and it can be easily overtaken by its pursuers, as it makes no great efforts to escape by flight, but trusts the discomfiture of its enemies to the discharge of a most noxious fluid. This fluid, which is of a deep yellow colour, is contained in a small bag placed at the root of the tail, and emits probably the most overpowering stench in the known world. It is so durable, that wherever a skunk has been killed, the place retains a taint for many days. "Mr Graham says that he knew several Indians who had lost their eyesight in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of inflammation, produced by this fluid having been thrown into them by the animal, which has the power of ejecting it to the distance of upwards of four feet. I have known," adds Sir J. Richardson, "a dead skunk thrown over the stockades of a trading <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POST">post</a> produce instant nausea in several women in a house with closed doors upwards of a hundred yards distant. The odour has some resemblance to that of garlic, although much more disagreeable. One may, however, soon become familiarized with it; for notwithstanding the disgust it produces at first, I have managed to skin a couple of recent specimens by recurring to the task at intervals. When care is taken not to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> the carcass with any of the strong smelling fluid, the meat is considered by the natives to be excellent food. It breeds once a-year, and has from six to ten young at a time." Not fewer than fifteen varieties of this animal have been described, and many of them under separate names, as distinct species. It is singular that the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUDSON_S_BAY">Hudson's <a </a>class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAY">Bay</a> variety should approach most nearly to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the Chinché of Buffon (Viverra mephitis, Gmelin), which, though said to be an inhabitant of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHILI">Chili</a>, is yet regarded by some observers as identical with the skunk of more northern regions, and to the same or closely related species we may also no doubt refer the so-called glutton of Quito (Gulo Quetensis), described by Humboldt.*

GENUS MYDAUS

Pages 170-171

Horsfield. Incisives 6; canines 1—1; molars 4—4; 5—5 = 34. Muzzle truncated, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> pig like. Tail very short. The only known <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of this genus is the Teledu of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JAVA">Java</a> (M. meliceps, Horsfield), classed as a Mephitis by Desmarest and others. In its dentition it certainly agrees closely with the mephitic weasels of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, but its <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> character and physiognomy are peculiar, its form being heavy, its neck strong and short, and its <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of progression almost entirely plantigrade. It emits an odour very similar to that of the skunk. "The Mydaus meliceps," says Dr Horsfield, in his excellent account of this curious animal, "presents a singular fact in its geographical distribution. It is confined exclusively to those <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> which have an elevation of more than 7000 feet above the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> of the ocean; on these it occurs with as much regularity as many <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> extended surface of Java, abounding with conical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POINTS">points</a> which exceed this elevation, affords many places favourable for its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RESORT">resort</a>. On ascending these mountains, the traveller scarcely fails to meet with our animal, which, from its peculiarities, is universally known to the inhabitants of these elevated tracts; while to those of the plains it is as strange as an animal from a foreign <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. A traveller would inquire in vain for the Teledu at Batavia, Semarang, or Surabaya. In my visits to the mountainous districts I uniformly met with it; and, as far as the information of the natives can be relied on, it is found on all the mountains. It is, however, more abundant on those which, after reaching a certain elevation, consist of numerous connected <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> ridges, than on those which terminate in a defined conical peak. Of the former <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> are the mountain Prabu and the Tengger Hills, which are both distinctly indicated in Sir <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STAMFORD">Stamford</a> Raffles' map of Java: here I observed it in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> abundance. It was the less <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> on mountain Gedé, south of Batavia; on the mountain Ungaran, south of Semarang; and on the mountain Ijen, at the farthest eastern extremity; but I traced its range through the whole <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>. Most of these mountains and ridges furnish tracts of considerable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, fitted for the cultivation of wheat and other European grains. Certain extra-tropical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> are likewise raised with success. Peaches and strawberries grow in considerable abundance, and the common culinary vegetables of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> are cultivated to great extent. To most Europeans and Chinese a residence in these elevated regions is extremely desirable; and even the natives, who in general dislike its <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLD">cold</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>, are attracted by the fertility of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, and find it an advantage to establish villages, and to clear grounds for culture. Potatoes, cabbages, and many other culinary vegetables are extensively raised, as the entire supply of the plains in these <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> depends on these elevated districts. Extensive plantations of wheat and of other European grains, as well as of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, are here found, where <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RICE">rice</a>, the universal product of the plains, refuses to grow. These grounds and plantations are laid out in the deep vegetable mould, where the teledu holds its range as the most <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> inhabitant of the soil. In its rambles in search of food, this animal frequently enters the plantations and destroys the roots of young plants; in this manner it causes extensive injury, and on the Tengger Hills particularly, where these plantations are more extensive than in other elevated tracts, its visits are much dreaded by the inhabitants; it burrows in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> with its nose, in the same manner as hogs; and, in traversing the hills, its nocturnal toils are observed in the morning, in small ridges of mould recently turned up. "The Mydaus forms its dwelling at a slight depth beneath the surface, in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">black</a> mould, with considerable ingenuity. Having selected a spot, defended above by the roots of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> tree, it constructs a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CELL">cell</a> or chamber of a globular form, having a diameter of several feet, the sides of which it makes perfectly smooth and regular; this it provides with a subterraneous conduit or avenue, about six feet in length, the external entrance to which it conceals with twigs and dry leaves. During the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> it remains concealed like a badger in its hole; at night it proceeds in search of its food, which consists of insects and their larvae, and of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> of every kind; it is particularly fond of the common lumbrici, or earthworms, which abound in the fertile mould. These animals, agreeably to the information of the natives, live in pairs, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> produces two or three young at a birth. "The motions of the mydaus are slow, and it is easily taken by the natives, who by no means fear it. During --- *Feuille Boreali-Americana, p. l. p. 55. *Recueil d'Observations sur la Zoologie. my abode on the mountain Prah, I engaged them to procure me individuals for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a>; and as they received a desirable reward, they brought them to me daily in greater numbers than I could employ. Whenever the natives surprise them suddenly, they prepare them for food; the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> is then scarcely impregnated with the offensive odour, and is described as very delicious. The animals are generally in excellent condition, as their food abounds in fertile mould. We may add, that the teledu is by no means ferocious in its manners, and, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> taken young, might no doubt be easily domesticated. An individual, retained for some <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> in confinement by Dr Horsfield, afforded him an opportunity of studying its disposition. It soon became gentle and reconciled to its situation, and never emitted its offensive <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EFFLUVIUM">effluvium</a>. In the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> state, however, its odour is so strong and volatile, that the entire neighbourhood of a village may be infected by a single animal in a state of irritation, and in the immediate vicinity of the discharge the smell is so violent as to produce fainting fits. The specimen from which Dr Horsfield made his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> ate voraciously of earthworms, but as soon as it had devoured ten or twelve it became drowsy, and, making a small <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GROOVE">groove</a> in the earth, it placed its snout in it and fell asleep.

GENUS MYGALE

Pages 163-163

Cuv. Differs from Sorex in having two very small <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> between the larger of the lower incisives, and in the upper incisives being triangular and flattened. Behind these incisives are six <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> small teeth, and four jagged molars. Pallas and Geoffroy St Hilaire differ in their descriptions of the dentition of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> they have respectively described. These animals are of aquatic habits, dwelling in holes to which they enter under <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and then proceed upwards to dry and comfortable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>. They feed on larvae and <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>, and, according to some authors, on the roots of the nymphura. The fur of the Russian species (*M. moscovita*, Geoff., *<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CASTOR">Castor</a> moschatus*, Linn.) is much esteemed, on account of its being composed, like that of the beaver, of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> silky <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, and of a softer felt beneath. It exhales a strong musky odour, which imbues the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of pike and other voracious fish which prey upon it. We are acquainted with only two species, that of Russia <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUST">just</a> named (extremely abundant in the environs of Woronech, where it is often entangled in the nets of the fishermen), and the Desman of the Pyrenees (*M. pyrenaicus*). It is said that these creatures, not being torpid in winter, suffer dreadfully during that inclement season, from the freezing of the waters. Many perish from suffocation in their subterranean abodes,—these having no <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AIR">air</a>. The species last named has as yet been found only in the neighbourhood of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TARBES">Tarbes</a> at the foot of the Pyrenees.

GENUS NASUA

Pages 167-167

STORR., CUV.** | Incisors | Canine | |----------|--------| | 6 | 1—1 | Molars | 6—6 | |------| Tail <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a>, covered with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, not prehensile. Six ventral mammae. No cecum. This genus contains the well-known South American animals called coatis, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> coati *mondis*, so frequently seen in our menageries. Individuals vary greatly in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and it is the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> of some observers, that the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-RED">red</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> coatis, *N. rufa* and *fusca* (*Viverra nasua* and *nasica* of Linn.), are identical. We have represented the so-called *Nasua rufa* on Plate IV., <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> 7. In a state of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> these animals dwell in the woods, preying on such small birds and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a> as they can overcome, and producing occasional devastation in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CANE">cane</a> plantations. They are often domesticated in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRAZIL">Brazil</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GUIANA">Guiana</a>, and Paraguay, but it is necessary to keep them chained, as they climb better than cats, and are always getting into mischief, from their restless <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> and habits (otherwise praiseworthy) of general inquiry, which induce them to poke their snouts into every unaccustomed hole and corner. A specimen at present in our possession is extremely <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a>, much attached to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>, and also very fond of strawberries, earthworms, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, eggs, chickens (either raw or roasted), young frogs, and green peas. We may here allude briefly to the genus *Potos* of Geoffroy (*Cercleptes*, Illiger), which contains only a single <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of a somewhat anomalous aspect. It is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> *maucoco* of Pennant (*P. caudivoleculus*, Desm.), frequently called the *kinkajou*. Its size is nearly that of a domestic cat, and its physiognomy is remarkably like a lemur's. A tame one kept by P. Cuvier was mild and fond of caresses. It loved obscurity, and slept much during the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>. It occasionally ate meat, but preferred a vegetable diet. It was a dexterous climber. According to Humboldt it is very abundant in New Grenada, and was among the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of those animals formerly reduced by the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABORIGINES">aborigines</a> to a domestic state. It is said to be a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> destroyer of the nests of wild bees, and makes <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of its long tongue to extract their gathered sweets. On this account it was named the *Carnivora honey bear*, by the missionaries.

GENUS PROCYON

Pages 166-167

Storr., Cuv. Incisors 6, canine 1—1, molars 6—6; = 40. Tail <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a>. Six ventral mamme. This genus contains the animals <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called racoons. We have no precise knowledge of more than two <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. The first is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RACOON">racoon</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> (P. lotor, Cuv. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-URSUS">Ursus</a> lotor, Linn.), a fox-like creature, with the gait of a bear. In a state of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> it sleeps throughout the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, prowling during the night in search of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, roots, birds, eggs, and insects. At low <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a> it frequents the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-shore, where it preys on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRUSTACEA">crustacea</a> and shell-fish. It climbs trees with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> facility. According to M. Desmarest it extends as far south as Paraguay. But it is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> species <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> crab-eating racoon (P. cancrivorus, Geoff.), which is the more characteristic of the southern portion of the New World. The genus Ailurus of Fred. Cuvier, may be here men- --- 1 The student who desires to complete his knowledge of this interesting animal, is referred to Martin's Voyage to Spitzbergen, Fabricius's Fauna Greenlandica, Pennant's Arctic <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, Scoresby's Account of the Arctic Regions, the Appendix to Parry's Second Voyage, and Richardson's Fauna Boreali-Americana, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> 1st. The same works may of course be consulted with equal advantage for the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of other arctic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a>. 2 Travels on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MISSOURI">Missouri</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARKANSAS">Arkansas</a>. tioned as allied to the racoons. It possesses, however, only one false molar instead of three. Its dentition is not distinctly known. One species only has been hitherto recognised, the *A. fulgens*, a native of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Northern <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>. It is an extremely beautiful animal, clothed in a soft dense fur, the upper parts of a bright <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CINNAMON">cinnamon</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-RED">red</a>, the under surface deep <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">black</a>. In size it resembles a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> cat, and dwells by preference among trees in the vicinity of streams and torrents, preying on birds and small quadrupeds. It offers in some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of the bears, civets, and racoons. (See Plate IV., figures 6 and 6a.) Another recently constructed genus is named *Ictides*, by M. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-VALENCIENNES">Valenciennes</a>. The three hindermost molars of the upper jaw are much smaller and less tuberculated than those of the racoons, especially the farthest back in each jaw, which is very small and almost simple. (See Plate IV., <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> 5.) The tail is long and densely furred, with an involved appearance as <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it were prehensile. Two species have been described.—*Ict. albifrons*, a native of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMATRA">Sumatra</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALACCA">Malacca</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JAVA">Java</a>; and *Ict. ater*, found chiefly in Malacca. They are not yet distinctly characterized or discriminated, and one or other of them is the *Binturong* of Raffles. It was observed to climb trees, with the assistance of its tail, which has uncommon strength. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a> Farquhar kept one alive for many years. It fed both on animal and vegetable food, was particularly fond of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, but also ate readily of fowl's heads, eggs, &c. It was most <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> during the night.

GENUS SCALOPS

Pages 163-163

Cuv. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> of this genus resemble those of the preceding, but their false molars are less numerous. The only known <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> is the shrew <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOLE">mole</a> (*S. canadensis*), a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">North</a> American animal, nearly eight inches in length, with a thick cylindrical body, no apparent neck, short concealed <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> strongly nailed <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. It resembles the European mole in its habits, leading a subterranean <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, forming galleries, and feeding principally on grubs and earthworms. According to Dr Godman, they exhibit the singular <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of coming to the surface daily exactly at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> of noon, and may then be taken alive by thrusting a spade beneath them, and throwing them out of their burrows. A tame one in the possession of Mr Peale was very lively and playful, would follow the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of its keeper by the scent (the eyes are very inefficient), and fed freely on fresh meat, whether cooked <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> raw. It would burrow for amusement in loose <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and after making a small circle, would return spontaneously to its keeper. Although widely spread over North <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, Dr Richardson does not think its existence probable beyond the 50th <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of latitude, at least to the eastward of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROCKY_MOUNTAINS">Rocky <a class=</a>"xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">Mountains</a>, because the earth-worm, its favourite food, is unknown in the countries of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUDSON_S_BAY">Hudson's <a </a>class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAY">Bay</a>.

GENUS SPALAX

Pages 197-197

Guldenstaedt. Aspalax, Olivier, Desm. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEETH">Teeth</a> as in the rats and hamsters, but the incisives more projecting and exposed. Legs very short; all the feet furnished with five toes, with flat thin nails. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-EXTERNAL">External</a> ears and tail scarcely perceptible. The singular animal (Mus typhlus of Pallas) which forms the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TYPE">type</a> of this genus, resembles the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOLE">mole</a> in its habits,—throwing up the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> from its burrows in the same manner, though furnished with much less powerful <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a>. It <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> nearly ten inches <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a>, has a thick cylindrical body, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> triangular head, and no apparent eyes. Beneath the skin, however, there are small <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POINTS">points</a> resembling eyes, although their functions, as organs of vision, are difficult to understand, in as far as they are covered over by skin and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>. "Whether the spalax be absolutely <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLIND">blind</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> whether it receives any perception of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> through the medium of the eye as an organ, does not sufficiently appear by what has hitherto been said by its describers. The presence of what may be called the vestige of an organ, seems perfectly consistent with other instances in which the application of such imperfect organ is not at all to be traced." On the contrary, it accords with that apparent unwillingness in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> to depart from prescribed laws. The total absence of an accustomed organ is much more anomalous in nature than the complete inutility of an imperfect one." It has been generally assumed that the Greeks described our <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> mole as blind, under the name of ἀσπαλάξ, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> authors, knowing that the sleek inhabitant of our pastures is possessed of eyes, though small ones, have prided themselves on their supposed correction of an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-ERROR">error</a>; but the observations of Olivier go to prove that the mole of the Greeks was not the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of western <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, but the animal in question, which spreads through <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR"><a class="</a>xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a> into <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> and the south of Russia, between the Tanais and the Wolga. The original error probably lay with the Latin writers, who translated the word ἀσπαλάξ into talpa, and then applied the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TERM">term</a> to the mole of Europe. We may add, however, that Professor Savi of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PISA">Pisa</a> is of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that the aspalax is to be regarded as identical with the species of mole (Talpa excisa) which he discovered in the Apennines, and which Baron Cuvier says is "tout à fait aveugle," by which we presume he merely means that its eyes are covered by the skin. M. <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Lucien Bonaparte likewise regards these species as <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a>. We may here briefly notice the genus Bathiergus of Illiger, which, with several attributes of the preceding genus, is distinguished by four molars on each side both above and below, by a small though perceptible eye, and a short tail. The sand mole (B. maritimus, Plate IX., <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> 2), as the larger species is usually called, is an animal of the size of a rabbit, which occurs abundantly along the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> shores of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> of Good Hope, where it sometimes excavates the ground in such a manner as to produce inconvenience, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not danger, to horsemen. Another species, called the Cape <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-RAT">rat</a> (B. capensis), is destructive in gardens and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> grounds. A third has been described under the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of B. hottentotus, by MM. Lesson and Garnot. For the genera Geomys and Diplostoma of M. Rafinesque, and a few other groups of the Rodential Order, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of which we cannot here detail, we must refer the reader to the works quoted below.

GENUS TALPA

Pages 164-164

Linn. Incisives 6, canine 1—1, molar 7—7; = 44. We need scarcely describe the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> aspect of an animal so well known as the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOLE">mole</a> (T. europaea), almost the only <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of which the restricted genus Talpa is now composed. There are few species, however, of greater <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> to the naturalist, whether he regards their singular economy and instinctive habits, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> their very peculiar organic structure. Moles present as it were the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TYPE">type</a> or perfect form of a subterranean dweller. The snout is pointed, yet strong and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a>, the head somewhat depressed, the eyes inconspicuous, the external ears wanting, the cervical ligament unusually strong, the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of the anterior extremity angular, and so extremely thick as to be almost as <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> as they are <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a>. The two bones of the fore-arm are fastened together, the paws are broad and shovel-shaped, with strong claws, and an elongated bone of the carpus communicates <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> solidity to their under edges. The clavicles are very powerful, and the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> muscles of the anterior extremity, especially the pectorals, are enormous. Although the organs of sight are feebly developed (they suffice, however, for whatever visual perceptions may be necessary to an almost constant dweller in subterranean darkness), the senses of hearing, touch, and smell, are acute. The galleries of the mole are constructed with admirable sagacity and art, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> brings forth in a dry and sheltered chamber, well furnished with grass and leaves. The exact <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of gestation is unknown, but as young are found in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> and autumn, it is obvious that she produces twice a-year. She is careful of, and much attached to, her young; but, except in relation to these, and during the pairing season, moles <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> a solitary and an isolated <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. They are extremely voracious,—their appetite for food, according to Geoffroy St Hilaire, amounting to an actual phrenzy. When kept for a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> in a state of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSTINENCE">abstinence</a> they become outrageous, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> dart with violence upon whatever prey is then presented,—plunging their heads into the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a> of birds and other animals, and satiating themselves with blood. They have been observed to refuse toads, but to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> upon frogs with avidity. With such violent propensities it may be easily conceived that they soon die of famine when debarred from food. At the same time their appetites are not so entirely carnivorous; at least several authors allege that they occasionally eat various tender and succulent roots, and the bulbs of the colchicum. Though deemed very injurious in gardens, and persecuted by farmers even in the open grounds, they do not want <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a> who espouse their cause as useful agents in the general economy of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>; and their undoubted destruction of grubs and mole-crickets must prove beneficial to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>. The female, indeed, while furnishing her nursery, is a somewhat too <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> reaper,—402 young stalks of corn, with the leaves entire, have been counted in her nuptial chamber. The existence of the optic nerve in moles is a greatly contested point among physiological naturalists. Daudanet and Dr <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GALL">Gall</a>, conceiving vision to be impossible in the absence of that nerve, presumed it to exist in those animals in a complete and normal condition. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CARUS">Carus</a>, Baily, and Treviranus, have sought to establish its existence in a rudimentary state; while its total absence is maintained by Serres and Desmoulins. Geoffroy St Hilaire presumes himself to have reconciled these various opinions with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of nature, by shewing that, although the optic nerve does not occur under the same conditions as it exhibits among the normal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a>, its analogue is found in a branch which proceeds from the eye to the fifth <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> writers have been accused of inaccuracy, in describing the mole as <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLIND">blind</a>; and this would certainly have been a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-ERROR">error</a> in relation to an animal, of which the eyes, though small, are so distinctly perceptible. It is true that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> twice repeats the assertion that the mole has no eyes; but we must remember that the true mole is extremely rare in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, and that the arvicolus of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> (translated mole) is another animal (Apalax typhlus), of which the eyes are in truth entirely covered by the skin. It is only in comparatively recent times that naturalists have become acquainted with a species, the remarkable conformation of which thus excuses, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it does not verify, the statement of the Stagyrite. The only other mole found in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> is one discovered among the Apennines by Signor Savi. It is said to be entirely blind, and has, in that <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a>, been named Talpa eoca by the Italian naturalist. It is somewhat less than the common species, and one of our correspondents states his belief that it occurs in France.

INSANITY

Pages 540-541

Insanity can only be defined in very general terms as a congenital mental deficiency. The degrees of this deficiency are infinitely varied, from the total absence of anything like human thought or reason up to the smallest amount of imbecility which distinguishes a naturally weak-minded person from one of sound mind. The history of some sciences and arts may with propriety be consigned to oblivion as the cumbrous record of ignorance and error; but the history of this department of study is that of the development of the human mind,—of man himself,—and is therefore deserving of study. The philosophy of mind, and by consequence that of

LET IT BE GRANTED THAT EVERY PHENOMENON

t it be granted that every phenomenon implies a corresponding reality; that the phenomena of the *ego* indicate the existence of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>; and the phenomena of the *non-ego,* that of a substantial universe; and the relation between the two, that of a being who is beyond relation—still, in no fact of consciousness is the reality given apart from the phenomena which are related to it. 3 The character of rational psychology, as distinguished from empirical, is thus stated by Wolf.—"De finibus psychologiae empiricae quod sit scientia stabilitatis principia per experimentum, unde ratio reddatur accurata qua in anima humana fluit . . . ." In psychologia rationali ex unico animae humano essentia derivantur a priori omnes aliae a posteriori observantur et ex quidquid observatis deducuntur." (Philosophiae Enucleatae, tomus secundus, sect. 111, 112.) Compare Herbert, *Allegoriae Metaphysicae,* sect. 29. 4 These three objects of metaphysical inquiry,—God, the world, the soul,—answer to Kant's three <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of pure reason; but he arrives at them in a different way; namely, by regarding them as all alike intimations of the unconditioned, suggested by the three kinds of logical syllogism—a derivation fanciful and extravagant, and which nothing but the profound genius of its author could have rescued from utter absurdity. Ontology, of an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> self, modified in no particular manner; of an abstract world, isolated from the special phenomena of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>; and of an abstract Deity, apart from those finite attributes by which he is manifested in relation to the finite consciousness of mankind, can be given in no phase of consciousness; for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they were, the relation and succession which constitute consciousness would be annihilated. Whether these three metaphysical ideas all stand on the same footing within the domain of consciousness itself, is a question which we shall have to ask hereafter; but, assuming for the moment that they do, and assuming that in each there is a legitimate passage from the phenomena presented in consciousness to the ultimate realities beyond, it is clearly begging the whole question, and anticipating the inquiry which <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> has not yet commenced, to start with the abstract notions of such realities, as if the problem had been already solved, and the passage found. Hence, like ontology in general, the three branches of ontology, if deductively treated, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> with words and not with things. Unable to verify their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FUNDAMENTAL">fundamental</a> assumptions by an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> to the facts of consciousness,—unable even to determine whether those assumptions represent thought <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEGATION">negation</a> of thought,—they can but torture words under the name of analysing notions, and arrive at conclusions which indicate no more than a consistent <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. Thought itself, in its bare and unmixed form, cannot be handled in any mental <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>. It must be contemplated either in the words which represent it, or in the things which it represents, or in the union of the two; and the whole <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between reasoning and logomachy depends upon a single criterion:—Can the relations of language, which our process exhibits as representing thought, be verified by an appeal to the facts of consciousness, of which thought itself is the representative? Such an appeal is manifestly impossible to those who commence their inquiries by assuming an abstraction of which consciousness does not and cannot take cognisance.
