Thus, to illustrate our remarks by special instances, the aim of rational psychology is to frame definitions exhibiting the essential <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the soul and its properties, as realities conceived by the intellect, underlying and implied by the phenomena presented in consciousness; and to prove by a demonstrative process that the notions thus defined necessarily flow one from another. Psychology is thus raised from a science of observation to one of demonstration; and its objects are transformed from phenomena presented in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> to realities contemplated by the intellect. The soul, by virtue of its essential nature as a simple substance, is shown to possess, of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>, certain attributes as rationally conceived and defined—such as sense, imagination, intelligence, will, spirituality, indestructibility, and so forth; and the same conclusions are even demonstrated of other spiritual natures which partake of the generic attributes of the human soul. The weakness of the whole process is, that it tacitly postulates as its starting-point a principle which is neither evident in itself, nor such as can be made evident by any process of thought. It assumes, that is to say, a transcendental <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> of the real nature of the soul, beyond and above those facts and relations which are manifested in consciousness. But how is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of such a definition to be guaranteed? Of the soul as a simple substance, apart from its particular modifications, consciousness tells us nothing. Its permanent existence is known only in conjunction with and by means of its successive modifications. How, then, is this abstract <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a> of the nature of the soul to be verified? It cannot be self-evident; for self-<a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> is nothing more than the instantaneous assent of consciousness; and the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSUMPTION">assumption</a> in question cannot be submitted to the judgment of consciousness at all. It cannot be demonstrable; for it could only be demonstrated by the assumption of a higher notion of the same kind, concerning which the same question would then have to be raised. It cannot be generalized from experience; for experience deals with the facts of consciousness only, and tells us not of what must be, but only of what is or seems to be. Unable to verify his fundamental definition by any reference to the reality which it is supposed to represent, the metaphysician is compelled to confine himself to the relations of the language by which it is represented. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CASE">case</a> is still stronger as regards the other two branches of deductive <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-METAPHYSICS">metaphysics</a>. Cosmology, as exhibited by Wolf, professes to deduce, from ontological principles, a demonstration of the nature of the world and the manner in which it is produced from simple substances. The world, according to this method, is represented as an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> whole, or entire system of causes and effects, which cannot be conceived as itself a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of any greater whole; and the office of cosmology is to deduce, from the abstract principles of being in general, the necessary relations which the world, as a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> being, must exhibit. It is thus based, not on an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of the mundane phenomena as they actually exist in the present system of nature, but on the general conception of the world, as a possible system, under which the actual system is included, as an individual under a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. Cosmology, as thus exhibited, can contain nothing more than an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a> of general notions, and can <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> to no conclusions but such as the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> has himself virtually assumed in his premises. The abstract notion of the world contains implicitly whatever attributes we choose to assume as its constituents; and the metaphysical or logical analysis of that notion can contain no more. For the world, as a possible system of realities, and not as an actual system of phenomena, is not an object of intuition, pure or empirical; and, without intuition, it is impossible to connect the concepts of the understanding with a single <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a>, beyond those which they contain in their original comprehension. 1 The following <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TABLE">table</a> of the contents of Wolf's *Psychologia Rationalis* will exhibit a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> summary of this method.—"De anima in genere et facultate cognoscendi in specie.—De natura et essentia animae.—De facultate sentiendi, sive sensu.—De imaginatone et memoria.—De attentione et intellectu.—De facultate appetendi.—De appetitu sensitivo et aversione sensitiva atque affectibus.—De appetitu et aversione rationali, seu de voluntate et noluntate.—De commercio inter mentem et corpus.—De systematis explicandi commercium inter mentem et corpus in genere.—De systemate influxus physicus.—De systemate causarum occasionalium.—De <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONIA">harmonia</a> praestabilita.—De veris omnium attributis, spiritu in genere, et animabus brutiorum.—De spiritu in genere et spiritualitate animae in specie.—De animae ortu, unione cum corpore, et immortalitate.—De animabus brutiorum." Compare Kant, *Kr. der r. v.* Transl. Dall., B. II., H. I. Hegel, *Enzyk.* sect. 31. 2 Wolf, *Cosmologia Generalis*, sects. 2, 7. The following are the questions discussed by Wolf in this <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a>, as constituting a metaphysical <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of the material world.—"De naturae mundi et universi usu.—De essentia mundi et ejus attributione.—De naturae mundi et universi compositione.—De essentia mundi et ejus compositione <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEX">sex</a> elementis.—De legibus motus.—De naturae universae et perfectione mundi.—De natura universa in genere, itemque naturali et supernaturali.—De perfectione mundi.—De ordine mundi atque naturae. 3 Kant, *Logica de Metaphysique traduite par Tissot*, p. 144. 4 Wolf, *Cosmologia*, sect. 49. 5 "Cosmology," says Hegel (*Enzyklop.* sect. 35), "treated of questions concerning the contingency or necessity of the world, its eternity or limitation in space and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a>, and the formal <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> of its changes; together with those concerning human freedom, and the origin of evil." It contemplated its object, however, not as a concrete whole, but only according to abstract definitions. Thus, for example, it discussed such questions as, whether the world is subject to chance or necessity; whether it is eternal or created. A portion of the questions here mentioned were sometimes transferred to other branches of metaphysics; but the method in all <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> was the same, and the results equally barren. This criticism is still more applicable to the system of rational <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a>. In this science, we are supposed to start from a nominal definition of the Deity, as the most perfect being, containing in his nature the sum of all possible realities in an absolutely perfect <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>. But here again the question arises.—How do we know that our conception at all corresponds to the nature of the being whom it professes to represent? The object, which the conception represents, is either given in some fact of consciousness, or it is not. If it is not given, I cannot compare the conception with its object; for <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> is itself an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACT">act</a> of consciousness, and cannot be applied to anything of which I am not conscious. If it is given, it must be given, like all other facts of consciousness, in the form of an object related to myself. By what <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, again, do I venture to transcend that relation, and assume that what is given in relation to me is identical with that which exists out of all relation? We are not, be it remembered, discussing the sufficiency of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> consciousness for the spiritual wants of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a>; we are only examining the claim of the metaphysician to found thereon a system of absolute and necessary truths. Such a system claims, in its very conception, a right to transcend consciousness. The form of consciousness is myself, and the facts of consciousness postulate my existence as their condition. By what warrant am I justified in reasoning from the relative to the absolute,—in identifying that which depends on me with that on which I depend. A conception of the Deity, in his absolute existence, appears to involve a self-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a>; for conception itself is a limitation, and a conception of the absolute Deity is a limitation of the illimitable.

MAGNUS

Pages 104-104

St. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAY">Bay</a> of, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and beautiful bay on the W. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the mainland of Shetland, about 8 miles wide at its mouth, and afterwards expanding to about 11 miles, and extending 7 miles inland. It affords excellent anchorage for the largest vessels. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PAPA">Papa</a>-Stour is at the S. side of its mouth.

MAGONTIACUM

Pages 104-104
or Mogontiacum, shortened into Moguntia, a town of Gallia Belgica, now Mentz or Mayence, situated at the confluence of the Rhine and the Maine.

MAHABALIPURAM

Pages 104-104

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, in Southern <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CARNATIC">Carnatic</a>. It is noted for the celebrated ruins of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Hindu <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> in the vicinity, dedicated to Vishnu, generally called the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">Seven</a> Pagodas, though it is not known for what reason, as no such <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> exists here. There is a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> rock, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> rather a hill, of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, about a 100 yards from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, covered with images, so thickly scattered as to convey the idea of a petrified town. On this hill a temple is cut out of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> rock, with figures of idols carved in alto-rilievo on the walls, and well finished. On an adjoining hill there is a gigantic statue of Vishnu asleep on a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BED">bed</a>, with a huge snake wound round in many coils as a pillow; the whole cut out of one solid stone. A <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MILE">mile</a> and a half to the southward of the hill are two pagodas, about 30 feet <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> by 20 wide. Near to these is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of an elephant as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> as <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and of a lion much larger than life. There are here also other pagodas, and curious monuments of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>. This town is said to have extended many miles to the eastward, into what is now covered by the sea; and there is every reason to believe that it was formerly a very large <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. N. Lat. 12. 37., E. Long. 80. 15.

MAHABULESHWA

Pages 104-104

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, a small town within the presidency of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BOMBAY">Bombay</a>, situate on the summit of the range of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> the same name. In <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTRAST">contrast</a> with most other hill stations in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, this is totally free from malaria, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> having, in many circumstances affecting <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, a decided superiority over the more depressed and sultry tracts in its vicinity, was some <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> since selected as a sanatory station for troops; but after a short <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TRIAL">trial</a> the project was abandoned, on the ground of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> being unsuited to the acute diseases most <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> among the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>. It is, however, much frequented by invalid officers, for whose accommodation there is a sanatorium containing eight sets of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>, and several detached bungalows. There are also about seventy private dwellings, many of them built of hewn <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of visitors is steadily on the increase. The station was established in 1828 by Sir John Malcolm, the governor of Bombay. There is a small <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, a subscription library, and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOTEL">hotel</a>; and the bazaar is well supplied. The elevation of the station above the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> is about 4500 feet. Lal. 17. 59., <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 73. 41.

MAHANUDDY

Pages 104-104

a river of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, which has its source in Nowagudda, one of the petty native states, on the S.W. frontier of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>. It proceeds with a very winding <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> towards the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAY">Bay</a> of Bengal, receiving in its course the contributions of the Hutseo and several other tributaries. Near the town of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUTTACK">Cuttack</a> it divaricates into the numerous branches inclosing <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> traversing the delta; the total length of its course being estimated at 520 miles. Its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> mouth is in Lat. 20. 20., <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 86. 50.

MAHARAJPOOR

Pages 104-105

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, a small town in the native state of Gwalior, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> possessions of Scindia's family. This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> was the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KEY">key</a> of the position of the Mahratta <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> on the 29th <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1843, when the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> took place between them and the British army under Sir Hugh Gough. The <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MAHRATTAS">Mahrattas</a> were driven from all <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POINTS">points</a>, lost 96 pieces of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>, and retreated to the fort of Gwalior. The loss of the British was severe, amounting to 106 killed, 684 wounded, and 7 missing. No <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> disparity of numbers existed between the contending parties, the British having a force of 13,000; and the Mahrattas numbering about 15,000. A monument at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CALCUTTA">Calcutta</a>, constructed from the cannon captured on the field, commemorates the victory. Lat. 26° 29', <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 78° 6'.

MAHE

Pages 105-105

in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, a French settlement and seaport on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Malabar, containing an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> of 2 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. It is situated at a short distance from <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TELLICHERRY">Tellicherry</a>, on the banks of a river, which is navigable for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> boats a considerable way up the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Small vessels can also <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BAR">bar</a>, where there is a secure harbour. The town is neat, and contains many good houses. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> export is <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>, which is produced in abundance in the surrounding country. It was taken possession of by the French in 1722, but was retaken by the British in 1761. It was restored at the peace of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1763, but was again taken in 1793. The British establishment, previously established at Tellicherry, was then removed to Mahe; but the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> having been restored to the French at the general pacification of 1815, the British establishment was replaced in its original station at Tellicherry. The Carmelites have a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> here. Pop. 2616. It is situated in E. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 75° 38', and N. Lat. 11° 42'.

MAHIM

Pages 105-105

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, is situated on the northern point of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BOMBAY">Bombay</a>. It possesses a small fort, originally intended for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> of the channel running between it and Salsette. The town of Mahim stands at the point where the island of Bombay is connected with that of Salsette by a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROAD">road</a> running partly on <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> of masonry, and partly on a causeway constructed by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, aided by a munificent contribution from Sir Jamsetjee Jejeebhoy, a Parsee merchant of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> wealth residing at Bombay. Here is the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> of a Mohammedan saint, with a mosque attached to it; also a Portuguese <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, with a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> for Roman Catholic priests depending on it. It is 7 miles N. of Bombay fort. E. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 72° 54', N. Lat. 19° 1'. MAHMUD I., <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SULTAN">Sultan</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>, the son of Mustapha II., was born at Constantinople in 1696, and succeeded his uncle Ahmed III. on the Ottoman throne in 1730. He prosecuted the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a> which had been begun in the former reign against Nadir Shah of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>. In 1734 the Russians commenced hostilities against the sultan, and in 1737 captured Oczakow and Kilburn. The Austrians joined them; but, after invading Wallachia, they were defeated at Krotska, and forced to accede to a disadvantageous peace in 1739. Not so <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> was the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> struck soon afterwards between the Ottomans and Russians, by which the latter were allowed to retain <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the possessions they had captured. Meanwhile, a peace had been concluded with Persia in 1736, but was broken in 1743, and restored soon afterwards on terms unfavourable to the Ottomans. Mahmud died in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1764. MAHMUD II., Sultan of Turkey, the younger son of Abdul-Hamed, was born at Constantinople on the 2d September 1789, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a>, according to another account, on the 20th <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1785. He passed his early years in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SERAGLIO">Seraglio</a>, engaged in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of Turkish and Persian literature until 1808, when his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Mustapha IV. was deposed and imprisoned, and himself raised to the throne, by Mustapha Bairaktar, pasha of Rusjuk. No sooner had he taken the sceptre than he appointed Bairaktar <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> vizier, and boldly proclaimed his intention of prosecuting the reforms for which his uncle Selim III. had been deprived of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>. He also restored the Nizam Jedid, or <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> organized according to European <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a>. Startled at these proceedings, the Janissaries rushed to arms, besieged the grand vizier in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, and clamoured for the head of the sultan. At this crisis, Mahmud ordered Mustapha IV. and his infant son to be strangled, and his four pregnant sultanas to be sewn up in sacks and thrown into the Bosporus. By thus becoming the sole <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> descendant of Osman, he Mahogany rendered his person sacred in the eyes of his subjects, and was enabled more effectually to quiet the tumult. Then began his unsuccessful war with Russia, which was terminated by the peace of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUCHAREST">Bucharest</a> on the 28th May 1812. Mahmud had for some <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> looked with a jealous eye upon the growing dominion of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALI">Ali</a>, the ambitious pasha of Jenina, and he now strained all his energies to effect his overthrow. But no sooner had he succeeded in crushing him in 1822, than the Greeks broke out into open rebellion. Aided by the forces of Mehmeh Ali, pasha of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>, the sultan suppressed this revolt with such sanguinary cruelty that <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, France, and Russia interfered; and when their interference had been slighted, their combined armaments attacked and routed the Turko-Egyptian fleet in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAY">Bay</a> of Navarino in 1827. Meanwhile, at Constantinople, a desperate rebellion of the Janissaries, in 1826, had ended in the complete subjugation and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DISPERSION">dispersion</a> of that order, and in the permanent establishment of an army organized according to the European system. Expecting that his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, under their new discipline, would now be able to cope successfully with the armies of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, Mahmud declared war against Nicholas of Russia in 1828. After his forces had been cut to pieces, and General Diebitsch had occupied <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ADRIANOPLE">Adrianople</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRUSSIA">Prussia</a>, Britain, and France had interfered to effect a reconciliation, he unwillingly signed the treaty of Adrianople in 1829. With a determination untamed by so many reverses, the sultan now began to muster all his strength for the purpose of curbing the restless ambition of Mehmeh Ali. The refusal of that pasha in 1832 to withdraw his troops from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a>, which his son Ibrahim had conquered in the preceding year, furnished Mahmud with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRETEXT">pretext</a> for war. Accordingly, he commenced hostilities, but, with his usual ill fortune, was defeated by Ibrahim at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HEMS">Hems</a> and Kouiah, and was only saved from total <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HUMILIATION">humiliation</a> by the intervention of a Russian army. The result of this mediation was the treaty of Unkari Skelesi, in which it was agreed that Russia should assist Turkey at any emergency with an armed force, and that Turkey in return should <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> the Dardanelles against all the foes of Russia. In 1834 another war between the sultan and Mehmeh Ali was prevented by the interference of the European powers. In the midst of all these distractions from abroad, Mahmud had completed the reorganization of his army, had constructed <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>, and had established postage <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> throughout the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. Ambassadors were also stationed at <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>; and women, for the first time, were allowed to appear in public. Still intent, however, upon taking vengeance upon Mehmeh Ali, he commenced hostilities in 1839, on the pretext of forcing that pasha to pay his arrears of tribute. His forces were defeated by Ibrahim near Nisibis; and he died on the 1st July 1839, before the news of the disaster reached Constantinople. He was succeeded by his eldest son, Abdul Mejid.

MAHOGANY

Pages 105-107

the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> of Swietenia Mahogani (Linnaeus); <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> Order, Cedrelaceae. The mahogany tree is a native of South <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUBA">Cuba</a>, St Domingo, Jamaica, and especially of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONDURAS">Honduras</a>, and is one of the most magnificent and valuable of tropical timber trees. It grows rapidly, yet its timber is very hard and heavy; its height is from 80 to 100 feet, with usually a very straight stem of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> diameter. It is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> imported in logs from 2 to 3 feet <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, of various lengths, not often exceeding 18 feet. That called Spanish mahogany is usually smaller, the logs being generally about 2 feet square by about 10 feet in length. The grain, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> curl, as it is called, is sometimes so exceedingly beautiful that it raises the value of a log to an extraordinary price. More than L1,000 has been realized several times by the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of a single log. Mahogany was introduced into England in 1595. By some the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DIS">dis</a>- Mahomet. covery of its value is attributed to the carpenter of Sir Walter Raleigh's ship; and another account states that it was first employed for cabinet-<a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> in England in 1720, by one Wollaston, a cabinet-maker in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, who being accidentally requested to make some small <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> from this wood for Dr Gibbons, a physician in that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, discovered its rare properties, which, on being made public, soon rendered both the workman and the material highly famous. It is chiefly imported from Honduras and Cuba. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> imports of the last five years are 38,000 tons, worth about £500,000. MAHOMET I., son of Bayazid I., was originally governor of the town and district of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMASIA">Amasia</a>, and, after the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his elder brothers, became <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SULTAN">Sultan</a> of the Ottomans, A.D. 1413. He restored the Ottoman empire, extended his conquests into Bosnia, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SERVIA">Servia</a>, and Wallachia in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and, after a reign of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> years, died A.D. 1421. MAHOMET II., Sultan of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ADRIANOPLE">Adrianople</a> in 1430, and succeeded his father, Amurat II., in 1451. Bent upon overturning the Greek empire, he broke the truce that subsisted between the Turks and the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">Emperor</a> Constantine, and in April 1453 besieged Constantinople with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> fleet and an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of 300,000 men. The Greeks, though only 10,000 strong, barricaded the mouth of their harbour with strong <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> chains, and offered a determined resistance. The emperor himself was slain, fighting <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAND">hand</a> to hand with the besiegers. At last, however, by conveying a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his fleet overland into the harbour, and by mounting a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> of boats with cannon, Mahomet was able, after a siege of fifty-three days, to storm the city on the 29th May. Three days devoted by his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> to massacre and pillage, rendered Constantinople desolate, and seemed to defeat Mahomet's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of making it his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>. Nevertheless, by granting to the Greeks <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> toleration and the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of one-half of the churches that had survived the sack, he induced many of them to re-inhabit the city. He also restored its fortifications, and erected at the mouth of the Hellespont the forts called the Dardanelles. In 1456 Mahomet, advancing westward, laid siege to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BELGRADE">Belgrade</a>, but was defeated and forced to retreat by John Hunnades, general to Ladislav, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KING">King</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a>. More successful in his invasion of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>, he subdued Corinth and the Morea. In 1461 he captured Trebizond, and thus overthrew the dynasty of the Comneni. The <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> of the Archipelago were added to his conquests in the following year. The Albanians, under their king <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SCANDERBEG">Scanderbeg</a>, had for some <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> successfully checked the advance of the Turks; but after the death of that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> in 1466, they too were subdued. From the republic of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> Mahomet wrested <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NEGROPONT">Negropont</a> in 1470. After taking the Crimea in 1475, he invaded <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> in 1480. No sooner, however, had he captured <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-OTRANTO">Otranto</a> than he received the news that part of his forces had been foiled in their attempt to take <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a>, by the knights who had fled thither after the sack of Constantinople. While he was preparing to retrieve that defeat he died in 1481. He was buried at Constantinople, and over his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> was written the following epitaph:—"I would have taken Rhodes and subdued Italy." MAHOMET III. began his reign in 1595, as the successor of Mourad III., by putting to death all his brothers. He gave himself up to idleness and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a>, and before he could be roused from his sloth his troops were beaten in Hungary and elsewhere. He set out for that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> with a large force, but after a few trifling successes, returned again to his capital, leaving his generals to prosecute the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a>. He died in 1603, while revolt raged in his Asiatic provinces, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MUTINY">mutiny</a> in his capital. MAHOMET IV., Sultan of Turkey, was born in 1642, and succeeded his father Ibrahim I. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> exploits of his reign were those of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> viziers Kuperli and his son Achmet. The Turks were defeated by the Hungarians at St Gotthard, in 1664, by General Montecuccoli. The war with the Venetians, begun in 1645, was ended in 1669, when the town of Candia, after a siege of two years, capitulated to Achmet Kuperli. Encouraged by the internal <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DISCORD">discord</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POLAND">Poland</a> under King Michael, the Turks successfully invaded that country in 1672; but in 1673 were routed by the famous John Sobieski, driven south of the Danube, and forced to sign a disadvantageous peace. In 1683 a horde of 200,000 men, under the grand vizier Kara Mustapha, marched westward, and encamped in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a>. After a siege of six weeks, all hope of relief had been abandoned, when Sobieski, now King of Poland, attacked the Turkish forces, drove them from their entrenchments, and cut them to pieces. This was the first of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of disasters that ended, in 1687, in an insurrection of the Janissaries, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPOSITION">deposition</a> of Mahomet IV. He died in prison in 1691. MAHOMETANISM. See MOHAMMEDANISM. <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MAHRATTAS">MAHRATTAS</a>. The Mahratta state comprehended a country in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HINDUSTAN">Hindustan</a>, very extensive, and of great natural strength, being interspersed with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, defiles, and fortresses, and well adapted for defensive war. It extended across the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a>, and, generally speaking, was in possession of the peishwa, Nagpoor Rajah, Scindia, Holkar, Guicowar, and other inferior chiefs. The Mahrattas were not originally a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> tribe, like the Rajputs; nor do they possess the same <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRACE">grace</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of person, being of a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> stature and badly made, and having more the character of freebooters than of soldiers. Their original country is said to have included Khandesh <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BAGLANA">Baglana</a> and part of Berar, and to have extended N.W. as far as the Nerbuddah River. Others, again, say that they are foreigners who came into India from the western parts of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> about 1200 years ago. Little is known of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the Mahratta people till about the middle of the seventeenth century, when they possessed a narrow tract of country on the western side of the peninsula, extending from N. Lat. 15. to 21. The founder of the Mahratta state, or at least the first person who raised this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-NATION">nation</a> from obscurity, was Sevajee, who was born about the year 1626, and died in 1680, and who claimed a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a>, but upon very doubtful grounds, from the rajas of Odeypoor. The father of Sevajee, named Sahoo Bhosila, or Bhoola, was an officer in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the last Muhammadan king of Bejaapoor or Visiapoor. The Mahratta country was originally divided amongst a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of principalities, ruled by independent chiefs, who at length acknowledged one leader, Sevajee. He was succeeded by his son Sambajee, who extended his conquests, but who was finally taken prisoner by Aurungzebe in 1689, and put to death. His son Saho, at the time of his father's death, was an infant and a captive. Saho was eventually liberated on the death of Aurungzebe, but found the succession contested by his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUSIN">cousin</a>, as stated in the article <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLAPOOR">COLAPOOR</a>. His power was usurped by the two chief officers of the state, the peishwa or prime minister Balajee, and the paymaster-general Ragoejee, who divided the empire between them. The former fixed his residence at Poona; the latter founded a new <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> at Nagpoor, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Gondwaneeh. Bajeerow, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> peishwa, died in 1759, and was succeeded by his son Ballajeeerow. In 1760 the Mahrattas had extended their conquests as far as the city of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DELHI">Delhi</a>, when a formidable rival appeared in Ahmed Shah Abdalli, the sovereign of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AFGHANISTAN">Afghanistan</a>, to dispute with them the empire of India. With the Afghans was fought, on the 7th of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1761, the great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of Paniput, in which the Mahrattas were speedily overthrown, with the loss of a great number of their chiefs. From this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> their power began to decline. Ballajeeerow died soon after the battle of Paniput, and was succeeded by his son Madhoorow, who died in 1772, and was succeeded by his son Narainrow, who was murdered the following year by his uncle Ragobah, who was opposed in his designs on the throne by a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of twelve chiefs. At the head of these was Ballajee Pundit, who became <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEWAN">dewan</a> or prime minister to the infant prince. Ragobah fled to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BOMBAY">Bombay</a>, where he solicited and obtained, by means of an advantageous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a>, the aid of the British <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>. But this aid was ineffectual in seating the murderer upon the Mahatta throne. His crime had brought upon him the general obloquy of the nation; and his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> to foreign aid united against him the whole confederate chiefs of the Mahatta empire. By the interference of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a> government, a treaty was concluded; but in 1777 the Bombay government again espoused the cause of Ragobah, and a war ensued which was terminated by a disgraceful convention, and Ragobah abandoned. A general war afterwards took <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> between the British and the Mahattas, and was terminated by a treaty in 1782, by which every conquest was restored, except the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of Salsette. At this period the Mahattas commenced hostile operations against all those independent states which lay between their territories and those of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a>; and in the course of six or <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years they were all subdued, by which the Mahatta frontier bordered with the British dominions. In 1785 they carried on an unsuccessful war with Tipper, and were obliged to purchase peace by the cession of several valuable provinces, all of which they recovered by their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> with the British in 1790. The posthumous and infant son of Madhurrow, who succeeded to the peishwship when he came to maturity, died in 1795, and the two sons of Ragobah contended for the office. The cause of the eldest <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>, named Bajeerow, was espoused by Scindia, by whose aid he was fixed on the throne; but he was permitted to enjoy nothing of the sovereignty but the name. In the year 1802 the united armies of the peishwa and Scindia were defeated by Holkar; and the former having taken refuge in the territory of the British, was, by their aid, reinstated on the throne, agreeing, in return, to a treaty offensive and defensive, and to receive into his pay a force of 6000 infantry, with the usual proportion of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a> attached, for the payment of which he assessed districts in the southern <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of the country. From this period the peishwa, murmuring under his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGRADATION">degradation</a> into a state of dependence, cherished schemes of hostility against the British. The first overt <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACT">act</a> of hostility was the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> of the Guicowar's <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a>, through the agency of his ambassador Trimbuckjee. But his intrigues and schemes being discovered, he vowed the strictest fidelity in future; and in 1815 he delivered up his prime minister to the British. He soon contrived, however, to escape to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Poonah; and the peishwa, no longer dissembling, joined the confederacy which had at that time been formed amongst the native princes of India, namely, Scindia, Ameer Khan, Holkar, and the Berar Rajah, for the destruction of the British power. But this confederacy was signally overthrown; the peishwa's armies were entirely routed; and he, reduced to the character of a wandering fugitive, at last surrendered himself a prisoner to Sir John Malcolm, on condition of an allowance being assigned him. It was now resolved by the Anglo-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> government to abolish the authority and the name of the peishwa, which had become a rallying point for the disaffected, and to occupy the whole of the Poonah dominions for the British nation, with the reservation of certain territories for the Satarah family. Thus was extinguished not only the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> influence, but the name and authority, of the Mahatta state.

MAI

Pages 107-108

ANGELO, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a> of the Roman <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a>, was born 7th <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1782, at Schilpario, a village of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BERGAMO">Bergamo</a>, in the Milanese territory. His parents were of the humblest <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PEASANT">peasant</a> class; and he was placed, along with the other boys of the village, at the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> school, for the purpose of being initiated in the usual branches of elementary <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>. At this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a>, however, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the recent suppression of the Jesuit <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DISPERSION">dispersion</a> of its members, a considerable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of ex-Jesuit priests were employed in the ordinary duties of the mission throughout <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. One of these, Father <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> Mozzi dei Capitani, a Milanese, who resided near Schilpario, was early struck by the remarkable abilities of Angelo Mai, and himself undertook to instruct him in Latin, Greek, and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>. About this time the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of Parma permitted the Jesuits to re-establish themselves at Colorno, in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of Parma; and Mai, who was then about seventeen, accompanied his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>, Father Mozzi, to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> there opened; and with four youths of his native village, entered the novitiate of the society in 1799. He completed the novitiate in 1801, but remained at Colorno until 1804, when the society was more solemnly (though still only provisionally) re-established in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>. To the college there founded Mai was sent as professor of Greek and Latin; but after somewhat more than a year and a half, he was transferred to Rome, when he completed his theological studies. Thence he was removed to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-ORVIETO">Orvieto</a>, where the bishop, M. Lambruschini, had invited the Jesuits to open a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. At Orvieto he was promoted to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>'s orders; and remained partly engaged in teaching, partly in prosecuting his private studies, till 1808, when he was recalled to Rome. In that year, however, on the occupation of the Papal States by the French, an order was issued by the viceroy of Italy, requiring all natives of the kingdom of Italy to return to their respective provinces, and Mai was obliged to repair to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>. As the Society was still unrecognised in the kingdom of Italy, Mai was compelled to seek for other occupation, and assumed the functions of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SECULAR">secular</a> priest. After a time, through the influence of his first protector, Padre Mozzi, he was named an associate of the Ambrosian College, and soon afterwards a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of the Ambrosian Library. It is to his connection with this library that he is mainly indebted for his literary reputation. Next to the unrivalled collection of the Vatican, the MS. treasures of the Ambrosian Library have <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> been celebrated in Italy for their number and importance. Enriched by contributions from the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a> of Bobbio, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LUCCA">Lucca</a>, Monte Cassino, and other <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> monasteries, the Ambrosian collection is now the depository of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> proportion of the literary treasures of the learned <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-BENEDICTINES">Benedictines</a> of Italy; and although many of its MSS. had already been published <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> collated by the industrious editors of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, yet at the time when Mai was enrolled as an associate, it still contained enough to stimulate his curiosity and to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> his learning. He had early acquired a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for this branch of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> under his first masters in the Jesuit Society, among whom were two learned Spanish fathers of some reputation in that department; and he now devoted a considerable time to a careful exploration of the Ambrosian MSS. His first publication was a Latin translation (accompanied by a critical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMENTARY">commentary</a>) of the recently discovered <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> of Isaacus, De Permutatiorum; but he speedily relinquished the more beaten track of an ordinary editor or translator, and devoted himself to the then almost unknown department of palimpsest; or re-written MSS.—a class in which the Ambrosian Library is peculiarly rich. Up to this time but two or three palimpsest fragments had been deciphered and made public. In the course of a few years Mai was enabled to print two volumes of meditated fragments of Cicero's Orations, some orations of Lysimachus and Isaeus, an interesting fragment of Plautus's lost <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a> the Vidularia, and, above all, a large collection of the letters and other writings of Cornelius Fronto, the preceptor of Marcus Aurelius. The MS. from which these relics of Fronto were recovered had formerly belonged to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> of Bobbio, and was a translation of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Acts of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNCIL">Council</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHALCEDON">Chalcedon</a>, written upon a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of palimpsest leaves, made up partly of an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> MS. of Pliny the Younger, partly of an old commentator on Cicero, partly of some of the works of Lysimachus, and partly of letters of Fronto addressed to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ANTONINUS_PIUS">Antoninus Pius</a>, Marcus Aurelius, Lucius Verus, and other friends,—all in a very disordered and mutilated condition, but yet sufficiently perfect to excite the curiosity of the learned throughout <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. The most interesting circumstance, however, of the discovery is, that when Mai, some years later, was removed to the Vatican Library, he had the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> to find the remainder of this very palimpsest translation of the Acts of Chalcedon, the counterpart of the Ambrosian palimpsest, containing above a hundred additional letters of the same correspondence. Meanwhile, the Jesuit Society had been formally revived by Pope Pius VII. on his restoration in 1814. But the services of Mai in his new position were so highly appreciated that, as he had never taken the solemn vows of the Order, he was induced to remain a member of the secular clergy. In 1819 he was invited to Rome to fill the office of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> keeper of the Vatican Library. Soon after his installation in this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> and congenial office, he discovered that a MS. of St Augustine's Enarrationes in Psalmos was a palimpsest, the original of which had been no other than the long-sought work of Cicero De Republica. The commentary itself, unfortunately, was imperfect. It extended only from the 119th to the 140th psalm (the commentary on the ten remaining psalms being deficient); and even in the portion which remained there were gaps to the amount of sixty-four <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-PAGES">pages</a>. Nevertheless, the skill and ingenuity of Mai recovered from these confused and obliterated fragments about one-fourth of the entire work, with which he interwove, in the edition which he published (Rome 1822), all the existing fragments of the original, collected from the numberless writers, sacred and profane, through whose writings they are scattered. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of the pope, however, in appointing Mai to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of the Vatican Library had been to engage him in a formal and systematic exploration of its contents, with a view to the publication of the most important remains of classical literature which still remain locked up in that great <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a>-house. Mai, extending the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, resolved to comprise in his collections the unpublished sacred as well as profane remains of the Vatican MSS., and, leaving to future scholars the task of critically editing, commenting, and translating, to secure for the world, in miscellaneous Collectanea similar to those of Muratori, Mabillon, Montfaucon, and their fellow-labourers, all that was really important among its edited MSS. in every department of literature. On this plan he commenced, in 1825, a magnificent 4to publication,—Scriptorum Veterum Nova Collectio et Vaticanis Codicibus Editæ,—which extended to 10 volumes, and comprises a vast number of unpublished remains of the Greek and Latin writers, sacred and profane. Several of the volumes are occupied with patristical remains. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, which is almost entirely from a palimpsest source, contains an immense number of fragments of the lost books of the historians,—Polybius, Diodorus Siculus, Dionysius of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HALICARNASSUS">Halicarnassus</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DION">Dion</a>, Appian, and others, even so late as Dexippus and Eumarius. In 1833 M. Mai was transferred from the office of Vatican librarian (in which he was succeeded by the celebrated linguist Mezzofanti) to that of secretary of the Propaganda; but he still <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> his literary labours. He followed up the Vaticana Collectio by another collection in 8vo, equally miscellaneous, and indeed entirely similar in plan,—Classici Auctores et Codicibus Vaticanis Editi, 10 vols. 8vo Malano (1828–35). In the year in which this work was brought to a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> he was elevated to the cardinalate, and soon afterwards was named prefect of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONGREGATION">Congregation</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>, and of that of the Council of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a>, and eventually cardinal librarian of the Roman church. The Classici Auctores was succeeded by a similar miscellany, but containing a larger amount of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, Speciellum Romanum, 10 vols. 8vo (1839–44). This collection, besides Greek and Latin writers, comprises also a few interesting Italian works, chiefly historical and biographical. His last publication was in 4to, Nova Patrum Bibliotheca (6 vols. 1845–53). It is almost exclusively patristical, and contains many highly important works, forming an indispensable supplement to almost all the existing patristical collections. Cardinal Mai had also undertaken to edit the celebrated Biblical Codex Vaticanus, and actually printed the text at the Propaganda press. He delayed its publication, however, with the intention of prefixing to the text an elaborate critical and historical introduction; but to the infinite disappointment of the learned, he died, leaving this great work incomplete, and indeed does not even appear to have made any progress in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> for it. Since his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, which occurred in his seventy-fourth year, at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALBANO">Albano</a>, September 8, 1854, no trace of the expected biblical dissertations has been discovered. It is highly probable that the anxious and unsettled condition of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> affairs at Rome during the years preceding his death, deprived him of the leisure or the spirit necessary for so laborious an undertaking. From the very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of Cardinal Mai's collections it <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> be understood, that in very many of the works which he printed he contented himself with the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> rough work of publication. But in those which he undertook to edit critically, and especially in the De Republica, he appears as a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASTER">master</a> in the art. Even those works the text of which alone he printed, are accompanied by learned and judicious prefaces, which exhibit an amount of erudition such as few <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> scholars can claim. His library was one of the most complete private collections in Rome. At his death he directed that it should be offered at half its estimated value to the Vatican Library, and that the proceeds of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALE">sale</a> should be applied to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> of his native village of Schilipario.

MAI-MAITCHIN

Pages 110-110

MAI-MAITCHIN. See KIACHT.

MAIANO

Pages 108-108

Benedetto da, an eminent sculptor and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a> in 1424. He first became known as an inlayer of wood, and in this capacity he was employed at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KING">King</a> Alphonso, and afterwards in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-HUNGARY">Hungary</a> by King Matthias Corvinus. Ambitious, however, to excel in a nobler art, he turned his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>, and returning shortly after to Florence, he was employed by the magistrates of that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of their audience chamber. While sojourning for a short <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> in Naples, he executed a bas-relief in marble of the Annunciation. On his return to Florence, Maiano commenced one of his masterpieces, the marble pulpit of Santa Croce, ornamented with sculptured representations of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of San Francesco. He was next employed in constructing the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of the Palazzo Strozzi. <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TURNING">Turning</a> his attention about this time to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, he built, in addition to other structures, the portico of Madonna della Grazie, near <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AREZZO">Arezzo</a>. After amassing a considerable fortune, Maiano died in 1498, and was buried in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of San Lorenzo in Florence.

MAIDA

Pages 108-108

a small town of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a> Ultra II., 8 miles S. of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NICASTRO">Nicastro</a>, and chiefly famous on account of a victory gained here by the English over a superior French force on 4th <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1806. Pop. about 3000.

MAIDENHEAD

Pages 109-109

MAIDENHEAD, a municipal borough and market-town of England, county of Berks, on the S. bank of the Thames, 14 miles N.E. by E. of Reading, 22½ miles W. of London. It consists of one street about a mile long, well paved, and lighted with gas. The town has a guildhall, which is a fine building; a chapel of ease; places of worship belonging to the Baptists and Wesleyan Methodists; a national school; and several charitable institutions. The manufactures are unimportant; but the wealth of the surrounding country, and the position of the town on the high road between London and Oxford, render it a place of considerable trade, the principal articles of which are meal, malt, and timber. The market is held on Wednesday, and there are also three annual fairs. The neighbourhood is highly cultivated, and is studded with gentlemen's seats and villas. The high road here crosses the river by a fine stone bridge, and the Great Western Railway by a very elegant one of brick. The borough received its first charter from Edward III., and it is governed by a mayor, four aldermen, and twelve councillors. Pop. (1851) 3607.

MAIDSTONE

Pages 109-109

MAIDSTONE, the county town of Kent, and a municipal and parliamentary borough, stands on a gentle slope on the right bank of the Medway, 34 miles E.S.E. from London. It was anciently called Caer Megaid, or Medwig (the City of the Medway); and afterwards, by the Saxons, Medwegestan and Medlestone, whence it acquired its present name. It was formerly in the possession of the archbishops of Canterbury; and their Gothic palace, dating from 1348, is still standing, though considerably altered from its ancient form. In the civil war Maidstone was taken by the parliamentary forces under Fairfax in 1648. A college was founded here by Archbishop Courtenay in the time of Richard II., but was suppressed about the time of the Reformation. Maidstone has always returned two members to Parliament since the time of Edward VI., from whom, and from various succeeding monarchs down to George II., it received charters. The town consists of four main streets, meeting in the market-place, together with several smaller ones. The sloping character of the ground on which it is built keeps the town clean and dry, and it is well supplied with water from the Medway. Of the public buildings, the chief is the parish church, built in the fourteenth century, and reckoned one of the largest edifices of the kind in England. It has recently been restored in a very splendid style. There are, besides, various other places of worship for different denominations. It has also a county hall, an extensive gaol, erected lately at the cost of L200,000, and covering 13 acres, a town-hall, a corn exchange, a theatre, ball-rooms, and other buildings. There is a school called All Saints College, founded in 1846, occupying a portion of the buildings of the college which formerly existed here; also a free grammar school, a Blue-coat and a Brown-coat school for clothing and educating poor children, national schools, &c. The only manufacture for which Maidstone is remarkable is that of paper, of which there are a number of mills in the neighbourhood. The surrounding country is extremely beautiful, by reason of its orchards and hop gardens; and the circumstance which has contributed most to the prosperity of the town is the fertility of the neighbourhood. The river is here crossed by an old bridge of seven arches, and is navigable for vessels of sixty tons up to the town. Maidstone is connected with London by a branch of the South-Eastern Railway, by which route the distance is 56 miles. Market-days, Thursday and Saturday. The borough is governed by a mayor, six aldermen, and eighteen councillors. Pop. (1851) 20,801.

MAILLA, JOSEPH-ANNE-MARIE DE MOYRIAC DE

Pages 109-110

MAILLA, JOSEPH-ANNE-MARIE DE MOYRIAC DE, a learned Jesuit, was born in Bugey, on the borders of Savoy, and appointed a missionary to China, whither he proceeded in 1703. At the age of twenty-eight he had acquired such skill in the characters, arts, sciences, mythology, and ancient books of the Chinese, as to astonish even the learned men of the celestial empire. Besides constructing maps of China, Chinese Tartary, and the Chinese provinces, Mailla also translated the Great Annals of China into French, and his MS. was transmitted to France in the year 1737. This work was published in 1737 in 13 volumes quarto, and is the first complete history of that extensive empire. Mailla died at Pekin on the 28th of June 1748, in the seventy-ninth year of his age.

MAIMBOURG, LOUIS

Pages 110-110

MAIMBOURG, Louis, a celebrated Jesuit, descended from a noble family, was born at Nancy in 1610. At the age of sixteen he entered the Society of Jesus, and was sent to Rome to study theology. On his return to France, he became a classical teacher in the college of Rouen; but afterwards devoted himself to preaching, and occupied in turn the principal pulpits in the kingdom. Not until Maimbourg had reached the middle stage of life did lie produce any of those historical works upon which his fame rests. In 1682 he appeared as a bold defender of the liberties of the Gallican church in his Traité Historique de l'Église de Rome, a treatise which caused the immediate expulsion of its author from the Order of the Jesuits by the command of Pope Innocent XI. As a compensation, however, for this misfortune, Maimbourg was presented by Louis XIV. with a pension, and with the abbey of St Victor at Paris as a place of retirement. He died there of apoplexy on the 13th August 1686, leaving unfinished his Histoire du Schisme d'Angleterre. A collection of Maimbourg's histories, published in 14 vols., Paris, 1686–87, includes, besides the work mentioned above,—Histoire de l'Arianisme, Histoire des Iconoclastes, Histoire du Schisme des Grecs, Histoire des Croisades, Histoire de la Décadence de l'Empire, Histoire du Grand Schisme d'Occident, Histoire du Luthéranisme, Histoire du Calvinisme, Histoire de la Ligue, Histoire du Pontificat de Saint Grégoire le Grand, et Histoire du Pontificat de Saint Léon. Although once in great repute, Maimbourg, as a historian, has no longer any authority; yet Voltaire, a critic by no means guilty of partiality to churchmen, says that Maimbourg "was formerly in too great vogue, and has been latterly in too great neglect."

MAIMONIDES, or BEN MAIMON MOSES

Pages 110-110

MAIMONIDES, or BEN MAIMON MOSES, a celebrated Jewish rabbi, was born at Cordova in Spain, probably about 1131. After receiving the elements of his education from his father, he studied philosophy and medicine under the learned Arabians Thophail and Averroes. He also pursued with avidity the ancient philosophers, especially Aristotle, and thus incurred the dislike and suspicion of his Jewish brethren. Soon after this he repaired to Egypt; and from remaining there during the rest of his life, he acquired the title of Moses Ægyptius. There he at first followed the vocation of a jeweller; but resorting afterwards to the practice of medicine, he became so eminent in this profession, that he was appointed chief physician to the Sultan Saladin. While holding this office, Maimonides is said to have also taught with great success in a school which he had founded. He died in Egypt at an advanced age. In addition to a thorough knowledge of philosophy and medicine, Maimonides possessed an acquaintance with mathematics, theology, and the jurisprudence of the Jews. He knew several languages, and wrote Arabic and Hebrew with facility. By his Jewish admirers he was surmamed "The Eagle of the Doctors," and "The Lamp of Israel." Of his numerous works three are chiefly notable. His "Moreh Nevuchim (Teacher of the Perplexed)", written originally in Arabic, but afterwards translated into Hebrew, is an exposition of the obscure words, allusions, types, and allegories in Scripture. A translation into Latin by the younger Buxtorf, 4to, Basel, 1629, has been retranslated into English by Dr Townshend, London, 1827. The original Arabic, accompanied with a French translation, has been published under the title, Le Guide des Egarés, traité de Théologie publié en Arabe avec Traduction et Notes par S. Munk, 8vo, Paris, 1856. The Arabic text of the Moreh Nevuchim exists in the Bodleian Library, Oxford. In Yad Hazakah ("The Strong Hand"), written in good Hebrew, Maimonides gives a digest of the Talmud, stripped of all its rabbinical fables. The best edition of this work is that in 4 vols. folio, Amsterdam, 1702. His Perush Ha-Mishna ("Commentary on the Mishna"), originally written in Arabic, has been often translated into Hebrew by different rabbis, and printed along with the Mishna. Part of this work, in the original Arabic, was published by Pococke, Oxford, 1655. MSS. of the works of Maimonides are found in the great libraries of Paris, Berlin, &c.

MAIN, MAINE, or MAYN

Pages 110-110

MAIN, MAINE, or MAYN (the ancient Moras), formed by the union in North Bavaria, about 14 miles N.W. of Bayreuth, of two streams, the Red and White Main, which have their sources in the Fichtelgebirge. It has a very irregular and winding course in a direction generally westerly, and falls into the Rhine nearly opposite to Mentz. It is about 280 miles in length, and is navigable as far as its junction with the Regnitz, near Bamberg, about 240 miles from its mouth. As early as 793 Charlemagne had projected the formation of a canal between the Alt-mühl and the Pegnitz, an affluent of the Regnitz, and so connecting the Main and the Danube; but it is only very recently that this has been effected. The chief tributaries of the Mayn are,—the Regnitz, Tauber, Mümling, and Geraprenz from the S., and the Rodach, Saale, Kinzig and Nidda from the N. The principal towns on or near its banks are Bayreuth, Bamberg, Würzburg, Aschaffenburg, Hanau, Offenbach, and Frankfort.

MAINE

Pages 323-324

a department of France, situated between 48. 28. and 49. 23. N. Lat., 3. 25. and 5. E. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>., and bounded on the N. by the departments of Aisne and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARDENNES">Ardennes</a>, E. by those of Meuse and Haute-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARNE">Marne</a>, S. by that of Aube, and W. by those of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a>-et-Marne and Aisne. The department, which has an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> of 3158 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles, consists of a bare plain, sloping from E. to W., with a few scattered hills, which do not rise higher than 1200 feet. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> consists of a thin layer of sand lying upon chalk, except in the W. and N.W. borders, and along the valley of the Marne, where the soil is rich and good. It is separated into two nearly equal parts by the River Marne, from which it takes its name; and is watered also by the Marne. Aisne in the N.E.; by its tributaries the Suippe and the Vesle in the N. and N.W.; and by the Aube and the Seine in the S., the latter of which merely touches it for a very short distance. Marne enjoys a temperate <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> and a pure <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>, although in the low and marshy tracts on the borders of the department fogs are very frequent. Cultivation is far advanced, and in a thriving condition. There are 500,000 acres of ploughed <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a>, 193,000 of woods and forests, 189,000 of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MEADOW">meadow</a> land, 45,000 of vineyards, &c. Corn is grown to a considerable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, especially oats and rye, which are more than sufficient for the supply of the wants of the department. Fruit trees are also numerous in Marne, and a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the department is covered with forests. But the most fruitful branch of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a> in this district, and that on which most care is bestowed, is the cultivation of the vine, for Marne occupies a part of the old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Champagne, so well known for the wines to which it has given name. This department produces annually about 15,400,000 gallons of wine. Many sheep are raised in Marne, and their breed has been much improved by crossing with the Merino and English breeds. The horned cattle and horses are small in size. Bees and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> fowls are kept in great numbers in the department. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> mineral productions are,—<a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">limestone</a>, chalk, flint, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MILLSTONES">millstones</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, clay of various sorts. The department is famous for the manufacture of woollen and other tissues, which centre chiefly at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RHEIMS">Rheims</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of trade are wines, together with corn, flour, brandy, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HIDES">hides</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, and the produce of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>. The department is crossed by the railway from <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-STRASBOURG">Strasbourg</a>, which enters Marne at Dormans, and leaves it at Sermazie, after a course of 68 miles.
