The borough received its first <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> in 1205. It is governed by a mayor, four aldermen, and twelve councillors; and it sends two members to Parliament. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARKETS">Markets</a> are held on Saturday, and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> three times a-year. Pop. of the municipal borough (1851), 3689; of the parliamentary borough, 5155.

MARLOW

Pages 321-321
GREAT, a municipal and parliamentary borough of England, county of Buckingham, on the north bank of the Thames, 23 miles S. by E. of Aylesbury, and 31 W. by N. of London. The town consists of two principal streets at right angles to each other, and meeting in a large square, besides several smaller ones. The principal buildings are the town-hall, and the parish church, opened in 1836, and surmounted by a lofty spire. There are also places of worship for Wesleyan Methodists, Independents, Baptists, and Roman Catholics; national schools; charity schools; and other benevolent institutions. The river is here crossed by a handsome suspension bridge, with a span of 75 yards. The town possesses paper-mills and breweries; and the trade, which is considerable, consists chiefly of corn, coals, and timber. The markets have been discontinued; but large fairs are held here for horses and cattle; and there are races in August. Marlow returns two members to Parliament. Pop. of the municipal borough (1851) 4485; of the parliamentary borough (1851) 5523.

MARLOWE

Pages 321-321

CHRISTOPHER, the "<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KIT">Kit</a> Marlowe" of Elizabethan wits and poets, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a> in 1564. His birth is registered under the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> of February 26, so that he was not two months older than his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> in the drama, Shakspeare. Marlowe's father was a shoemaker, but he had <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> enough to obtain for his son admission into <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KING">King</a>'s School, Canterbury, which insured him five years' liberal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> and a sum of L4 per annum, equal to L20 of our present <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MONEY">money</a>. He was entered as a pensioner of Bennet <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">College</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 17, 1581, and took his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of M.A. in 1587. Before this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> Marlowe had written the first <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his tragedy of Tamburlaine, which was attacked in 1587 by Greene and Nash as an attempt to "outbrave better pens with the swelling <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOMBAST">bombast</a> of blank <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>." In the prologue to his play Marlowe had challenged <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to his innovation: "From jigging veins of rhyming mother-<a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, And such conceits as clownage keeps in pay, We'll <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> you to the stately <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-TENT">tent</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a>, Where thou shalt hear the Scythian Tamburlaine Threatening the world with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> astounding terms." Marlowe kept his word with the audience. The tragedy is full of extravagant scenes in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SCYTHIA">Scythia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MOROCCO">Morocco</a>, &c., in which Tamburlaine is drawn in a chariot to which captive kings are harnessed, and even <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> is represented as afraid to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACE">face</a> the conqueror! There is great power of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, and some gorgeous local <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, in the drama, and its success was unprecedented. A <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> part was soon produced, and both were printed in 1590. Tamburlaine was followed by the Tragical <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a> and Death of Dr Faustus, the Massacre at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, the Rich Jew of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a>, and the Troublesome Reign and Lamentable Death of Edward the Second. Marlowe also aided Nash in another tragedy, Dido <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>. Besides his plays, all of which were highly successful, Marlowe translated part of the poem of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HERO">Hero</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEANDER">Leander</a>, from Musaeus (afterwards completed by Chapman), the first book of Lucrece, and Ovid's Elegies,—the last in so licentious a style that it was burned by order of the Archbishop of Canterbury. The beautiful little pastoral song, "Come live with me, and be my <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOVE">love</a>," quoted in Izaak Walton's Angler, was also of Marlowe's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>. He had thus not only the tragic pomp and "mighty line" of the dramatic muse, but the gentler graces of the poet and lover of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. His <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> strength, however, consisted in depicting the passions—in awakening terror, pity, grief, and remorse, which, before his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, were unknown to the English stage. The latter scenes of Faustus, and the death-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of Edward II., are unsurpassed, even in Shakspeare, for their strong interest and sublimity. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">Passages</a> of fine poetical and rhetorical <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> also relieve his darker delineations of character and daring flights of imagination; and there is little doubt that, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> Marlowe had lived till his powers had been chastened and matured, Shakspeare might for once have found a rival. But Marlowe was wild and dissipated, entertaining atheistical opinions, according to his wretched associate in debauchery, Robert Greene, and numerous zealots; and he was cut off by a violent death when little more than twenty-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> years of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>. One Francis Archer, a serving-<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and rival in Marlowe's "lewd love," as Meres states, had invited him to a feast at <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPTFORD">Deptford</a>. A quarrel probably arose, for Marlowe attempted to stab his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOST">host</a> with his dagger, while the other seized him by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WRIST">wrist</a>, and turned the dagger so that it entered Marlowe's eye, and pierced him to the brain. He died shortly afterwards, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 16, 1593. It is usual to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TERM">term</a> Marlowe the precursor of Shakspeare. He had the priority in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of sonorous and energetic blank verse. They were, however, of the same age; and as the great dramatist had produced at least twelve of his original plays before 1598, it is <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> to infer that he had begun to write some time before Marlowe's death in 1593. He may have been engaged even as early as 1587, when Tamburlaine appeared, in adapting his historical dramas of Henry VI. and Richard III., and the Taming of the Shrew; all which are modelled so closely on the old plays that above 2000 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> have been appropriated entire by Shakspeare. Many passages in these old plays are also found in Marlowe's Edward II. Stage effect was then chiefly studied; the plays were produced to be acted, not read; and so many additions were made—at least to the inferior dramas—by subsequent writers engaged by the managers, that considerable uncertainty hangs over their literary history. That Shakspeare had at first "beautified" himself by "feathers" taken from Greene <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> Marlowe, or both, we have shown by extracts given in the life of Greene; but his style—the garb, as it were, of his unapproachable genius—was soon distinctly formed, and the characteristics of Marlowe are also manifest in his best plays. The individuality of either cannot be mistaken; and Marlowe, however inferior, has the striking merit of originality and command of the grander elements of tragedy.

MARMADE

Pages 321-322

a town of France, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of an arrondissement of the same name in the department of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">Lot</a>-et-Garonne, is pleasantly situated on the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the Garonne, which is here crossed by a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> with a single <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>, 30 miles N.W. of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGEN">Agen</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARMANDE">Marmande</a> has rather an antiquated appearance, many of the houses being <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>-framed; but it is at the same <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> neat, clean, and regular, and has several fine squares and public fountains. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> buildings are the town-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> chiefly carried on here are those of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a>, woollen stuffs, brandy, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>. The Garonne is navigable as far as Marmande, and the harbour is very good. The trade is very flourishing, and consists of corn, flour, wines, <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, &c. Marmande is an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> town. Having supported the cause of the Albigeois, it was taken after a disastrous siege, in 1219, by <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> VIII. and Amaury de <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MONTFORT">Montfort</a>, when most of its inhabitants were put to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>. It was afterwards besieged in 1577 by Henri IV. (Pop. (1851) 8257).

MARMONT

Pages 322-322

AUGUSTE FREDERIC <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOUIS">LOUIS</a> VIETTE DE, Duc de Raguse, Marshal of France, was born at Chatillon-sur-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a> on the 20th <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1774. At the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of fifteen he entered the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a> as sub-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a> of infantry, and in 1792 passed with the same <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RANK">rank</a> into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>. In the following year his skill and bravery before <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TOULON">Toulon</a> introduced him to the notice of Bonaparte, and laid the foundation of his fortunes. He was promoted to the rank of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> in 1794, and having entered the army of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a> in 1795, he showed <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> valour at the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLOCKADE">blockade</a> of Mayence. He then accompanied <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NAPOLEON">Napoleon</a> as his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> aide-de-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAMP">camp</a> in the Italian <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> of 1796; and by his brave and skilful conduct at Lodi, Castiglione, and Saint Georges, earned his promotion to the rank of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLONEL">colonel</a>, and the distinction of being sent to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> with the captured colours. His rise became more rapid amid the toils and perils of the Egyptian expedition in 1798. For the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> he acted during the capture of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a> he was created a general of brigade; and after he had distinguished himself at the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of the Pyramids, he was appointed commander of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>. He returned with Bonaparte to France in 1799, and was a zealous supporter of that general on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of the 18th Brumaire. Shortly after this he was appointed a councillor of state and commander-in-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the reserve of the artillery. In this latter capacity he superintended the famous crossing of the Great St Bernard in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> of 1800. His important share in the victory of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARENGO">Marengo</a>, which was gained in the following <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, raised him to the rank of a general of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>. Appointed commander of the army in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a> in 1806, Marmont defeated the Montenegrins, Greeks, and Russians, at Castel-Novo, and governed the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> with so much tact and success, that he received the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> de Raguse in 1808. In the following year he was summoned by Napoleon to assist in the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a> against <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, and won his marshal's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BATON">baton</a> on the battle-field of Wagram. The organization of the Illyrian provinces was a result of that decisive victory, and Marmont was appointed their governor. From this office he was called in 1811 to supersede Massena in the command of the army in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>. There his administration was characterized by his usual ability, but not by his usual success. He was defeated by <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WELLINGTON">Wellington</a> at the battle of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALAMANCA">Salamanca</a> in 1812, and escheched by wounds and fatigue, he was forced to return to Paris. Summoned into <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTION">action</a> once more in 1813, Marmont fought at Lutzen, Bautzen, and Wurtzen; and while covering the retreat of the French after the disastrous battle of Leipzig, he was again wounded. In 1814, with a comparatively small force, he resisted for several hours the entrance of the allies into Paris, and not until he was nearly overborne by the numbers of the enemy did he agree to evacuate the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. Yet so much odium did he incur on account of this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAPITULATION">capitulation</a>, that he was excepted by name from the general amnesty which Napoleon proclaimed on his return from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELBA">Elba</a>. Marmont accordingly retired to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AIX">Aix</a>-la-Chapelle during the Hundred Days, and did not return to Paris until after the battle of Waterloo. He was then nominated a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAJOR">major</a>-general of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>; and in 1817 he was commissioned as the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KING">king</a>'s lieutenant to allay an insurrection in Lyons. About this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> he retired into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and devoted himself to agricultural pursuits until 1825, when he was despatched as <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> extraordinary to congratulate Nicholas on his accession to the throne of Russia. During the Revolution he commanded, though very unwillingly, the king's troops. Having thus become the object of popular indignation, he was driven into exile on the expulsion of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> X., and his name was struck off from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIST">list</a> of marshals. He latterly devoted much <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> systems of different countries. Part of his information on this subject he published in his Esprit des Institutions Militaires, Paris, 1845. He died at <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> in 1852. Two volumes of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a>, written by himself, were lately published in Paris.

MARMONTEL

Pages 322-323

JEAN FRANCOIS, a celebrated French writer, was born in 1723 at the picturesque village of Bort in the Limousin, in a family little removed above the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of peasantry. He owed the early <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> to private <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> and gratuitous public institutions. After studying at the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of the Jesuits at Clermont, he went to <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TOULOUSE">Toulouse</a>, where he delivered lectures in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> with considerable reputation, and gained an academical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a>. An accidental correspondence with Voltaire finally led to his departure for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1745, where he obtained the personal acquaintance of that highly popular writer, who at that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> extended the most friendly encouragement to all young men possessed of any talents for <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>. There Marmontel commenced his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAREER">career</a> of letters by gaining a prize for a poem on a subject proposed by the French Academy, La Gloire de <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. perpetuelle dans le Roi son Successeur. But in that <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> afforded the most ample field for the acquisition of wealth and eminence, and he accordingly next turned his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to theatrical <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>. His first tragedies, Dionysius and Aristomenes, obtained a flattering reception, but were soon forgotten; and his succeeding ones, Cleopatra, the Heraclides, and Numitor, had no success whatever. La harpe, who was a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> dramatic critic, condemns them all as bad, except the Heraclides, which he calls a tolerable tragedy of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> rank. In fact, Marmontel does not appear to have been endowed with any great talents for poetry <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> dramatic composition. His dramatic writings, however, gained for him at once both friends and fortune, and he found himself suddenly elevated from the verge of utter want, and at once plunged into all the bustling intrigue of the first literary circles, and into all the glare and dissipation of fashionable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>. His time was occupied with rehearsals, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOVE">love</a> intrigues, and parties of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>. By addressing flattering verses to the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KING">king</a>, and gaining the favour of other persons of influence, Marmontel obtained the situation of under-secretary of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> buildings. This employment fixed his residence at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-VERSAILLES">Versailles</a> for five years, during which time he contributed <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> to the Encyclopedie, which were afterwards printed together in alphabetical order, under the general <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Elements de Litterature. He afterwards commenced the Contes Moraux, written originally for the Mercure de France, which were subsequently collected and printed by themselves. Many of these tales, on which the fame of Marmontel principally, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not solely, rests, bear reference to the original idea with which they commence, being for the most part intended to expose some absurdity or extravagance of character. In most of them he displays a very happy <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> in the manners and in the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>; and it is only to be regretted that he has occasionally given too <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> Marmora, a colouring to conceptions of the most beautiful simplicity. As lively pictures of French manners, both simple and fashionable, they are admitted to be unrivalled. Having been suspected of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> a satire against some powerful nobleman, in the Mercure, of which he had now become the sole manager, he was, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, shut up for a few days in the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BASTILLE">Bastille</a>, and on his release deprived of his agreeable and lucrative situation. He next translated into prose the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHARSALIA">Pharsalia</a> of Lucan, and added to it a supplement, in which he details the events of Caesar's wars in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, and concludes with his last <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. His next publication was a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROMANCE">romance</a> called Bélisaire, which, on its first appearance in 1768, attracted universal attention, and involved the author in a dispute with the Sorbonne, who published a censure of it; which was opposed by the arguments of Turgot, and by the epigrams and squibs of Voltaire. He some time afterwards produced his Incas of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERU">Peru</a>, and, irritated as he was by the recent anathemas of the Sorbonne, his great object in this new romance was to show, that all the evils inflicted by the Spaniards on the Indians had their origin in that fanaticism which he was desirous to bring into still deeper detestation. In these latter works he unluckily abandoned the simplicity which charmed so much in his Moral Tales, for a tone too highly rhetorical and turgid. In 1763 Marmontel had been admitted, after considerable opposition, to the much-envied <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of a member of the French Academy, and in 1783 he succeeded D'Alembert as its perpetual secretary. The situation of historiographer of France, and the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> in the Lyceum, which he successively obtained, fully indemnified him for the loss of the Mercure. He was in the full enjoyment of affluent circumstances, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> felicity, and literary reputation, when the French Revolution suddenly changed the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>. During its alarming progress he led a retired <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, and though reduced to indigent circumstances, remained secure amidst all the violent events of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>. In 1797 he was chosen a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a> to the National <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASSEMBLY">Assembly</a> by the department of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EURE">Eure</a>, but he died soon afterwards, of an apoplectic attack, at his cottage near <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ABBEVILLE">Abbeville</a>, on the 31st <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> 1799. After his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> were published the Nouveaux Contes Moraux, 4 vols. 8vo, 1801; also a tolerable Histoire de la Régence du Due d'Orléans, 2 vols. 8vo, 1805; besides his Mémoires d'Une Perce, pour servir à l'Instruction de ses Enfants, 4 vols. 8vo, 1804,—perhaps the most attractive and amusing of all his writings,—containing, however, among many agreeable and happy sketches, much <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARADOX">paradox</a> and self-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a>; with a vast gallery of portraits of the most distinguished names of his time in France, ranging from Massillon to Mirabeau. Many of his pieces are of very doubtful morality.

MARMORA

Pages 323-323
Sea or, lies between European and Asiatic Turkey, between 40. 18. and 41. 5. N. Lat., 26. 40. and 30. 5. E. Long. It is 172 miles in length by 55 in breadth. At the east end it terminates in two long and narrow gulfs,—that of Izmid to the N., and that of Mudanich to the S. It communicates with the "xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">Black Sea at the N.E. by the Bosphorus or Straits of Constantinople, and with the Archipelago on the S.W. by the Dardanelles. The shores of the Sea of Marmora are beautiful in scenery and well cultivated; but those on the Asiatic side are bolder and more precipitous than those on the European. In some places the depth is very great; at a point 5 miles N. of Marmora Island no soundings have been obtained at 355 fathoms; and it is believed that in the centre the depth is very much greater. It is fed by several streams, of which the most important are the Karasu, Jatiçi, and Chortu from Europe, and the Salataderç, Gweimenshar, Mukhalitch, and Hyla from Asia. The navigation of the sea is safe, and not accompanied with much difficulty; and there are numerous good harbours on the northern shore and under the islands. This sea is not subject to tides; but a current runs through it from the Black Sea to the Mediterranean, varying in strength and swiftness at different seasons. The principal island, Marmora, which has given name to the sea, is celebrated for its marble quarries, from which in ancient times Cyzicus and other neighbouring cities, and in modern times Constantinople, have been supplied with building materials. The island of Marmora is occupied by a mountain range of no great height, and has a very barren appearance, although some wine is here produced. It is thinly inhabited, mostly by Greek Christians; and the town of Marmora, which stands on the S.W. coast, is chiefly built of wood. The island has a circumference of about 45 miles, and was anciently known by the names of Proconnesus or Elephoonenus, on account probably of the deer with which it was then stocked. The other islands are,—Rahi, Liman-Pasha, Papa or Kalolimano, and the group called Prince's Islands or Demonesi. The Sea of Marmora was called by the ancients Propontis, and was believed by them to lie due N. and S., so that the Dardanelles and the Bosphorus were placed on the same meridian.

MARMORICE

Pages 323-323
or Marmarás, a town of Anatolia, situated on the S.W. coast of Asia Minor, 27 miles N. of Rhodes. It is irregularly built, and the houses are mean; but it occupies a fine position at the head of a large bay. In the vicinity are the ruins of the ancient Physeus. The harbour is large and good, but the entrance is extremely narrow. The export trade is considerable in timber, honey, turpentine, wax, &c. At the mouth of the bay stands the cape of the same name. Lat. 36. 43. N., Long. 28. 20. E.

MARNE

Pages 323-323

a river of France, rising in the hills of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LANGRES">Langres</a>, and following a course nearly <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to that of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SEINE">Seine</a>, flows first N.W. and then W., until it falls into that river a short distance above <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, after a course of about 280 miles. The greater <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of its course lies in the departments of Haute-Marne and Marne; but it also traverses those of Aisne, Seine-et-Marne, and Seine-et-<a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOIRE">Loire</a>. It receives on the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> the Ornain at Vitry, after a course of 48 miles; and on the left the Blaise, the Petit-Morin, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a>-Morin. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> on the Marne are,—Langres, Chaumont, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JOINVILLE">Joinville</a>, Saint-Dizier, Vitry-le-François, Châlons, Mareuil, Epernay, Château-Thierry, Ferté-sous-Jouarre, and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MEAUX">Meaux</a>; and the river is navigable as far as Saint-Dizier, 210 miles from its junction with the Seine. The Marne is joined to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a> by means of a canal, which follows for a considerable distance the course of the Ornain. It crosses the Meuse at Voidé, the Moselle at Toul, and enters the Rhine at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-STRASBOURG">Strasbourg</a>, its whole length being about 89 miles. Communicating with this canal another has been constructed from Vitry to Dizy, along the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the Marne, for 38 miles, on account of the rapid and winding character of this part of the river. There is also a third canal of 35 miles in length, which opens a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> between the Marne and the Aisne.

MAROS

Pages 324-325
or Marosch, a river in the Austrian empire, rises in Transylvania, in Mount Magos, a branch of the Carpathians, flows through Transylvania in a S.W. and W. direction, enters Hungary, and forms the northern boundary of the Banat, till it enters the Theiss opposite to Szegedin after a course of about 350 miles. During the earlier part of its course it is inclosed among high cliffs, but further down it flows through a wide plain. The country which it washes on either side is rich in minerals; gold and silver being found to the north, and iron, lead, and copper to the south. Its principal affluents are,—on the right side, the Aranyos; and on the left, the Nyarad, Kokel, Sebes, and Strebl. The most important towns on its banks are Arad, Karlsburg, and Szaza; and it is navigable as far as Karlsburg.

MAROS-VASARHELY

Pages 325-325
or Szekerly-Vasarhely, a free town of Transylvania, capital of a county of the same name, is situated near the Maros, 53 miles N.N.E. of Hermannstadt. The town is fortified, and occupies several small hills; the streets are wide, and the houses small, but for the most part well built. It is chiefly remarkable for its large and excellent public library of 80,000 volumes, which includes many fine editions of the ancient classics, and is kept in a handsome building. There are also here five churches, two convents, a Roman Catholic gymnasium and seminary, and a Protestant college. Maros-Vasarhely is also the seat of the Royal Table, the highest legal tribunal in Transylvania; and is in consequence a place of resort of large numbers of students and practitioners of law. In the neighbourhood is a garrisoned castle. Much tobacco is grown in the vicinity, in which the town carries on a considerable trade. Pop. 10,000.

MAROT

Pages 325-325

Clement, the best French poet of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAHORS">Cahors</a> in 1495, being the son of John Marot, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-VALET">valet</a>-de-chambre to Francis I., and poet to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> of Bretagne. He enjoyed his father's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> as valet-de-chambre to Francis I., and was page to Margaret of France, wife of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of Alençon. In 1521 he followed that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> into <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and was wounded and taken prisoner at the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PAVIA">Pavia</a>; but on his return to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> he was accused of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a> and thrown into prison, where he wrote his Enfer, and revised the Roman de la Rose. Delivered by the protection of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KING">King</a> Francis I., he at length retired to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of the Queen of Navarre, then to that of the Duchess of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FERRARA">Ferrara</a>, and in 1536 returned to Paris; but having declared openly for the Calvinists, he was obliged to fly to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GENEVA">Geneva</a>, which he at length quitted for Lyons, where he renounced Calvinism; and after having taken <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> in the Italian <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> of 1535, under Francis I., he retired to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a>, and died at <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TURIN">Turin</a> in 1544, aged fifty. His versés are filled with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> beauties. La Fontaine acknowledged himself his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a>, and contributed greatly to restore to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> the works of this <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> poet. Marot, besides his other works, translated part of the Psalms into <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, a production which was condemned by the Sorbonne, but subsequently <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> by Beza. Michael Marot, his son, was also the author of some verses; but they are not comparable to those of John, and much inferior to those of Clement Marot. The works of the three Marots were collected and printed together at the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAGUE">Hague</a> in 1731, in 3 vols. 4to, and in 6 vols. 12mo.

MAROWINE

Pages 325-325
or Maroni, a river of South America, rises in the Serra Tumucumaque, flows in a northerly direction, forming the boundary between French and Dutch Guiana, and falls into the Atlantic after a course of about 300 miles, in 5° 52' N. Lat., and 53° 50' W. Long. For about 15 miles up it is navigable for small boats; but the number of small islands, rocks, and quicksands that obstruct its course, prevent any vessel of large size from entering; and in the upper part of its course it is so much interrupted with rapids as to be totally unnavigable. It receives on the right the Rio Siburique and the Rio Waki, and on the left the Rio Tapahon.

MARPURG

Pages 325-325

Friedrich Wilhelm, an eminent musical critic and writer on the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> and practice of music, was born at Seehausen, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRANDENBURG">Brandenburg</a>, in 1718. He received a good <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, and early applied himself to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of music. When about thirty years of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> he was appointed to an office under <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a>, and from that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> devoted his leisure to the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> and publishing of works on music. He published several editions of his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> on the art of playing the harpsichord, and of his work on thorough-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BASS">bass</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>; also several editions and a French translation of his work on fugue-writing, Abhandlung von der Fuge, &c.; which French translation was again published by Choron in his Principes de Composition, &c., 1808, and in his Nouveau Manuel de Musique, &c. It has been objected to Marpurg's work on fugue-writing, that he did not clearly understand the true principles of canonical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a>, nor of those most important parts of the fugue, the subject and the answer. Also, that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> order of the objects treated of is quite <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INVERTED">inverted</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> counterpoints being placed after fugue, and canons after double counterpoint. Choron rectified this confusion in his Nouveau Manuel de Musique. In 1758 Marpurg published a good work on the composition of vocal music, Anleitung zur Singcomposition. In 1763 appeared his introduction to music in general, Anleitung zur Musik überhaupt, &c. In 1757-74-76-79 he published four works on theoretical music and on <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TEMPERAMENT">temperament</a>. Besides these, he published several critical and historical works relative to music, and some of his own musical compositions. He also edited two collections of pieces for the harpsichord, and a collection of fugues by celebrated German composers. He died at Berlin on 22nd May 1795.

MARQUESAS

Pages 325-326
or Mendaña Islands, a group of islands in the South Pacific Ocean, situated between 8 and 11° S. Lat., and 138° 30' and 143° W. Long. The number of the islands is twelve; and they extend to a length of 200 miles from N.W. to S.E.; being divided into two smaller groups, one lying to the N., and another to the S. The principal islands in the southern group are,—Santa Dominica or Hiwaoa, Santa Christina or Tahuna, San Pedro or Motane, and Hood's ss="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">Island or Tiboa, of which the average length is about 10 miles. Of the northern group, the largest is Noukahivah, 20 miles in length and 70 in circumference; and the other principle ones are,—Uahuga or Washington Island, Uapoa or Adam's Island, Motouiti or Franklin Island, and Obivaoa. These islands present a mountainous and rugged appearance; their coasts, which are bold and precipitous, being unprotected by any coral reefs, are exposed to the sea, which beats on them with violence; and the centre of each island is occupied by a ridge of rocky "xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains, rising in the larger islands to the height of 2000 or 3000 feet. From these mountains branches stretch out, reaching down to the sea, and dividing the surface of the islands into numerous small valleys. The soil in these parts is rich, consisting of clay mixed with vegetable remains; but on the higher grounds it is thin, and produces only a coarse sort of grass. Considerable portions of the islands are covered with forests of cocoanut, bread-fruit, papaw, and other trees. The natural productions of this group closely resemble those of the Society Islands; but the fan palm, which is unknown in these islands, is found in the Marquesas. Cultivation is practised to a considerable extent; the principle articles of produce being cotton, sugar, tobacco, potatoes, bananas, and plantains. The inhabitants supply vessels with vegetables and live stock, in return for which they obtain muskets and ammunition for their own use and that of the neighbouring islands. The climate is warm, and the thermometer generally ranges between 64° and 80°. Abundant showers of rain fall in winter, but thunder-storms seldom take place; and sometimes for a period of ten months the islands are without rain—an event which invariably produces a famine. The trade wind from the E. blows frequently here, especially in autumn; but winds from the N. in summer, and from the N.W. in winter are very common. The inhabitants are of a copper colour, are remarkable for the symmetry of their limbs, and though not tall, their appearance is strong and healthy. While the inhabitants of each valley are governed by a single independent chief, yet the possessor of Resolution Bay, one of the best and most frequented harbours, by means of his traffic with Europeans, has acquired considerable influence over the neighbouring princes. This chief took under his protection two English missionaries, who settled here in 1835. The open practice of idolatry has been given up, yet the people still retain many of the manners and superstitions of paganism. They are, however, generally honest and well disposed to Europeans; and the ideas formerly entertained of their cruelty and cannibalism have been found by later visitors to be unfounded. These islands were first visited in 1596 by Mendafia, who discovered four of the southern group, and called them Marquesas de Mendoza, after Don Garcia de Mendoza, then viceroy of Peru. Hood's Island was discovered by Cook in 1776, and the others by the Americans in 1797. In 1842 these islands came under the protection of France. Pop. estimated at 20,000.

MARQUIS

Pages 326-326
or MARQUESS, a title of honour next in dignity to that of duke. The office of marquis is to guard the frontiers and limits of the kingdom, which were called the marches, from the Teutonic word marche, a limit, as, in particular, were the marches of Wales and Scotland whilst they continued hostile to England. The persons who had command there were called lords marchers or marquesses, whose authority was abolished by statute (27 Hen. VIII. c. 27), though the title had long before been made a mere design of honour. The first English marquis was Robert de Vere, Earl of Oxford, created Marquis of Dublin in 1385 by Richard II. This title was first known in Scotland in 1599, when the Marquises of Huntly and Hamilton were created. Since the Revolution, this title has been given as a second title on conferring a dukedom. A marquis is created by patent; his mantle is double ermine, three doublings and a half; his title is most noble; and his coronet has pearls and strawberry leaves intermixed round, of equal height.

MARRACCI

Pages 326-326

Ludovico, a learned Italian, who was born at <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LUCCA">Lucca</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a> in 1612. He applied himself principally to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of languages, especially Greek, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, Syriac, Chaldee, and Arabic, which last he taught for some <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> at Rome. Pope Innocent XI chose him as his confessor, placed <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> confidence in him, and would have advanced him to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> dignities <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> Marracci had not opposed it. Marracci died at Rome in 1700, aged eighty-<a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a>. The great <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> upon which his reputation chiefly rests is his edition of the Koran in the original Arabic, with a Latin version under the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Alcorani Textus universus ex correctionibus Arabum exemplaribus summa fide atque pulcherissimi characteribus descriptus, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a>, 1698, in 2 vols. folio; the first contains the Prodomus, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> the Koran, with critical and grammatical notes, which are highly esteemed. The version of the Koran by Marracci, with notes and observations by himself and others, and a synopsis of Mohammedan <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, by way of introduction, was published by Heineccius at Leipzig, 1721, in 8vo. Marracci had also a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAND">hand</a> in the Biblia Sacra Arabica Sacra Congregationis de Propaganda Fide jussu edita, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AD">ad</a> usum Ecclesiarum Orientalem, Rome, 1671, in 3 vols. folio.

MARRAST

Pages 326-326

Armand, a French journalist, and one of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> authors of the republican <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of 1848, was born in the south of France in 1802. His <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAREER">career</a> as a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> writer began at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1827, and he soon became distinguished as a defender of the practical school of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> as opposed to the eclecticism of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUSIN">Cousin</a>. In 1830 he established the newspaper La Tribune, which during several years was the acknowledged organ of the ultra-Liberals. For some fierce invectives in this periodical against the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> Marrast was at different times prosecuted; and for a pamphlet entitled Vingt Jours de Secret he was compelled to flee to England. In 1836, when Carrel was slain in a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUEL">duel</a>, Marrast succeeded him as chief editor of Le National, and speedily converted that organ of moderate and philosophical Republicanism into a vehicle of vigorous but scurrilous tirade. By his bold and persistent attacks upon the government and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a>, he was a chief <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> in accelerating the Revolution of 1848. Accordingly, he acted a prominent <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> in the new government, became <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the National <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ASSEMBLY">Assembly</a>, and was re-elected to the same office at the end of several successive months. As rapid, however, in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> as in his rise, Marrast was soon forced to flee from the vengeance of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-RED">Red</a> Republicans, and living in retirement, he was almost forgotten, when his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1852, introduced his name once more to the public. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">MARRIAGE</a>. See HUSBAND AND WIFE.

MARRUCINI

Pages 326-326

a people of Central <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, inhabited a narrow strip of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a> extending along the banks of the River Arturnus (Pescara), from the Adriatic to the Apennines, and bounded on the S. by the territory of the Frentani. Their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, on account of its eastern exposure, was more fertile than the neighbouring districts. Teate (<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIETI">Chieti</a>), situated on the Arturnus, was their most important <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. The Marrucini were of Sabine origin. They were an independent people, although they almost invariably appear in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> as allies of the neighbouring tribes of the Marsi and Peligni. Along with these they became confederates of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> in 304 B.C., and revolted at the commencement of the Social <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">War</a>. Their district was included in the Fourth Region of Augustus.

MARS

Pages 327-327

MARS, the Roman god of war, was originally called Mars or Marus, and was identical with the Sabine and Oscar deity Mamers. Among the Romans he came gradually to be viewed in three different characters, and to receive different names corresponding to these characters. He appears to have been regarded originally as the father of Romulus, and accordingly was considered one of the tutelary divinities of Rome. In this character he was called Quirinus, a name derived from the Quirinal Hill, on which his ancient temple stood. But, as the founder and patron of Rome, Mars was naturally supposed to preside over agriculture, the favourite calling of the primitive Romans. He was therefore worshipped as a rustic deity, under the title of Silvanus. Another honourable vocation, however, in ancient Rome was the art of warfare. For the same reason, therefore, that Mars was held to be the god of agriculture he was supposed to be the god of war. In this last character he was worshipped under the name of Gradivus by priests called Salii. Mars was generally painted as an armed warrior of a fierce aspect, riding in a chariot, and brandishing a spear. His shield (anicle) is said to have fallen from heaven in the reign of Numa, and was carefully preserved as the symbol of the perpetuity of the Roman power. To lessen the chances of its being stolen, it was placed among eleven other shields exactly like it. At the ancient temple of Mars, near Reate (Rieti), the responses of the god were communicated by the mouth of his sacred bird the woodpecker (picus). He was also worshipped with great honours at Tuder (Todi), in a sanctuary still seen in ruins. Of the numerous temples dedicated to him at Rome, the most famous was that of Mars Ultor, built by Augustus in the Forum Augusti. The quadrupeds sacred to Mars and most acceptable to him in sacrifice, were the horse and the wolf. The name of his wife was said to be Nerio or Neriene. At an early period he was identified with the Greek god Ares. The month of March and the Campus Martius were named after Mars.

MARSALA

Pages 327-327

MARSALA (the ancient Lilybeum), a seaport of Sicily, in the province of Trapani, is situated on the low promontory of Cape Boeo, on the W. of the island, 18 miles S.S.W. of Trapani. The town is of a square form, and surrounded by old fortifications, which, though at present neglected, might easily be rendered capable of defence. The ancient harbour was good, but is now filled up, and the present one is about a mile S. of the town. Marsala is traversed by a straight and broad street, called the Cassaro, in which stands a large cathedral, with sixteen handsome Corinthian columns of marble. The town has sixteen other churches, many convents, three abbeys, a gymnasium, seminary, hospital, &c. Among the curiosities of the place may be mentioned an old castle, a church with a tower which perceptibly vibrates by the ringing of the bell, and a few remains of aqueducts and tombs of ancient date. The harbour was so highly esteemed by the Saracens as to have received from them the name of Morsa Alla (the Harbour of God). In modern times Marsala derives its chief importance from its trade in the wine grown in the neighbourhood, which is much prized. The quantity produced in the neighbourhood is calculated to amount to 30,000 pipes, of which about two-thirds are exported principally to England, the United States, and the West Indies. Small quantities of corn, cattle, oil, &c., are also exported from Marsala. Pop. about 21,000. MARDSDEN, WILLIAM, an eminent oriental scholar, was the son of a merchant in Dublin, and was born in 1754. After studying at Trinity College in that city, he obtained an appointment in the civil service of the East India Company, and set sail for Bengoolen, Sumatra, in 1771. There he soon rose to the office of principal secretary to the government, and was at the same time intent on acquiring that intimacy with the Malay language, and that knowledge of the country, which were afterwards the sources of his literary reputation. Returning to England in 1779 with a pension, he retired into literary seclusion; and in 1782 produced The History of Sumatra. Marsden was appointed in 1795 second secretary, and in course of time first secretary, to the Admiralty. In 1807 he retired again into private life, and devoting himself to study, published in 1812 his Grammar and Dictionary of the Malay language, and in 1817 his translation of the Travels of Marco Polo. A pension of L1,500, which he had received on his retirement from office, he voluntarily resigned in 1831 for the behoof of the public. In 1834 he presented his rich collection of Marseille, oriental coins to the British Museum, and his library of books and oriental MSS. to King's College. He died of apoplexy in October 1836. Marsden's other works are—Numismata Orientalia (Eastern Coins), 4to, London, 1823-25; Catalogue of Dictionaries, Vocabularies, Grammars, and Alphabets, 4to, London, 1796; and several papers touching the language, manners, and antiquities of the East, in the Philosophical Transactions and the Archaeologia. MARSEILLE, a town of France, capital of the department of Bouches-du-Rhone, is situated on the Mediterranean, 30 miles W.N.W. of Toulon, and 475 S.S.E. of Paris. This city was founded about the year 600 B.C. by a colony of Greeks from Phocæa in Ionia, and was called by them Massalia, which was afterwards changed by the Romans into Massilia, from whence was derived its modern name. (See Massilia.) After the fall of the Roman Empire, Marseille was at different times under the power of the Visigoths, Ostrogoths, and Franks. In the year 720 the greater part of the town was taken and sacked by the Saracens; but the upper city held out until Charles Martel and his brother Childebrand came to the rescue and expelled the Saracens. After this period Marseille continued to increase in wealth and prosperity, though much harassed and threatened by pirates, especially during the reign of Louis le Débonnaire in the ninth century. Up to the time of William I., Viscount of Marseille, this city had preserved a republican form of government; but under that prince and his successors, till the twelfth century, the government was monarchical, though this change exercised no adverse influence on the progress of the arts, industry, and commerce of Marseille. For some time after the restoration of the republican constitution, Marseille formed one of a confederacy of similar small states, including those of Arles, Grasse, &c., and after a struggle for six years against the Counts of Provence, was finally obliged, in 1243, to recognise their authority. Soon afterwards, however, Marseille was involved in a war with Charles of Anjou, brother of Louis IX., which ended in its falling into the hands of that prince. Under the House of Anjou, Marseille continued until the year 1482, when Charles du Maine, the heir of the line of Anjou, bequeathed Marseille to Louis XI., with a stipulation that the time-honoured liberties of the city should be respected. In the year 1524 Marseille was besieged by the imperialists under the Constable de Bourbon, but the inhabitants made a desperate resistance, and succeeded in repelling their adversaries. Marseille was made by Louis XIII. a station of the French navy, and provided with a dockyard and arsenal; and the good effects of this were seen in the clearing the Mediterranean of the pirates which infested it. In the reign of Louis XIV., a sedition broke out here, of which the ringleader was Noiselles; but the "Great Monarch" having made his appearance in 1660, quelled the sedition, and deprived the city of its peculiar privileges, erecting at the same time the citadel of St Nicolas. In 1720 and 1721 Marseille suffered from a fearful visitation of the plague, which, although it had frequently made its appearance previously, had never been so destructive as on this occasion, when it carried off between 50,000 and 60,000 victims. Marseille hailed with joy the beginning of the first French Revolution, but the event did not correspond to the hopes entertained at the outset, and the commerce of Marseille was almost ruined in the commotions of that unhappy period. After the Restoration, however, the city recovered its former commercial importance, and is now daily increasing in wealth and magnificence. The situation of Marseille is not only very convenient for commerce and navigation, but is extremely beautiful and picturesque. It is built on the slope of the hills which surround the excellent harbour in a semicircular form. The Marseille town consists of two distinct parts, an old and a new; the former, which occupies the site of the ancient Massilia, is situated on uneven ground to the N. of the harbour, and is irregularly and ill built, with narrow and dirty streets. The new town, on the other hand, consists of broad and straight streets, as well as splendid and elegant squares, which rival in magnificence those of Paris. The division between the old and new town is marked by a public promenade called the "Cours," lined with trees, and adorned with numerous fountains, and which, along with the streets of Aix and Rome, forms a thoroughfare extending in a straight line through the city, from the triumphal arch at the northern extremity, to an obelisk which stands near the gate by which the road from Rome enters Marseille. Another favourite promenade is the Rue de la Canebière, a broad street extending from the Cours to the harbour, and commanding a view of the shipping. The walls which formerly inclosed Marseille have been converted into boulevards; and beyond these the town has extended, and is still rapidly extending itself, in all directions. On a hill to the S. stands the fort of Notre Dame de la Garde; and the entrance of the harbour, formerly closed during the night by a chain, and hence called "La Chaîne," is protected by the Fort St Jean on the N., and St Nicolas on the S. The approach is still further guarded by the fortified island of If, which has long served as a state prison, as well as by the islands of Pomègue and Ratoneau, which are also fortified. The harbour of Marseille, which was in ancient times called Lacydon, is of a rectangular shape, and is about 1020 yards in length by 327 in breadth. It is secure and convenient, and surrounded by a number of excellent quays, which are always thronged with a busy crowd of men of all nations. Although the harbour can accommodate 1200 vessels, it has been found insufficient for the numbers of those frequenting it, and a new harbour has been accordingly constructed, called La Joliette, opposite to Fort St Nicolas. The neighbourhood of Marseille is extremely dry and barren; and although there are numerous bastides or country houses in the vicinity, the only attraction which these possess is the view of the sea, to which Marseille owes not only its wealth, but a great part of its beauty. The public buildings of Marseille are not so numerous as might be expected; and the view of the city from an eminence is remarkably destitute of spires, domes, and other indications of large and handsome buildings. The cathedral, which is called the "Major," or the church of St Victor, is of very great antiquity, but is by no means an elegant or imposing structure, and its castellated towers give it the appearance rather of a fortress than of a place of worship. The Hôtel de Ville stands on the northern side of the harbour, and is a rather heavy building, said to be the work of the celebrated Puget, but which was in all probability executed by some inferior hand. One of the finest buildings in Marseille is the Hôtel de la Prefecture. The only others that deserve notice are the new market-house, the theatre, resembling the Odeon at Paris, and the Palais de Justice. In the neighbourhood is the chapel of Notre Dame de la Garde; which contains an ancient olive-wood statue of the Virgin, held in the highest veneration by sailors and fishermen, and a modern one of silver; besides many votive pictures. The church of St Madeleine, also in the suburbs, is an elegant building, and has two light steeples and a fine front. The town contains altogether about twenty Roman Catholic churches, two Greek ones, one Protestant church, and a synagogue. There is a museum and picture gallery, in the former of which are to be seen a few remains of the ancient city of Massilia, which are not of much interest, and do not ascend to a higher antiquity than the time of Julius Caesar.
