But this cannot be admitted as evidence in support of the point in question; for, what- --- 1 Clausen, Kirchen-verfassung, Lehre und Ritus des Catholischen und Protestantischen, p. 723. 2 Hensil, de Christi generatione, ap. Suicer. Thes. Eccl. ii. 305. 3 Bishop Pearson on the Creed, p. 174, folio ed.; Edwards' Exercitations on Scripture, p. 143; and Pott, Preleg. in Epist. Jacobi, Nov. Test. Koppenhagen, vol. ix., p. 90, &c. 4 Life of Christ, Eng. tr., p. 32; Comp. De Wette on Matt. i. 25, in his Exegetisches Handbuch. 5 Lightfoot, Hor. Talus, in loc.; Winer, Real-Wörterbuch; and Kitto's Bib. Cyclopaedia, art. Magdala. Mary may be the conclusion to which we come as to the nature of that diabolical possession which prevailed in the days of our Lord, one thing is certain in regard to it, which is, that to be afflicted with it did not imply in the individual so visited any peculiar moral depravity; so that, though the case of Mary Magdalene was one of unusual severity (the number seven being the number of completeness), it by no means follows from this that she was not a virtuous, nay, pious female. On the contrary, the evidence from Scripture seems rather to favour the supposition that she was a person at once of blameless character and respectable station. She is introduced to us for the first time in the society of Joanna, the wife of Chuza, steward of Herod's household (ἐπιτρόπος, προσεκτος δουλος), with whom she was associated in ministering to the wants of our Saviour "out of their substance" (ἐπαγωγα, ὁπερ συμβαίνει); and from the language used by Mark (ch. xv. 41), it would seem as if this had been the usual practice of these pious females whenever he paid a visit to Galilee. Had she been, as is commonly supposed, a mere common prostitute before her conversion, it is difficult to understand how she should either associate with persons of such rank as Joanna, or be possessed of the means of such liberality towards Christ. On the occasion of our Lord's going up to Jerusalem from Galilee, immediately before his death, Mary Magdalene was one of those by whom he was followed; nor does she seem to have left him as long as he continued upon earth. She was one of those who beheld him from a distance when he was hanging upon the cross (Mark xv. 40); and when he was taken down and buried, it was she and Mary Salome who sat over against the sepulchre and beheld where he was laid (Matt. xxvii. 61; Mark xv. 47). From the sepulchre she returned with her companion into the city to procure materials for embalming his body; and having rested on the Sabbath, they came at the dawn of the third day to perform this office of respect to their departed Lord. Contrary to their expectations and fears, they found the stone which they had seen placed upon the mouth of the tomb rolled away, and free entrance afforded to its interior. Stooping down and looking in, they were startled to find the body of Jesus gone; but as they wondered, an angel appeared, who informed them of his resurrection, and at the same time commanded them to carry the tidings of this event to the rest of the disciples (Matt. xxviii. 7). Amazed and perplexed, they fled from the sepulchre, and announced to their company what they had seen; upon which Peter and John hastened to satisfy themselves of the correctness of their report, by returning with them to the place where Jesus had been interred. When the others returned home, Mary seems to have remained by the empty sepulchre to weep; and "as she wept," we are told, "she stooped down and looked into the sepulchre, and seeth two angels sitting, the one at the head and the other at the feet, where the body of Jesus had lain." By them she was asked the cause of her tears; to which she answered, that it was because they had taken away her Lord, and she knew not where they had laid him. During this conversation, Jesus himself drew near and addressed her; but, stupified with grief, she did not at first recognise his voice, and, intent upon gazing into the sepulchre, she answered his inquiries as to what she wept for, and what she sought, without turning herself, under the impression that he was the gardener. To recall her recollection, Jesus addressed her by name; upon which she immediately recognised the well-known voice, and turning herself, exclaimed, "Rabboni, which is to say, Master." After a brief conversation, he sent her to announce to the disciples that she had seen him, and that he was about to ascend to heaven. This command she obeyed; and from this time forward we find no mention made of her in the New Testament. As to certain traditionary accounts of subsequent actions and journeyings in which she is said to have been engaged, they bear too obviously the marks of mere legendary fiction to be worthy of notice. Mary, the sister of Martha and Lazarus. These three individuals composed the members of a family, than which none was more beloved and honoured by our Lord in the days of his flesh. Their residence was at Bethany, a village not far from Jerusalem, where Martha seems to have been a housekeeper; and thither our Lord was in the habit, apparently, of frequently retiring during the intervals of his public labours. The name of Mary is first introduced, in connection with that of her sister, in the account given of a visit paid by Christ to their abode, during one of his journeys; on which occasion, whilst Martha busied herself in caring for the hospitable entertainment of her guest, Mary sat at his feet to receive his instruction (Luke x. 38, &c.). The next mention that is made of her is in the touching and striking account given by John (ch. xi. 1-46) of the death and resurrection of Lazarus; and she appears for the last time shortly subsequent to this, on the occasion of an entertainment given to our Lord, a few days before his crucifixion, by Martha, when she anointed his feet with precious ointment, and wiped them with the hair of her head (John xii. 1-9). Mary, the mother of James and Joses, and Simon and Judas. She is the same who is elsewhere called the wife of Cleophas (John xix. 25), or Alphæus, these two being only different modes of Hæcizing the Hebrew חפלא, Chafpal. The common opinion is that she was the sister of the Virgin Mary, an opinion founded on John xix. 25. But as it is not very probable that there would be two sisters in one family of the same name, it seems better to adopt the suggestion of Wieseler (Theol. Studien und Kritiken, 1840, p. 648), that in this passage four persons are enumerated—Mary, Mary's sister (whose name is not given), Mary the wife of Cleophas, and Mary of Magdala. Mary, the mother of John Mark. (Acts xii. 12.) Mary I., Queen of England, was the daughter of Henry VIII. and Catherine of Aragon, and was born on the 18th of February 1516. She ascended the throne on the 6th of July 1553, married Philip II. of Spain on the 25th of July 1554, and died on the 17th of November 1558. (See England.) Mary, wife of William III., was the eldest daughter of James II. and Ann Hyde, and was born in 1662. She married the Prince of Orange in 1677, shared the throne with her husband in 1688, and died in 1694. (See Britain.) Mary, Queen of Scots, was the daughter of James V. of Scotland and Mary of Lorraine, and was born on the 8th of December 1542. She married the Dauphin of France, afterwards Francis II., on the 24th of April 1558; assumed the personal government of Scotland on the 19th of August 1561; married Lord Darnley on the 29th of July 1566, and Bothwell, on the 15th of May 1567; was forced to retire from the throne on the 17th of June 1567; was imprisoned by Elizabeth in 1568, where she remained till her execution on the 8th of February 1587. (See Scotland.) MARYBOROUGH, a town of Ireland, capital of Queen's county, is situated on a small tributary of the Barrow, 50 miles S.W. of Dublin. It is struggling and meanly built, consisting chiefly of one long irregular street. --- 1 For a complete investigation of this point, see Lardner's Letter to Jonas Hanway, Esq., Works, vol. v., 4to ed. See also Macknight's Harmony, sect. 43.

MARYBOROUGH

Pages 341-341

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUEEN_S_COUNTY"><a class="xref</a>" href="vol18.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, is situated on a small tributary of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BARROW">Barrow</a>, 50 miles S.W. of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>. It is struggling and meanly built, consisting chiefly of one <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> street. --- 1 For a complete <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> of this point, see Lardner's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LETTER">Letter</a> to Jonas Hanway, Esq., Works, vol. v., 4to ed. See also Macknight's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">Harmony</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SECT">sect</a>. 43.

MARYLAND

Pages 341-343

one of the United States of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, bounded on the N. by <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PENNSYLVANIA">Pennsylvania</a>, E. by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DELAWARE">Delaware</a> and the Atlantic, and S. and W. by <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a>, from which it is separated by the River <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POTOMAC">Potomac</a>; and extending from 38° to 39° 44' N. Lat., and from 75° 10' to 79° 20' W. <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. Its form is very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>; its greatest length is 190, and its greatest breadth 120 miles; <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> 93,56 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. The surface of Maryland may be regarded as consisting of two distinct parts. The one comprehends the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> lands in the W. of the state, traversed by several ridges of the Alleghany <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">Mountains</a>, and extending in a narrow strip of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a> eastward as far as the lower falls of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>. The other portion, which is low and flat, is subdivided into two parts by Chesapeake <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BAY">Bay</a>. These are called respectively the Western and the Eastern Shore; the former consisting of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> formed by the estuary of the Potomac and Chesapeake Bay, and the latter of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of that peninsula lying between Chesapeake Bay and the Atlantic. Of this last, the north-eastern part is occupied by the state of Delaware, while the southern extremity belongs to that of Virginia. In the mountainous district the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> ridges are South-East Mountain <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> Parr's Ridge, terminating at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUGAR">Sugar</a>-Loaf Mountain on the Potomac. In a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> nearly <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to this range, extends Catoctin Mountain, reaching the river at the Point of Rocks. Further up, the river is crossed at Harper's Ferry by the Blue Ridge or South Mountain, and at Hancock by the Kittatinny. In the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> W. of the state rise the main ridges of the Alleghany Mountains, besides Rugged Mountain, Wills Mountain, and other detached chains. None of these ridges have any <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> elevation; and the valleys which <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LIE">lie</a> between them are remarkable for the fertility of their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> and the mildness of their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>. The eastern and western shores of the state are very similar to each other in soil and productions. The soil is alluvial, and consists in general of a mixture of sand and clay; and though not very fertile by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, is easily rendered productive by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of manure, which is supplied in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantities by the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARL">marl</a> beds in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The climate is temperate, and in general salubrious, with the exception of some of the low-lying country near Chesapeake Bay, from which rise noxious exhalations, especially during the months of autumn. The principle feature in this part of the state is the Bay of Chesapeake which divides the whole region into two parts from N. to S., and gives the outline of the state a very irregular appearance. This great estuary has a total length of 180 miles, of which 120 are in this state, and a breadth varying at different places from 7 to 20 miles. It is navigable for the largest vessels throughout its entire length, and it abounds in fine fish and oysters. It receives many rivers of various sizes, and its coasts are deeply indented by numerous bays and creeks. The surface of the bay is studded with many <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, the most considerable of which is <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KENT">Kent</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">Island</a>, opposite the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ANNAPOLIS">Annapolis</a>, about 12 miles in length. The Potomac River, the largest of those that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> into Chesapeake Bay, and which forms the boundary between this state and that of Virginia, rises in the Alleghany Mountains, and flows in an irregular course, first nearly E. and afterwards S. and S.E., till it enters the Bay of Chesapeake towards its southern extremity between Point Look-out and Smith's Point. Its width at its mouth is 7½ miles, and it is navigable for the largest vessels as far up as <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>; while by means of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> the falls which occur not far above this are avoided, and the river rendered navigable for boats as far as <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>, 191 miles above Maryland. <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WASHINGTON">Washington</a>. The scenery of this river is very fine, especially at these falls, which, though not very high, are among the most interesting objects of the kind in the States; and at Harper's Ferry, where the river rushes through a defile in the Blue Mountains. The principal affluents of the Potomac in this state are the Monocacy River, Antietam and Conococheague Creeks. Besides these are—the Patuxent, which flows in a direction nearly the same as the Potomac, rising in Parr's Ridge, and falling into Chesapeake Bay, and is navigable as far as <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NOTTINGHAM">Nottingham</a>, 50 miles up; the Patapsco, falling into the bay near <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BALTIMORE">Baltimore</a>; the Susquehanna, which is for the greater part of its course a Pennsylvanian river, but which falls into Chesapeake Bay in this state. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ELK">Elk</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHESTER">Chester</a>, Choptank, Nanticoke, and Pocomoke, all flow to the eastern shore, and are navigable for 30 or 40 miles. The only river in Maryland which does not flow into Chesapeake Bay is the Youghiogheny, which rises in the mountains of the extreme W., and flows northwards into the Ohio. In a geological point of view, the whole of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> region of Maryland consists of recent formations, containing many interesting fossils; while the mountain district consists of metamorphic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STRATA">strata</a>, such as gneiss and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MICA">mica</a>, slate, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANITE">granite</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">limestone</a>, &c.; and is rich in coal and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a>. Maryland contains a considerable <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of forest land; the principal trees are—oak, pine, chestnut, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CEDAR">cedar</a>, ash, beech, poplar, and elm. The principal agricultural productions of this fertile and well-cultivated district are <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, wheat, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> corn; besides which large quantities of oats, rye, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, hay, potatoes, peas, beans, &c., are raised. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of farms in the state in 1850 was 21,860, comprising 2,797,905 acres of cultivated land; and the total value of the farms, with their machinery and implements, was L18,676,233. The live stock in the same year included 75,684 horses, 219,586 head of cattle, and 177,902 sheep; and amounted in total value to L1,166,174. In the agricultural produce for the year ending <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1, 1850, the principal items are the following:—Wheat, 4,494,680 bushels; rye, 226,014 bushels; Indian corn, 10,749,858 bushels; oats, 2,242,151 bushels; tobacco, 21,407,497 lb.; potatoes, 973,932 bushels; and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>, 3,806,160 lbs. In the aggregate amount of tobacco produced, Maryland is the third of the States; and in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POPULATION">population</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of Maryland are numerous and important. There were, in 1850, 24 cotton factories, employing 3022 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, and producing stuffs to the value of L1,441,772; 38 woollen factories, employing 362 hands, and producing stuffs to the value of L61,488; 51 furnaces, forges, &c., employing 2699 hands, and producing 39,855 tons, valued at L523,519; and 116 tanneries, producing <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> to the value of L229,820. Total number of manufactories in the state (1850), 3863; <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> invested, L3,073,588; hands employed, 30,124; value of raw material, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-FUEL">fuel</a>, &c., L3,609,738; value of produce, L6,870,355. The improvements in the internal communications of this state have been very extensive, and Maryland has in this department displayed more energy and enterprise than caution and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a>. There are three extensive canals—the Chesapeake and Ohio Canal, which has only been completed as far as Cumberland, a distance of 200 miles from its commencement at Alexandria, and which cost up to the year 1839 more than L145,833; the Susquehanna Canal, communicating with the interior of Pennsylvania; and the Chesapeake and Delaware Canal, which affords a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PHILADELPHIA">Philadelphia</a>. There are also many <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RAILWAYS">railways</a> in the state. Of these the Baltimore and Ohio, and the Baltimore and Susquehanna <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, with their several branches, are the principal, and have a total length of 514 miles. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of Maryland is very great, owing to the Maryland, facilities for trade afforded by its excellent harbours, its navigable rivers, canals, and railways. The principal <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of export are,—flour, wheat, pork, and tobacco; and the total value of goods exported from the state in 1850 was £1,451,633. The imports for the same year amounted in value to £1,275,886. For the year ending June 30, 1855, the respective values were,—exports, £2,165,413; imports, £1,623,781. The number of vessels built in the state in the year ending June 30, 1855, was 122, with a tonnage of 22,524. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-FISHING">Fishing</a> is carried on in Chesapeake Bay, and large quantities of fish are taken, consisting principally of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HERRING">herring</a>, shad, eels, perch, mullet, &c. The state of Maryland is divided into 21 counties; and the principal <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> are,—Baltimore, Cumberland, Frederick, Hagerstown, and Annapolis. Though not the largest town, Annapolis is the capital of the state. The present <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of Maryland, which was settled by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of 1851, consists of a Governor, elected for four years, with a salary of £750 a-year; a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SENATE">Senate</a> of 29 members, also elected for four years; and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUSE">House</a> of Representatives of 74 members, elected for two years. There are three districts in the state, from each of which in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-ROTATION">rotation</a> the governor must be chosen. The franchise extends to every <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-WHITE">white</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MALE">male</a> above the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of twenty-one, a citizen of the United States, and who has resided for a year in the state, and six months in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> or town for which he votes. The qualifications for members of the legislature are, that they shall be not less than twenty-five years of age for the Senate and twenty-one for the House of Representatives, and have resided three years in the state and one in the district for which they are elected. The judicial establishment consists of an orphans' <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> in each county, composed of three judges, elected by the people for four years; eight circuit courts, each presided over by a judge elected for ten years; and a court of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a>, with four judges elected from as many districts for ten years, one of whom is appointed <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> by the governor and Senate. Judges must retire at the age of seventy. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> institutions in Maryland consist of an aggregate of 909 churches, with <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> amounting to £829,476. The proportions of places of worship belonging to the different sects are as follows—Baptists, 48; Episcopalians, 133; Friends, 26; German Reformed, 22; Lutherans, 42; <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-METHODISTS">Methodists</a>, 479; Moravians, 12; <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRESBYTERIANS">Presbyterians</a>, 57; <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>, 65; Union <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a>, 10; <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> sects, 10. The educational establishments consisted in 1850 of 11 colleges, with 91 teachers and 992 students; 907 public <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, with 1005 teachers and 33,254 scholars; and 224 <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a> and other schools, with 489 teachers and 10,677 scholars. The total number attending school in the state in 1850 was 62,063; and the number of adults unable to read or write was 41,877. The amount of the public funds expended for purposes of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> was in the same year £15,862; and the amount raised by <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TAXATION">taxation</a> was £18,055. The principal public institutions in the state are at Baltimore, and consist of a state <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENITENTIARY">penitentiary</a>, a lunatic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a>, &c. The amount of the state debt of Maryland, September 30, 1856, was £3,114,985; the total receipts for the year ending at that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a>, £256,359; and the total expenditure for the same year, £256,356. The earliest settlement of Europeans in the territory of this state was in 1631, when William Claiborne founded a colony on Kent Island. The district was named Maryland from Henrietta <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARIA">Maria</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I., who granted a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> for the territory to <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Baltimore, a Roman Catholic, in 1632. A colony, composed chiefly of Roman Catholics, fugitives from religious <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PERSECUTION">persecution</a>, settled at St <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MARY">Mary</a>'s in 1634 under Leonard Calvert, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of Lord Baltimore. The government was liberal and democratic, the legislative functions being exercised by the lord proprietary and the representatives of the people. A contest, however, soon arose between the governor and the people about their respective <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> in the legislature; the former endeavoured to force on the colony a system of laws framed by himself, and the latter resisted this attempt, restricting his power to a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of veto on any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> passed by the people. The governor ultimately gave way, and the constitution of the colony became of a more popular character. During the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the civil <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a> in England, the governor, a Catholic, and an adherent of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KING">king</a>'s, expelled from the colony a number of Puritans, who settled in Virginia, but afterwards returned, and attempted to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> the supremacy in Maryland. After partial successes on both sides, the legislature passed in 1649 an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACT">Act</a> of Toleration, in which Catholics, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-QUAKERS">Quakers</a>, and Puritans, who had now all in turn experienced the evils of persecution, had a share. Soon afterwards the adherents of the Commonwealth, which was now in power in England, having gained the upper <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAND">hand</a> in the colony, and reinforcements having been sent to their assistance, the lord proprietary was overthrown, but not until after a bloody <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. After the restoration of Charles II., the government was restored to the Baltimore family, with whom it <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> till the Revolution of 1688. After that event the affairs of the colony were managed by governors appointed by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, until 1715, when Benedict Leonard Calvert, the heir of the Baltimore family, who had embraced the Protestant <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, was reinstalled as governor of the colony. After this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> Maryland continued to make progress in population and manufacturing industry, though the policy of Great <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, which was calculated to repress the progress of the colony, was felt as a great hindrance. Long and tedious disputes were carried on between Maryland and Pennsylvania, which were only finally settled in 1783, when the frontiers were adjusted as they at present stand. No remarkable engagement took <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> here in the revolutionary war; but Annapolis was the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of some of the meetings of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONGRESS">Congress</a> and of Washington's resignation of the command at the end of the war. Maryland is a slave-holding state; and though after the Revolution there was a strong tendency to emancipation, all public <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> of that kind were checked by an article in the constitution of 1836. ### Population in 1850 | | Male | <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FEMALE">Female</a> | Total | |----------|--------|--------|-------| | Whites | 211,187| 206,756| 417,943| | Free Coloured | 35,192 | 39,531 | 74,723 | | Slaves | 45,944 | 44,424 | 90,368 | | **Total**| **292,323** | **290,711** | **583,034** |

MARYPORT

Pages 343-344

a seaport and market-town of England, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>, is situated near the mouth of the Ellen, 29 miles S.W. of Carlisle. The town is neat and well built, and has entirely risen within the last century. The only public buildings of importance are the town-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, the market-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BRIDEWELL">bridewell</a>, which are elegant edifices. Maryport has a chapel of ease, and places of worship for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRESBYTERIANS">Presbyterians</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-METHODISTS">Methodists</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INDEPENDENTS">Independents</a>, Baptists, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-QUAKERS">Quakers</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ROMAN_CATHOLICS">Roman Catholics</a>. The town has also national and British <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>' <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-READING">reading</a>-room and library, and a savings-<a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a>. The inhabitants are principally employed in ship-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, and the manufacture of sail-cloth, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a>, cordage, and other <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> for ships. The trade of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is very considerable, consisting chiefly in coal, which is conveyed through Maryport from <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTHUMBERLAND">Northumberland</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DURHAM">Durham</a> to Scotland and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>. In 1855 283,603 tons were shipped here. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COKE">Coke</a>, lime, and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a> are also exported; and the imports consist of cattle, <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a>. The harbour is dry at low <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a>. A steamer plies between this town and <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LIVERPOOL">Liverpool</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">Man</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a>, every <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEEK">week</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, and every fortnight in win- Marysville ter. The town had in 1855, 105 vessels, of 15,987 tons burden; and during that year the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of vessels that entered the harbour was 273, with a tonnage of 39,052; and of those that left, 2654, with a tonnage of 229,658. The market-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> is Friday; and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> are held twice a-year. Pop. of the chapelry (1851), 5698.

MARYSVILLE

Pages 344-344

a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POST">post</a>-town, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of Yuba, in the state of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CALIFORNIA">California</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, is situated on the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of the River Yuba, about a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MILE">mile</a> above its confluence with the Feather River, and 100 miles N.E. of Benicia. Steamers ply regularly between Marysville and San Francisco, touching at Sacramento. Pop. (1853) 8000.

MASACCIO

Pages 344-344

a celebrated painter of the Florentine school, was born in 1402 at San Giovanni in Valdarno. His real name was Tommaso Guidi, but his unfitness for the cares of ordinary <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> procured for him at an early <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> the nickname of Masaccio, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> "Helpless Tom." Receiving the first <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LESSONS">lessons</a> in his art from Masolino da Panicale, he was employed under that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASTER">master</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> the Brancacci chapel in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of the Carmine at <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>. He also carefully studied the sculptures of Ghiberti and Donatello, and learned <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol8.html#article-PERSPECTIVE">perspective</a> from Brunelleschi. About 1430 Masaccio seems to have visited Rome, and there, according to Vasari, he was employed in the execution of several important works. On the return, however, of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PATRON">patron</a>, Cosmo de' Medici, from exile in 1434, he went back to Florence, and was engaged to complete the paintings of the Brancacci, left unfinished by the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his old master Masolino. He died, however, in 1443, before he had fulfilled his engagement. The suddenness of his death, and the envy in which he was known to be held by his rivals, combined to originate the suspicion that he had been poisoned. Ever working with a clear perception that painting is simply a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, Masaccio surpassed all his contemporaries in the easy postures of his figures, in the simplicity and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of his draperies, and in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> and harmonious colouring. So unprecedented was his skill in foreshortening, and his knowledge of perspective, that he may be said to have introduced a new era in the annals of painting. The frescoes in the church of the Carmine at Florence were his masterpieces, and were zealously studied by Raphael and other <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> painters of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. In his epitaph, written by Annibal Cavo, it is said that Michael Angelo was the teacher of other painters, but the pupil of Masaccio.

MASANIEMO

Pages 344-345

the abbreviated name <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> given to Tommaso Aniello, a fisherman born at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMALFI">Amalfi</a> in 1622, who, at the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of twenty-five, became <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the celebrated revolution in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> which bears his name. While under Spanish dominion that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> was subjected to the greatest misgovernment. The ambition of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> III. and Philip IV., both of whom required extraordinary funds to carry on the wars of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOMBARDY">Lombardy</a> and Catalonia, scarcely surpassed the avidity and selfishness of the exacting viceroys employed by them to plunder the Neapolitans. A confused and embarrassed administration; a corrupt magistracy; venal employees who enriched themselves as a reward for other services; an oppressive distribution of taxes, which rendered a system of violence necessary in levying them; a ready compliance with all the arbitrary acts of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, who set the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> at defiance and enjoyed a total immunity from all burdens of the state; and last, though not least, an organized system of brigandage, which the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> was as powerless and unwilling to check as the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a> were interested in upholding—such was Naples under the vice-regal government of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. This state of things, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> hateful to the Neapolitan people, reached its height under his excellency the Viceroy Ponce de Leon, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> d'Arcos. Taxes were multiplied, more especially on the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol8.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of daily consumption; and in 1647 even fruit, which in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> forms almost the only food of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> portion of the populace, did not escape this galling impost. Fish had been taxed a few years before; and the young Masaniello, accustomed, in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of his calling, to dispute with the tax collectors, had, from his fearless dealing with these universally hated functionaries, become a favourite with his own class and with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> people in general. One <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> when his wife, detected with <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONTRABAND">contraband</a> flour, was imprisoned and fined, he assembled a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of young men, armed them with sticks, and urged them to take advantage of the crowds at the approaching festival of the Madonna del Carmine to make a solemn and public protest against these oppressive taxes. On the 7th of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, however, some country people coming as usual to Naples to sell fruit, were compelled by the tax collectors to pay the duty beforehand. The market people revolted, and one of them, trampling the fruit under his feet, cried out indignantly that he would rather destroy his fruit than submit to such exaction. A crowd assembled, partly from curiosity, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ANGER">anger</a> ensued, and the companions of Masaniello fanned the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> which soon burst forth. The agitation increased by degrees until it became general. The officials, who had prudently retreated, were now panic-struck; still the insurrection wanted a chief; and Masaniello resolved at once to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> the opportunity. He made his way among the crowd, and with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> that drowned all other sounds, cried, "Away with the tax on fruit! <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> to bad rulers!" "Away with them!" shouted the multitude; "Long live Masaniello!" In a moment the infuriated mob drove off the functionaries, who were looking on in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MUTE">mute</a> astonishment, burned the tax-collectors' offices, and proceeded to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> to besiege the viceroy, who had, however, already taken refuge in the Castel Nuovo. The people must vent their rage on something; so Masaniello directed that the houses of the nobility should be burned, but threatened death to any who should attempt to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> a single object from the flames. This order was blindly obeyed. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRISONS">prisons</a> were thrown open, and one Perrone, who afterwards became Masaniello's civil genius, was set at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, together with all the thieves and malefactors of the town. The viceroy sent a messenger, who promised everything; but Masaniello, not satisfied with simple promises, demanded the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> granted by <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V., prohibiting the imposition of new taxes, except by a special <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KING">king</a>. A hundred thousand men were now at the command of the intrepid fisherman, whom they followed and promptly obeyed. A perambulating throne <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PLATFORM">platform</a> was erected, consisting of a rough <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>-raised dais, placed on a waggon drawn by four strong horses. On this he sat, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAP">cap</a> of the fisherman on his head, and dressed in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> garb of his calling. This simplicity increased the enthusiasm of his followers, and Masaniello found himself the animating <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> of thousands. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Filomarini, Archbishop of Naples, came as a mediator from the viceroy, and was received with marks of respect. Hopes were entertained that the insurrection would be checked, when the nobles, headed by the Duke of Monteleone, and his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Caraffa, assembled 200 brigands, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> them to assassinate Masaniello. Two hundred shots were fired at him while seated on his throne, but, by an extraordinary chance, not one reached him. This inflamed the popular fervour to a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of fanaticism, while <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> were ready with their marvellous explanations. The assassins were seized and executed. None were spared—not even those who denounced their instigators. Two hundred heads, fixed on <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>, now bristled round the throne-like erection on which Masaniello, the people's idol, sat. The two noblemen were pursued, but the duke made his escape; while the prince, having fallen into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the mob, was beheaded and quartered; his head, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> the inscription "Giuseppe Caraffa ribelle e traditore della patria," being Masaniello placed conspicuously among the others. Judicial, regal, administrative powers were all now centred in Masaniello's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> and single hand. He ordered the nobles to be disarmed, and the people to receive each <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a> a sword, a musket, ample ammunition, and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>. He established a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POLICE">police</a>, and decreed that all judgments should be referred to him, on which he gave prompt and impartial verdicts. At last, through the intervention of the Archbishop of Naples, he consented to treat with the viceroy. He now began to despise his red cap and fisherman's dress, and assumed a gaudy attire glittering with silver and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>. The people were amazed when they <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SAW">saw</a> him, thus adorned, head a cavalcade, equally splendid, on his way to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of the Madonna del Carmine to negotiate a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> with the viceroy. He styled himself "Capo del Popolo," and with this <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> he altered, modified, and rescinded, as he thought proper; none daring to oppose him. Finally the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> terms were settled:—1st, The total abolition of all the taxes imposed since the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> of Charles V.; 2d, Absolute equality of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> among all classes of citizens; 3d, General amnesty to all who had taken <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> in the insurrection; 4th, That the Neapolitan people should remain armed till the ratification of the treaty by his Catholic Majesty the King of Spain. He then exacted an oath from the Duke d'Arcos, and <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> to the people, declared his mission accomplished, his desires fulfilled, and that henceforth he would follow his trade as a fisherman. Having said these words, he threw off his rich attire, fell at the feet of the viceroy, professed <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a> to the king, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOVE">love</a> to the people, <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> to his country, and rejected all proffered rewards. This imposing <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> called forth the deafening shouts of the multitude that thronged the church, who begged him to retain the authority he had for several days exercised so successfully. The Duke d'Arcos showed him the greatest respect, praised his skill in statesmanship, and, to celebrate the restoration of peace, invited him to a solemn banquet at the royal palace. Masaniello's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAR">star</a> now began to wane. His conduct at the banquet was boastful and extravagant, some say showing signs of an unsound mind, caused by overjoy at his success, or, as other historians affirm, by a poisoned drink given him by the viceroy. Masaniello, now arrogant, overbearing, and arbitrary to his fellows, lost that simplicity which had made him their idol. At the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the fourth day of his power, two hundred thousand men would have given their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> for him; on the eighth day there were as many disaffected. The Duke d'Arcos, who had been plotting to bring about this state of things, seeing the moment had now arrived to get rid of the spirited tribune without danger to himself, on the 16th of July placed four men in ambush. They fired upon the unfortunate leader, who fell <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> dead. Hated as much as he had been loved, his body was insulted even by his old friends. The hired assassins, emboldened by this feeling, showed their zeal by severing his head from his body, and holding it by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, presented it to the viceroy, who ordered it to be thrown into the castle <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-MOAT">moat</a>. One day, however, had scarcely passed when a more <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> feeling returned. The greater part of the people deplored the effects of sudden ambition on the mind of their chief, pitied him, wept for his untimely fate, and were ashamed they had not taken immediate <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> on his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MURDERERS">murderers</a>. His body was exhumed, and with the head joined to it, was placed on a bier, covered with a regal purple robe, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of laurel on the brow, a sceptre in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> hand, and amid the solemn tolling of all the church bells it was carried in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROCESSION">procession</a> through the twelve districts of the town, followed, according to one historian, by 400,000 people. The viceroy, by a stroke of policy, sent his own <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-PAGES">pages</a> in state, and ordered that funeral honours should be rendered to the "Capo del Popolo," whose body, after having lain in state several days, was finally buried with all the pomp reserved to men of the highest <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RANK">rank</a>. The Duke d'Arcos, when the popular excitement had subsided, was perfidious enough to persecute numbers of the lower orders who had taken part in the revolution, thus causing the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of Masaniello to be more than ever regretted. To this day he is held in high esteem by the liberal party of the lazzaroni of Naples, who regard him as the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> of their class, and the standard of popular heroes. The most complete account of this remarkable episode in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> was contained in a manuscript of the Padr Filippini dell' Oratorio in Naples. The monks consented only lately to publish this interesting <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOCUMENT">document</a>. It is entitled "Diario di Francesco Copeclatro contenente la storia delle cose avvenute nel Reame di Napoli negli anni 1647-50, ora per la prima volta messo a stampa, etc dal Marchese Angelo Granito, Napoli, 1854, presso G. Nobile." (v. r.)

MASBATE

Pages 345-345

one of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PHILIPPINE_ISLANDS">Philippine <a clas</a>s="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">Islands</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> Archipelago, situated to the S. of Luzon and W. of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SAMAR">Samar</a>, in the middle of the Bisaya <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>. The shape of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> is triangular; it is about 70 miles in length, by 20 in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> breadth; and its <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> is computed at 1225 <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. It consists for the most <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROCKY_MOUNTAINS">rocky <a class=</a>"xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, with only a small portion of cultivated <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a>, and is very thinly populated. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> article of produce is <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RICE">rice</a>. The island contains the harbours of Barreras and Catayungan.

MASCALI NUOVO

Pages 345-345

a town in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Catania, is situated at the foot of Mount Etna, on a small river about 2 miles from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and 18 miles N.N.E. of Catania. The town is ill built, and, though formerly flourishing, is now in a declining condition. <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol4.html#article-FISHING">Fishing</a>, however, is still actively carried on; and there is some trade in lime, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LAVA">lava</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, corn, wine, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>. The surrounding <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> is fertile, and contains many thriving villages. A little to the N.W. stands the village of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASCALI">Mascali</a> Vecchio. There have been found here many curious remains of antiquity, especially of the Saracenic <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>. Pop. about 4000.

MASCARA

Pages 345-345

a town of Algeria, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-ORAN">Oran</a>, pleasantly situated on the S. slope of the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATLAS">Atlas</a> range, 45 miles S.E. of Oran. It was formerly the residence of Abd-el-Kader, and was strongly fortified and defended by a castle. It was taken and burnt by the French in 1835, and was again taken by them in 1841, since which <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> it has remained in their possession. It has been much improved since it came into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the conquerors, and is now strongly garrisoned. Pop. (1851) 4915, of whom 3210 were natives.

MASCHERONI

Pages 345-346

Lorenzo, an Italian mathematician, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BERGAMO">Bergamo</a> in 1750. Intended for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, he devoted his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the classical languages, and studied so successfully, that at the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of eighteen he was appointed professor of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> in the university of his native <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>. From this situation he was promoted to the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> of Greek at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PAVIA">Pavia</a>. Chancing, however, in his twenty-seventh year, to take up a book on <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, he conceived so intense an enthusiasm for that science, that he forthwith renounced all other studies for its sake. His former success attended him in this new pursuit, and he was soon appointed professor of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GEOMETRY">geometry</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of Mariano at Bergamo. In 1796 he published at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a> his Geometry of the Compass, a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> which secured for him the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a> of Bonaparte. Mascheroni, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> though he was, became a zealous promoter of the revolution that attended the invasion of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> by the French. Accordingly he was elected a member of the legislative body of the Cisalpine Republic. In 1798 he was sent to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> the French system of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WEIGHTS_AND_MEASURES">weights and <a class</a>="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>, and to apply it to Italy. His zeal, however, in discharging this duty, was the cause of an illness which closed his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAREER">career</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>. 1800. Mascheroni's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> work, *The Geometry of the Compass*, was translated into French by M. Carette, Svo, Paris, 1798. (See Fifth Dissertation, § I.)

MASHAM

Pages 346-346

a market-town of England, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">North</a> Riding of <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, on the Ure, 16 miles S.S.E. of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RICHMOND">Richmond</a>. It has a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> in the early English style, surmounted by a lofty spire, several Dissenting places of worship, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> school, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>' institute, a library, a literary and several benevolent <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOCIETIES">societies</a>. The inhabitants are chiefly employed in the manufacture of woollen stuffs and in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLAX">flax</a>. Pop. (1851) 1139.

MASINISSA

Pages 346-346

a celebrated African <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, son of Gala, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Numidian tribe of the Massyli, was born about 239 B.C. Receiving his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>, and thus becoming interested in the welfare of that <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, he incited his father in 213 B.C. to form a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> with the Carthaginians. In the same year, accordingly, Masinissa, at the head of a troop of Numidian cavalry, sailed for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, and served most devotedly in the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a> against the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. But the check which the Punic fortunes received at Silpia in 206 B.C. shook his fidelity, and he resolved to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> over to the Romans on the first safe opportunity. This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> was strengthened by the generosity which his nephew Massiva had experienced from Scipio, and probably also by the intelligence that Sophonisba, the beautiful <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of Hasdrubal, to whom he had been betrothed, was about to be wedded to Syphax, the prince of the Numidian tribe of the Massyli. Meanwhile an event had occurred in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a> that accelerated the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEFECTION">defection</a> of Masinissa. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of his native <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, which, after the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his father Gala, had passed in rapid succession to his uncle Esacles, and his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUSIN">cousin</a> Capusa, was seized at this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> in the name of an infant <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of the latter by Mezetulus. On hearing of this usurpation, Masinissa crossed to Africa, rallied around his standard the old <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> of his father, defeated Mezetulus in a pitched <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, and forced him to flee, along with his <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WARD">ward</a>, into the dominions of Syphax. No sooner, however, was Masinissa seated on his ancestral throne, than he recalled the two fugitives, and by his favours disarmed their hostility. But a more formidable foe immediately appeared in the person of Syphax. Instigated and backed by the Carthaginians, that prince invaded the Massylian territories, and annihilated in quick succession those armies which had been hastily mustered to oppose him. Thus stripped of his sovereignty, and driven from his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, Masinissa was obliged to skulk with a few followers near the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-shore, until the landing of Scipio in 204 B.C. gave him the opportunity which he had for some time wished, of identifying his cause with that of the Romans. He joined the invaders with a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his shattered forces, and by his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> fidelity, and his knowledge of the habits of the enemy, contributed in no small <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> to the two victories gained over Hasdrubal and Syphax. On the capture of Cirta, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a> of the Massyli, Masinissa obtained possession of Sophonisba, the wife of Syphax, and, with her own consent, married her. But Scipio severely censured his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> with so determined a foe of the Romans; and Sophonisba, by the advice of her newly espoused husband, poisoned herself to escape the ignominy of falling into the power of her enemies. The grief of Masinissa for this untoward event was allayed by his reinstalment into the sovereignty of the Massylians. From the quiet possession of his power, however, he was soon summoned by the arrival of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HANNIBAL">Hannibal</a> in Africa. In the decisive conflict of Zama which followed (202 B.C.), he made a brilliant <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> at the head of his Numidian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, drove the cavalry of Hannibal from the field, and was thus the first to turn the tide of battle against the Carthaginians. For this important <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> he was rewarded in the following year with the greater part of the kingdom of Syphax. Firmly fixed in his possessions, with the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of King of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMIDIA">Numidia</a>, Masinissa now devoted his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to the organization of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> and the improvement of his people. Yet at times his ambitious spirit, and his reliance upon the powerful support of Rome, incited him to provoke by aggressions the humbled Carthaginians. In all these disputes the Romans acted as mediators, and uniformly favoured the Numidian king. At length in 150 B.C., the Carthaginians, indignant at the intrigues which Masinissa had been carrying on against the welfare of their city, commenced acts of hostility. Masinissa accordingly marched into their territories, and though deserted by several of his chiefs, he adroitly circumvented the enemy, and forced them to capitulate. He died in 148 B.C., at the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of ninety, while Roman ambassadors were on the way to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> to demand reinforcements for the third Punic war. In accordance with his dying request, his kingdom was divided between his three sons, Micipsa, Gulusa, and Massanabal. Masinissa displayed all the qualities that render a prince the favourite of semi-barbarian subjects. Not destitute of skill in strategy, he also possessed a dauntless valour in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, and an unshaken <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-MAGNANIMITY">magnanimity</a> under reverses. He shared the hardships and fare of the meanest soldier; and till within a short time before his death, he underwent with surprising agility all the warlike exercises of youth. His attempts to civilize his people were highly praiseworthy.

MASKELYNE

Pages 346-348

NEVIL**, a most industrious and accurate astronomer, born in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONDON">London</a> on the 6th of October 1732, was the son of Mr. Edmund Maskelyne, a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> of respectable family in Wiltshire. At the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> he was sent to Westminster School, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to apply with diligence to the usual pursuits of that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, until the occurrence of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> solar eclipse of 1748, which made a strong <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a> on his mind, and was the immediate cause of his directing his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, and beginning with great ardour the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> as subservient to that of astronomy. It is remarkable, that the same eclipse is said to have made an astronomer of Lalande, who was only three months older than Maskelyne. He soon afterwards entered as a member of Catherine <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HALL">Hall</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, but in a short <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> removed to Trinity. He took the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of Bachelor of Arts with great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> in 1754, and proceeded regularly afterwards through the succeeding stages of academical <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RANK">rank</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>. He was ordained in 1755 to a curacy at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BARNET">Barnet</a>, and the next year he obtained a fellowship at Trinity. In 1758 he was elected a fellow of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>; having previously become intimate with Dr Bradley, and determined to make astronomy the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> pursuit of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, feeling its perfect compatibility with an enlightened <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a> to the duties of his own profession. In 1761 he was engaged by the Royal Society to undertake a voyage to St Helena in order to observe the transit of Venus. He remained ten months in that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, but the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> prevented his observing the transit to advantage; and the faulty <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> of the plumb-line of his <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUADRANT">quadrant</a>, which was of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> then usually employed, rendered his observations on the stars less conclusive with respect to annual <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PARALLAX">parallax</a> than he had expected. His voyage was, however, of great <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a>, by promoting the introduction of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> observations for ascertaining the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol10.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a>; and he taught the officers of the ship which conveyed him the proper use of the instruments, as well as the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of making the computations. He performed a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> voyage in 1763 to the island of Barbadoes in order to determine the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RATES">rates</a> of Harrison's watches, and also to make experiments with <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRVINE">Irvine</a>'s marine <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> on board of the "Princess Louisa," <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ADMIRAL">Admiral</a> Tyrrel; acting at the same time as chaplain to the ship. The chair he found of very little use for observing the Maskelyne, eclipses of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>'s satellites; and the maker of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHRONOMETERS">chronometers</a> was not satisfied with his report of their performance, fancying that he was too partial to the exclusive employment of lunar observations for determining the longitude. The liberality of the British <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, however, bestowed on Harrison the whole reward that he claimed; and Maskelyne having been appointed to the situation of astronomer-royal, and having thus become a member of the Board of Longitude, was extremely <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> in obtaining a few thousand pounds for the family of Professor Mayer, who had computed lunar tables, and a compliment of L300 for Euler, whose theorems had been employed in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a>. The merits of Mayer's tables having been fully established, the Board of Longitude was induced to promote their application to practical purposes by the annual publication of the Nautical Almanac, which was arranged and conducted entirely under Maskelyne's <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> for the remainder of his life. He was also actively employed, without any other <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> than the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of science and of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, in almost every decision which was required of the Board of Longitude; and he had to give his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the merits of an infinite <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of fruitless projects which were continually submitted to his judgment. He must of course have made many enemies amongst the weak and illiberal; but the universal impartiality and the general accuracy of his determinations were acknowledged by all candid persons; and it must be admitted, that the longitudinal speculators of Great <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> in those days submitted to discouraging remarks from persons in authority, with wonderful fortitude and with great personal civility. During the forty-<a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years that he held the situation of astronomer-royal, he acquired the respect of all <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> by the diligence and accuracy of his observations, which he never neglected to conduct in person whenever it was in his power, and he required only one assistant. The French had a handsome <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> to amuse the public by its exterior magnificence; but the establishment of the observers was never arranged in so methodical a manner as that of the English national <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-OBSERVATORY">observatory</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of their labours were never systematically made public, the attempt which was once made by Lemonnier in his Histoire Céleste having been interrupted and discontinued. Dr Maskelyne, on the other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, obtained leave from the British government to have his observations printed at the public expense under the direction of the Royal Society, who are the legal visitors of the observatory, appointed by the royal sign <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MANUAL">manual</a>. The early observations of Flamsteed and of Bradley were considered as private <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>. Flamsteed published his own, and Bradley's were very liberally bought by his family, and afterwards printed by the university of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, who are still as liberal in bestowing them where they are likely to be employed for the benefit of science. Flamsteed was the astronomer-royal from 1690 to 1720, then Halley to 1750, Bradley to 1762, and Bliss to 1765, when Maskelyne was appointed. He took his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a>'s degree in the year 1777. He made several improvements in the arrangement and employment of the instruments, particularly by enlarging the slits through which the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> was admitted; by making the eye-glass of his transit <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TELESCOPE">telescope</a> moveable to the place of each of the wires of the micrometer; and, above all, by marking the time to tenths of a second, which had never been attempted before, but which he found it practicable to effect with surprising accuracy, as the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of the observations at the different wires sufficiently demonstrated. The object of his expedition to Schelliken is well known. Bouguer had made an unsuccessful attempt to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTRACTION">attraction</a> of a mountain in South <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, and had been obliged to conclude that the mountain was hollow, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the eruption of a volcano, the attraction being Maskelyne too little sensible.
