"There is a certain science," says Aristotle, "which contemplates being in so far as it is being, and the attributes that belong to it essentially as such. This science is not the same with any of those which are called particular sciences; for none of these inquires generally concerning being as being, but each selects some separate portion of being, and contemplates the properties of that alone; as, for example, mathematics. But since we are seeking for the principles and highest causes of things, it is clear that these must have some nature to which they properly belong. We must therefore take as the object of our inquiry the first causes of being as being." A similar conception of the great problem of philosophy had been previously exhibited by Plato in his sketch of the office of dialectic—a science which, though differing in name and method, is in its purpose and aim identical with the first philosophy or theology of Aristotle. In the sciences of geometry and arithmetic, he tells us, certain principles of numbers and figures are assumed by hypothesis as self-evident, but not investigated, by any process of reasoning; and from these assumptions the proposed questions are demonstrated. But in dialectic the same hypotheses are employed, not as first principles, but as stepping-stones to some higher truth and absolutely first principle, which is grasped by the intellect without hypothesis, as that on which all other reasoning ultimately depends. The problem of metaphysics, as conceived by both these philosophers, may be perhaps more clearly stated in modern language as follows:—"To determine the relation that exists between the subjective necessities of thought and the objective necessities of things." In mathematical demonstration, for example, we start from certain axiomatic principles, of which, as mathematicians, we can give no other account than that they are self-evident; that is to say, that we are compelled by the constitution of our minds to admit them. But this opens a further question. What is the relation of self-evidence to reality? Is the necessity, of which I am conscious, of thinking in a certain manner any sure guarantee of a corresponding relation in the objects about which I think? In other words, are the laws of thought also laws of things; or, at least, do they furnish evidence by which the laws of things can be ascertained? Is thought identical with being, so that every mode of the one is at the same time a mode of the other? Is thought an exact copy of being, so that every mode of the one is an adequate representative of some corresponding mode of the other? Or, finally, is thought altogether distinct from being, so that we cannot issue from the circle of our ideas, to seize the realities which those ideas are supposed to represent? Does anything exist beyond the phenomena of our own consciousness? and, if it does exist, what is the path by which it is to be reached? The ancient and mediæval metaphysicians adopted almost unanimously the a priori method of reasoning downwards from the assumption of abstract principles of being,—as the moderns have laid the foundation of the inverse method of reasoning upwards from the phenomena of thought. A short analysis of the principal subjects treated of in the Metaphysics of Aristotle will serve to exhibit the details of the former method, as far as our present limits will permit. In the order of the books we shall follow the common arrangement, which, though far from unexceptionable, is perhaps not more liable to objection than others which have been proposed in its place. The first book comprises a psychological account of the nature of science and its origin in the human mind, followed by a history of the researches of previous philosophers into the principles and causes of things. To this is subjoined a kind of appendix (the book known as A minor), containing an argument in favour of the existence of a first principle of things, and consequently of the possibility of attaining to a knowledge of it; with a caution concerning the method to be pursued, and the necessity of accommodating the mode of reasoning to the nature of the object. The second book commences with a list of questions, which are to be answered in the course of the treatise, and which may be regarded as furnishing a sort of table of contents to the rest of the work. They may be briefly summed up as follows:—1. Do the principles of being and those of demonstration belong to the same or to different sciences, to one science or to many? 2. Are there other substances besides objects of sense; and, if so, of how many kinds? 3. To what science does it belong to take cognisance of identity and difference, similarity and dissimilarity, priority and posteriority, and such like? 4. Are the principles of things to be sought in their genera, or in the material elements of individuals, or does there exist a cause or causes other than matter, and separable from it? 5. Are there the same principles of things perishable and imperishable, and are all principles themselves imperishable? 6. Are being and unity the essence of all things, or must other elements be added? 7. Are the principles of things universal or individual, potential or actual, active or passive? 8. Are numbers, lines, figures, and points substances or not; and, if substances, do they exist separate from the objects of sense? A further development of the difficulties involved in these questions occupies the remainder of this book. The third book is occupied with the sketch of a science of being as such, which has for its object both the principles of things and the laws of reasoning. In it the philosopher maintains the truth of the logical principles of contradiction and excluded middle against the objections of Heraclitus, Anaxagoras, and others, and establishes the distinction between being and appearance, and consequently between truth and error. The fourth book is an explanation of the various significations of several philosophical terms. The terms defined are,—principle, cause, element, nature, necessity, unity, being, substance, identity, distinctness and diversity, similarity and dissimilarity, opposition and contrariety, priority and posteriority, power, quantity, quality, relation, perfection, limitation, in respect of and in itself (καθ' ὅ and καθ' ἀλο), disposition, habit, passion, privation, possession, derivation, part, whole, imperfection, genus, falsehood, accident. --- 1 Metaph. iii. i. The same view is also exhibited more fully in v. 1, in a passage too long for quotation. 2 Republic, vi., p. 510. 3 The correspondence, however, is by no means exact. Michellet observes,—"En général, il faut remarquer que l'énumération et le développement des problèmes contenus dans ce livre ne répondent pas exactement à leurs solutions données dans les autres livres. Car beaucoup de problèmes sont transposés; quelques-uns n'y sont qu'effleurés; plusieurs y sont réunis, à cause de l'affinité qu'il y a entre eux; d'autres encore sont traités en différents endroits." (Essai Critique, p. 131.) The division of the questions themselves admits of considerable variety. Michellet and Haurisson enumerate as many as seventeen. Mr Maurice (Moral and Metaphysical Philosophy, p. 183) reduces them to six.

METAPONTUM

Pages 636-637
or Metapontium, a city of Magna Graecia, was situated on the Tarentine Gulf, 14 miles from Heraclae, and 24 from Tarentum. It was colonized by Achaeans about the beginning of the seventh century B.C.; but some ascribe it to a much earlier origin. In the early period of its history Metapontum was in all probability in alliance with Sybaris and Crotona, cities likewise of Achaean origin; and it was imbued to a considerable extent with the opinions and doctrines of Pythagoras, who retired to this city and spent there the last days of his life. His tomb was still to be seen there in the time of Cicero. The Metapontines assisted the Athenians in their Sicilian expedition (415 B.C.), being at that time in a flourishing condition of wealth and prosperity. They embraced the side of Pyrrhus in his war with the Romans, and after its conclusion fell under the Roman yoke. When Hannibal invaded Italy the Metapontines, after the battle of Cannae, were well disposed to him; but, on account of a garrison of Romans, were unable openly to desert to him till 212 B.C., when the city was occupied by a Carthaginian garrison. When Hannibal was compelled to leave Italy he removed, along with his own troops, the inhabitants of Metapontum; and from that time the city disappears from history. Some remains of it are still to be seen.

METASTASIO

Pages 637-639

Pietro, whose original name was Pietro Trapassi, was born in Rome, 3d <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1698. His father, Felice Trapassi, a native of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASSISI">Assisi</a>, had been forced by the poverty of his family to enter the Corsican regiment of the pope, had subsequently married, supported himself by copying legal documents, and saved <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MONEY">money</a> enough to open a shop in Rome, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARTNERSHIP">partnership</a> with a friend, for the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SALE">sale</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>, and other things of the kind. His mother was Francesca Galasti of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>. They had two sons, the elder of whom, Leopoldo, afterwards became an advocate, and distinguished himself as a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> polemic; and two daughters. Pietro from his earliest years showed an extraordinary <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> for improvisation, and was accustomed to entertain his playmates in the street with impromptu rhymes. The celebrated jurist Gravina, having accidentally heard him so engaged while passing his father's shop one <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, was so much interested by his precocious talent, and by the sweetness and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MODESTY">modesty</a> of his manners, that he proposed to his parents to adopt and educate the boy as his own son. The proposal was accepted. Gravina, who was a Grecian and a pedant, changed his name to Metastasio, from the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EQUIVALENT">equivalent</a> to tropassamento. Intending to educate him for the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BAR">bar</a>, where he thought his powers of improvisation and eloquence might be turned to most account, he sent him to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUSIN">cousin</a> Caroprese, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a>, to be taught Greek and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. In a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to Mattei, the poet dwells on these youthful studies with enthusiasm. Gravina did not, however, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-INTERDICT">interdict</a> what was his own favourite employment, the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-READING">reading</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> poets, nor the practice of improvisation; and the handsome, modest, and vivacious boy was loved and admired in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> and Crotona by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> to which the influence of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> admitted him. He relates in one of his letters that he was accustomed at this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> to engage in poetic contests with the most distinguished improvisatori; but the excitement being found prejudicial to his <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, Gravina caused him to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BREAK">break</a> it off, and apply himself more closely to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the Greek poets and of the early Italian writers, and to the cultivation of a correct style. For this course of conduct Metastasio afterwards expressed his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a>, censuring the practice of improvisation as extremely injurious to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and labour. At the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of twelve he translated the Iliad of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOMER">Homer</a> in ottava rima; and two years later he composed the tragedy of Giustino, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of his patron's dramas,—stiff and feeble imitations of the Greek,—borrowing the plot from the Italia Liberata of Trissini. An edition of this tragedy is extant, printed in 1713. In a letter to Calsabigi, who superintended the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> edition of his Metastasio <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> in 1755, he expresses his regret that this immature production had been included. Yet it is not without beauties prophetic of the Olimpiade. The story is simple and affecting, and the plot is developed with much clearness. In 1714 Caroprese died, leaving Gravina his heir, who in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> went into Calabria and rejoined his adopted son. These mingled occupations of poetical and legal study Metastasio pursued till the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his benefactor in 1718. The blow was severely felt by the poet, who composed on the occasion an elegy entitled La strada <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ALLA">alla</a> gloria, which he recited, amid the tears of the audience, to the literary society founded by his distinguished patron. Gravina bequeathed him his Roman <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, amounting to 15,000 scudi (between L3000 and L4000); and finding himself at the end of two years nearly penniless, he resolved to resume his legal studies. With the view of opposing a powerful <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a> to his inclination, and escaping the seductions of society, he went to Naples, and placed himself under the tuition of the eminent lawyer Castagnola, whose aversion to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> was such that Metastasio was compelled to observe the strictest secrecy in his favourite pursuits. His genius was, however, too well known, and too highly appreciated by the refined society in which he moved, to permit him <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> to resist the struggles of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, seconded by admiration and flattery. He composed an epithalamium of 100 stanzas, in ottava rima, on the occasion of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> of the Marchese Pignatelli; and on the same occasion, perhaps, his first musical drama, Endimione, in 1721. But the event that fixed his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DESTINY">destiny</a> was the following:—The birthday of the Empress <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, consort of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> VI, occurring during her pregnancy, the viceroy wished to celebrate it with unusual splendour, and requested Metastasio to write an <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-OPERA">opera</a>. The latter complied, exacting a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROMISE">promise</a> of strict silence with regard to the author's name, and produced Gli Orti Esperidi, which was received with the most unusual and unbounded applause. The viceroy was so highly gratified that he presented the poet with 200 ducats. At first every one was ignorant of the author, and supposed it to be the work of some Roman poet; not even the composer, Porpora, nor the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ACTORS">actors</a> knew. But <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MARIANNA">Marianna</a> Bulgarelli, known as "La Romana," from her birthplace, who had performed the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Venus with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> success and profit, succeeded in discovering him. Gli Orti Esperidi was published, with the name of the author, the same year at Naples. The opera of Angelica, also composed by Porpora, was produced on the same occasion in 1722. It is not clear whether it was before <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> after the production of Angelica that Metastasio finally determined on abandoning the legal profession. He quitted the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Castagnola, and went to live with La Romana and her husband. She introduced him to Porpora, from whom he received instructions in the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of music, and doubtless much insight into the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a> adaptation. From La Romana herself he confesses to have learned much. Mattei asserts, as from good authority, that the finest situations in his next work, Didone Abbandonata, written for the carnival 1724, were suggested by this accomplished actress. This opera, composed by Sarro, and produced at Naples in that year, and afterwards composed by Vinci, and produced at Rome and <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> in the following years, rapidly spread the fame of Metastasio over the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> as the great dramatist of the age. In 1727 La Bulgarelli took leave of the stage, of which she had been now for eighteen years an ornament, and returned to her native <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, taking with her her husband and her cicileo. Catone in <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-UTICA">Utica</a> was written for the Roman stage in 1728, and was Metastasio's first (<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we except Giustino) and last attempt in regular tragedy. The reception it met with convinced him that it was impossible to harmonize the requirements of the musical drama with those of tragedy; he changed the conclusion, adapting Metastasio. it to the powers of his actors and the taste of his audience, and never forgot the lesson. *Catone* was composed by Vinci for Rome, and next year by Leo for Venice. *Ezio*, *Alessandro nell'Indie*, and *Semiramide* rapidly followed, extending his fame, but not much improving his circumstances. Feeling himself partially dependent on La Bulgarelli, and with no very brilliant prospects, he became despondent, when in September 1729 he received a letter from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a> Pio of Savoy, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VIENNA">Vienna</a>, commissioning two dramas, and inviting him thither to occupy the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-POST">post</a> of imperial poet, with an annual salary of 3000 florins. This appointment he owed to his fame, to the influence of the Princess Althan, and the generosity of Zane, who retired on a pension. Metastasio welcomed it with eagerness. He merely requested time to complete his Roman engagements, chiefly the *Artaserse*; and having done so, he took a tender farewell of his family, and of the faithful Marianna, whom he never <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SAW">saw</a> again, and repaired to Vienna in April 1730. He was received with cordiality in the house of Niccolò de Martinez, *cerimoniere* of the apostolic nuncio, where he <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to reside till his death. The dramas which he produced in the year succeeding his arrival, *Adriano in Siria* and *Demetrio*, both composed by Caldara, and performed within a few days of each other, had great success. That of *Issipile*, written in the following year, moved the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> from his customary reserve, and procured the poet his personal congratulations. His fame increased with the operas of *Giuseppe*, *Demofonte*, and the *Divine Olimpiade*, which successively appeared in 1733. To the plaudits of the *Olimpiade* the emperor added the more <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> recompense of a treasurership in Naples, of which, however, he was in a few years bereft by the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a> of the succession. His <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> at this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> may best be read in his letters to La Bulgarelli, written with great expansion and confidence. His <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> was in his work: the scenes which touched his audience had first moved himself. "I send you," he writes, "a sonnet composed while I was <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> a pathetic <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> (it was the ninth scene of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ACT">act</a> of the *Olimpiade*), with which I was so much affected, that I found myself in tears." He sends her directions for the representation of *Demetrio* in Rome, asks her for suggestions and for advice, and talks of the applause he was receiving. While engaged on the *Clemenza di Tito*, February 1734, the news of Marianna's death reached him. For some time he was quite overpowered. She bequeathed him her whole fortune, amounting to 25,000 Roman scudi, which he at once made over to the widower. There cannot be much doubt as to the nature of his connection with the actress. The pious expressions he makes <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of on the occasion, in a letter to a friend (Burney, vol. i., p. 109), are not sufficient to refute an inference so entirely warranted by all the facts, and by the state of society then, and unfortunately still, existing in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. His immediate and generous renunciation of her legacy procured him great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>. That act was one quite in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> with the tenor of his whole life. From this time onward Metastasio's life was laborious and peaceful, little disturbed in outward appearance by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> distractions that followed the death of Charles VI, in 1740, or that of Charles VII, in 1744. On the former occasion he received excellent and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> proposals from various courts, but he adhered to the fortunes and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MARIA">Maria</a> Theresa, whom he had taught Italian, and who was personally attached to her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a>. During this period he produced his best works, writing only at the command of the court, and writing rapidly. He told Burney that the opera of *Achille in Sciro*, produced in 1736 on occasion of the marriage of Maria, was written in eighteen days, and that of *Ipermestra*, in 1744, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a>. The operas of *Temistocle* and *Attilio Regolo*, with the exception of the *Olimpiade* perhaps his best works, belong to this period; *Temistocle* being produced in 1738, and *Re-Metastasio-golo* being interrupted in 1740 by the death of the sovereign. This continual labour, and the ungenial <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> of Vienna, brought on in 1745 a serious illness, which obliged him to suspend his exertions. His malady was chiefly a nervous one, and he suffered from it more or less till his death. An occasional visit to his native <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> would perhaps have better reconciled his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> to the severity of the Austrian climate, of which he so often bitterly complains; but excepting an annual visit to the seat of the Princess d'Althan in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MORAVIA">Moravia</a>, he never stirred from Vienna. His days were spent in the society of the Martinez, and of a few congenial friends. Burney, who visited him in 1772, gives an interesting account of his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of life and his conversation (*State of Music in Germany*, &c., vol. i., p. 298 ff.); but the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a>, almost the only, source of information about him during this latter period are his own delightful letters. These give a fine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of the nobleness, generosity, and kindness of his disposition. His most intimate friend was the celebrated singer Farinelli, to whom he writes as his "twin <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>" (*gemello*), and who appears to have deserved and reciprocated his affections. These letters also show how thoroughly he had studied and comprehended the requirements of the composer, and with what care and judgment he adapted his dramas to the necessities of music. The ancient poets he read assiduously. Ovid was his particular favourite, as we might guess from the frequent occurrence of Ovidian sentiments in his works. In spite of the care of Gravina, he does not appear to have ever mastered the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> sufficiently to enable him to appreciate their tragic writers. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a> he has left of them proves this; and he confesses to the difficulty he had of reading the *Poetics* of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, of which he has also left an imperfect <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a>. Of the Italians, his great favourite and model was Tasso, to whom he revolted at an early age from the Ariostisti, and Marino, the so-called depraver of Italian poetry, whom he always read before sitting <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to work. Metastasio died in Vienna on the 12th of April 1782. A fever, caught by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> himself on the occasion of the pope's visit, carried him off in twelve days. He was buried in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of St Michael. He left the younger Martinez heir to his real property and a fortune of 130,000 florins, with deduction of 2000 for each of the two <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a> and 3000 for each of the three brothers of the legate. He had survived all his Italian relatives. The dramatic works of Metastasio are of the very highest excellence in their kind. Judged simply as dramas, and in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of Shakespeare, Corneille, and Racine, they <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a> be pronounced exceedingly defective in point of characterization, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a>, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>; but regarded as compositions to be set to music, they are unequalled. What are excellences and necessities in the spoken drama, become, when transferred to the sung drama, difficulties in the way of the composer and the audience. On the other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, the improbabilities of incident and situation which would shock an audience in the spoken drama, tend to heighten the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> derived from music; the music itself, the greatest improbability, being already conceded. In estimating his powers, all those <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POINTS">points</a> in which Metastasio falls infinitely short of the real dramatists must be taken into account; but in estimating the value of his works, it matters little whether he was deficient in true dramatic genius, or voluntarily renounced its <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>. One thing only is to be regretted, that Metastasio did not exercise more judgment in the choice of his subjects; we may <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> all his sentiments, incidents, and motive, but not that they should be introduced into <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, or attached to great historical <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>. Caesar, Amilcar, and Regulus, are too distinctly marked and too incongruous with the subject to be made the heroes of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOVE">love</a> story. With such a choice, besides, the defects of Metastasio, in his letter of thanks to Zeno, says that the latter was his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MASTER">master</a> and model. Apostolo Zeno rescued the Italian opera from the debasement into which it had sunk, and which is so admirably described in Marcello's *Teatro alla Moda*. He is a poet of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> ability, if not of first-rate genius. He as much surpasses his pupil in force of characterization, simplicity and strength of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a>, and accuracy of historical colouring, as he falls short of him in sweetness, delicate clearness, and musical adaptability. It is in these that Metastasio's great merit consists. His songs are already music. "He exerted himself to fulfill every demand of music. He shortened the recitative; he enlivened the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-DIALOGUE">dialogue</a>. And as his mother tongue, now in the highest <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> refined, was quite at his command, he made of the Italian rhythm a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-SYLLABLE">syllable</a> music, which is single in its kind." (Bouterweck, *Gesch.* ii., p. 493.) The Italian critics have almost deified Metastasio. In respect of style, perhaps, they are the only proper judges; but it is impossible to agree with all that Andres, Arteaga, and Baretti have uttered in his praise. The sweetness, harmony, and lyrical rendering and finish of many of Metastasio's arias and canzonettes are quite unequalled; and one is rather surprised to learn the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> coolness with which he was accustomed to set to work. Of the canzonette *La Partenza* and that to Nice, *Grazie agl' innamor tui*, are perhaps the finest, as they are the most celebrated. Metastasio, late in life, counted forty editions of his works in his own library. The best are,—the Paris edition of 1755, in 9 vols. 8vo, published under the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of Calasibigi; the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TURIN">Turin</a>, 1757, 10 vols. 4to, founded on the former, and frequently reprinted till 1780, when the Herissant edition, in 12 vols. 4to, appeared at Paris, under the care of Pezzana, from a copy of the Turin edition corrected by the author. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTE">Conte</a> Pajala published the posthumous works at Vienna in 1795. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GENOA">Genoa</a> edition of 1802 and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a> of 1811 are the most valuable.

METELLUS

Pages 639-640

the name of a noble family of the Cæcilian gens. Of this family the following are the most notable members: Quintus Cæcilius Metellus Macedonicus, who was appointed praetor in 148 B.C. Having received <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a> as his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, he routed and captured Andriscus, the pretended <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-KING">king</a> of that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. He then turned his arms against the Achaeans, and encountering their praetor Critolaus near Thermopylae, gave him a severe defeat. After gaining a victory over the Arcadians near Charonea, he returned to Rome in 146 B.C., and was honoured with a triumph and with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SURNAME">surname</a> of Macedonicus. Elected to the consulship in 143 B.C., Metellus was intrusted with the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-WAR">war</a> against the Celtiberians in nearer <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>. During the two years of this command he maintained with a steady <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAND">hand</a> the severest <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> among his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a>, and the most skilful <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TACTICS">tactics</a> against the enemy. His censorship in 131 B.C. was rendered notable by his proposing that every Roman should be forced by <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> to marry. The speech with which he introduced this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> was <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> afterwards read by Augustus in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, and has been partly preserved by A. Gellius in his *Noctes Atticae*. Metellus lived to be universally respected, and to see his four sons enjoy the highest honours and the highest offices in the state. He died in 115 B.C., after exhibiting in his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> felicity which <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> writers have considered remarkable and almost unexampled. Quintus Cæcilius Metellus Numidicus, who became <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> in 109 B.C., and was sent into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NUMIDIA">Numidia</a> to carry on the war against Jugurtha. No sooner had he assumed the command than the Roman cause, which was formerly on the descendant, began forthwith to prosper. He routed the enemy near the River Mathal, ravaged the country without opposition, and by an artful system of intrigues kept the Numidian king in a restless terror for his life. In the following year, however, he was forced by the wary strategy of Jugurtha to protract the war. This delay was employed by his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>, the ambitious Marius, to ruin his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> reputation. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> was, that in a short <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> the low-born Marius superseded the aristocratic Metellus in the consulship and the command of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. On his arrival at Rome in 107 B.C. Metellus was received with <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> applause, and was honoured with a triumph and with the <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Numidicus. During his censorship in 102 B.C. his zeal for the aristocracy led him to attempt to expel from the senate two inveterate plebeians Servilius Glanecia and Appuleius Saturninus. In 100 B.C. the latter obtaining the tribunate, returned the blow of Metellus, and by the aid of Marius, who was then consul, succeeded not only in depriving him of his seat in the senate, but in effecting his banishment. With cheerful resignation Metellus set out to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RHODES">Rhodes</a>, carrying along with him his friend Cælius Praconinus, the rhetorician, and bent upon burying all gloomy thoughts in the deep problems of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. He was roused, however, from his studies in the following year by the news that the popular party had suffered a severe check by the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Saturninus, and that his own banishment was repealed. Not long after his return to Rome, Metellus is supposed to have been poisoned. Quintus Cæcilius Metellus Pius, who received the surname of Pius from his affectionate endeavours to effect the recall of his father Numidicus from banishment. He was elected praetor in 89 B.C., and gained his first distinction as one of the leaders of the Marsic war. From carrying on hostilities against the Samnites he was summoned in 87 B.C. to defend Rome from Marius, who had returned from exile, and was marching towards the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> to wreak vengeance on his enemies. Deeming it imprudent to dare so redoubtable a foe, Metellus repaired to <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, and did not return to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> till 84 B.C. He was among the first to greet Sulla on his landing at Brundusium in 83 B.C., and was one of the most effective lieutenants of that general in his protracted struggle with the Marian party. In 82 B.C. he gained three successive victories over the forces of Carbo; and in 79 B.C. he was sent as proconsul into Spain to check the victorious <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAREER">career</a> of Sertorius. His <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a>, however, of that country, and the increasing infirmities of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, rendered him unfit to cope with the alert movements and guerrilla strategy of his enemy. Only after a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years was his military reputation redeemed by a victory over Sertorius. He returned to Rome in the following year to celebrate a triumph. Metellus Pius had been consul along with Sulla in 80 B.C., and he had also been appointed pontifex maximus. He died about 63 B.C. Quintus Cæcilius Metellus Celer, who was elected to the praetorship in 63 B.C. In this capacity he was intrusted with the command of the three legions that guarded the Picentine and Senonian districts during the Catilinarian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSPIRACY">conspiracy</a>. Anticipating the attempt of the rebel army to escape into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAUL">Gaul</a>, he threw himself into the passes of the Apennines, and thus compelled Catiline to turn back upon his pursuers, and to hazard that <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> which issued in his defeat and death. In 60 B.C. Metellus was elected to the consulship, and exerted the entire power of his office in opposing the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> of Pompey, who was at that time considered the deadliest foe of the aristocracy. So determined, indeed, was his opposition, that he chose to be dragged to prison by order of the tribune rather than sanction an agrarian law for the provision of Pompey's soldiers. With the same unflinching resistance did he meet the agrarian law of Caesar in 59 B.C. His death happened in the same year, not without raising suspicions that he had been poisoned by his wife Clodia, the profligate sister of Clodius. Quintus Cæcilius Metellus Pius Scipio, who was the adopted son of Metellus Pius, and became tribune of the people in 69 B.C. In 52 B.C. Pompey took his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> Cornelia in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol6.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, and chose himself as his colleague in the consulship. Metellus now became a puppet in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of his ambitious son-in-law. In 49 B.C. he proposed in the senate that Caesar should be commanded to disband his troops, on pain of being treated as a public enemy. On the outbreak of the civil war which followed the execution of this proposal, the command in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYRIA">Syria</a> was allotted to Metellus. No sooner had he taken possession of his province than his vicious character and his inability to govern burst forth into strong manifestation. The most exorbitant taxes were wrung from the people; the country was overrun by swarms of pillaging soldiers, and the blackest crimes passed unchallenged. From this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of ruthless oppression he was summoned in 48 B.C. to play a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> in the impending struggle between Pompey and Caesar. He joined his son-in-law shortly after the skirmish at Dyrrhachium, and commencing forthwith to portion out the honours which the coming victory would leave at the disposal of his party, he became involved in a hot quarrel with some of his comrades touching his own claims to succeed Caesar in the office of pontifex maximus. On the fatal <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> of Pharsalus he led the centre of the Pompeian army, and after he had seen his ambitious hopes scattered in the rout of his <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> squadrons, he repaired to Africa to seek the aid of Juba, King of Numidia. The partizans of Pompey in that country placed him at their head. He was engaged in using his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a> in his old practice of pillaging and oppressing when Caesar arrived, towards the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the year 47 B.C. In the following year Metellus was completely defeated at Thapsus. Escaping on board of a small fleet, he was intercepted by a squadron under P. Sittius, and was on the point of being captured when he stabbed himself; and then flung himself into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>.

METEMPSYCHOSIS

Pages 640-647

a word of Greek origin signifying the passage <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-OR">or</a> transmigration of souls, is applied to a peculiar system of doctrine, of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> antiquity, respecting the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-DESTINY">destiny</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>. According to the more general forms of this system, the souls of men after <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> are supposed to enter successively into various bodies, and to animate various existences, which differ only in their <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> forms. It is equally difficult for <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAN">man</a> to believe in the ultimate annihilation of his spirit and to conceive of a future state of existence totally different from the present, independent alike of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> and of the laws of organized <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Accordingly, the mind seeks naturally for some <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of reconciling these two antagonistic conceptions—some system of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>, no <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> how obscure, whereby "the longing after <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">immortality</a>" may be gratified, and the instinctive shrinking from annihilation find itself respected. And hence the origin of metempsychosis: the first form in which the doctrine of the immortality of the soul is presented to the human mind. Metempsychosis was maintained by the Egyptians, the Hindus, and the Greeks. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a> informs us (lib. ii., sec. 123), that the Egyptians were the first to adopt the doctrine of the soul's immortality; and it is generally to them that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of the metempsychosis is attributed. They held that the human soul immediately after death entered into some animal, called into existence at the same instant, and that after having successively assumed the forms of all the animals which inhabit the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAND">land</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AIR">air</a>, it returned, after completing a cycle of 3000 years, into the body of a man, to recommence eternally the same endless pilgrimage. With the Hindus, again, the idea of metempsychosis is more metaphysical, more universal, than that of the Egyptians, and is closely allied to the idea of emanation maintained by that highly <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SPECULATIVE">speculative</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RACE">race</a>. As matter is the last <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of the emanations of Brahma, it follows that life, which is the union of the soul with matter, is essentially an evil. This being the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CASE">case</a>, all the developments of life, such as actions, sensations, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, pain, &c., must of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> share in the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGRADATION">degradation</a>. Accordingly, the proper business of the soul is to die to everything earthly—to elevate itself by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a> to that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> repose in the bosom of the Deity from which it originally came forth. The soul must expiate in this world the sins of its previous life; and in order to purification, the impenitent are at death condemned to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> from one body into another of a more or less perfect form, according to the upward or downward tendency of their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. Such is the doctrine taught in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> of Vaiseshika. According to the Vedanta system, again, the soul is not an emanation but a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Brahma; a spark from an eternal fire. It knows neither birth nor death; it endures itself only for a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-TIME">time</a> in a corporeal envelope, where it is afflicted by the darkness of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a>, and subjected to the sufferings attendant upon evil. It visits various bodies in succession, and the circle of its metamorphoses embraces all organized nature, from a plant up to a man. Divine knowledge alone can extricate it from this circle of sorrow and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HUMILIATION">humiliation</a>; and this knowledge can only be attained by the soul stripping itself of all personality both of feeling and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WILL">will</a>; after which it precipitates itself into the bosom of the Deity, as a river discharges its waters into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>. It is a current <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> that the idea of metempsychosis passed from <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> into <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>; but this <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> is not well founded. For not only are traces of this doctrine to be found in the latter <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, as the name of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-ORPHEUS">Orpheus</a> will suggest, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LONG">long</a> previous to any authentic intercourse between those two nations, but Herodotus himself expressly distinguishes between the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol1.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> partizans of metempsychosis in Greece; between the doctrine current in the country before the time of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-PYTHAGORAS">Pythagoras</a> and the form of it introduced by that <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, who was the first Greek speculator initiated in the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> science of the Egyptian priests. But whether original or borrowed, the doctrine as found in Greece was in complete <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> with the genius of the Greek people. It was removed alike from the cloudy mysticism of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-INDIA">India</a> and from the miraculous naturalism of Egypt. It was Pythagoras who gave the doctrine its most precise form. He limited the metamorphoses of the soul to animal life, and, instead of a fortuitous entrance, he maintained that each individual soul passed into that particular form of organized animal existence which was most in harmony with its own faculties and condition. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>, in adopting this Pythagorean doctrine, attempts in the *Phaedo* to establish it from two sources, and thus elevates it into the class of philosophical <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a>. His first <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> is drawn from the general order of nature, and the other from the human consciousness. Nature, says Plato, is governed by the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> of contraries; death succeeds life, and life must succeed death. Again, we find <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of the same state of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRE_EXISTENCE">pre-existence</a> in the fact of reminiscence. That intellectual suggestiveness and inventive power so frequently noticeable in the subtler workings of the understanding, by which the mind makes such swift conquest of whole territories of the realm of knowledge, are only to be attributed to the fact that all this knowledge was once fully comprehended in a previous state of existence. But how far Plato insisted on this doctrine, or whether it was ought more than a piece of suggestive <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-HYPOTHESIS">hypothesis</a>, it is difficult to determine. We find the idea of metempsychosis assuming new developments during the later stages of Greek speculation. We encounter it subsequently in the school of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>, in the bosom of Judaism, and in a father of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. The hypothesis of a pre-existent state was, with <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol8.html#article-ORIGEN">Origen</a>, a favourite mode of explaining certain biblical difficulties; and the same argument, particularly in its bearings on original sin, has been recently revived by an eminent American divine. METEOROLITE. This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TERM">term</a> is derived from the Greek πτερόν, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-METEOR">meteor</a>, and ἀστος, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, and denotes a stony substance, exhibiting peculiar <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> of which to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> is usually accompanied by the appearance and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-EXPLOSION">explosion</a> of a fire-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BALL">ball</a>. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LUMINOUS">Luminous</a> meteors have in all ages been observed in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>. It is also well known that their disappearance has frequently been attended with a loud noise; but that they should moreover terminate in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FALL">fall</a> of one or more <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> bodies to the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-EARTH_S">earth's</a> surface, is a position so repugnant to our ordinary conceptions of the tenor of physical events, that we cannot admit it as a fact upon slight or scanty evidence. One passage may be cited from the books of the Old <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a> in corroboration of the descent of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STONES">stones</a> from the atmosphere. In the 11th <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VERSE">verse</a> of the 10th <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> of Joshua we find—"And it came to pass, as they fled from before Israel, and were in the going <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to Beth-horon, that the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> down <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-GREAT">great</a> stones from heaven upon them unto Azekah, and they died." <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> from sacred we turn to the early <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of profane <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, we shall find the annals of public events very copiously interspersed with notices of such strange appearances. Through the midst of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> which envelopes the history of the beatai we discern some characters which correspond with those of meteorolites. Thus in the Aethusa, a poem falsely ascribed to Orpheus, the crōngaros is said to be "rough, heavy, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BLACK">black</a>." Damascus, in an extract of his Life of Isidorus, preserved by Photius, relates that the beatai fell on Mount Libanus, in a "glow of fire." A fragment of Sanchoniathon, preserved by Eusebius in his Preparatio Evangelii (i. 10), moreover informs us, that these stones were fabricated by the god Uranus or Heaven, one of whose four sons was named Beatai. In the same chapter we are told that Astarte found a "<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STAR">star</a>" which had "fallen from heaven," and honoured it with consecration in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TYRE">Tyre</a>. The stone denominated "the mother of the gods," if we can believe Appian, Herodian, and Marcellinus, "fell from heaven." Aristodemus, cited by the Greek scholiast on Piniar, asserts that it fell encircled by fire, upon a hill, at the feet of the Theban bard. It is said to have been of a black <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and of an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> shape. Herodian expressly declares, that the Phoenicians had no statue of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> polished by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, but only a certain stone, circular below, and terminated acutely above, in the form of a cone, of a black colour, and that, according to report, it "fell from heaven," and was regarded by the people as the image of the sun. Amongst various instances which might be selected from Livy is that of a shower of stones on the Alban Mount, in the reign of Tullus Hostilius, or about 652 B.C. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SENATE">senate</a> was assured that stones had really fallen, "hand alter quam quem grandinem venti glomeratam in terras agunt." But one of the most remarkable <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a> which occurs in the records of antiquity is that which is mentioned in the 58th chapter of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SECOND">second</a> book of Pliny's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="../1842/vol15.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> History, of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> stone which fell near Egospotamos in Thrace, in the second year of the 78th Olympiad, or, according to our <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRONOLOGY">chronology</a>, about 467 years before the Christian era. Pliny assures us that this extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MASS">mass</a> was still shown in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, and that it was as large as a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CART">cart</a>, and of a burned colour. According to Plutarch, in the Life of Ly-sander, the inhabitants of the Chersonesus held the Thracian stone in great veneration, and exhibited it as a public show. This event is also recorded in that curious <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DOCUMENT">document</a>, The Parian <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CHRONICLE">Chronicle</a>, among the Arundelian marbles, in these terms—"From the time when the stone fell at Egospotamos, and the poet <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SIMONIDES">Simonides</a> died at the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of ninety, during the archbishopship of Thengenesides at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATHENS">Athens</a>, is 205 years." Pliny gives another instance of an aerolite which fell in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LUCANIA">Lucania</a> about 56 B.C.; Meteoro-lite and Caesar records the descent of another at Accilla 46 B.C. From this period till near the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of the fifteenth century, any historical notices which we have been enabled to collect are so vague and scanty, that in this abridged view of the subject we may pass them over in silence. Professor Bantenschoven, of the central school of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLMAR">Colmar</a>, first directed the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of naturalists to some of the old chronicles, which commemorate, with much naïveté, and in the true spirit of the times, the fall of the celebrated stone of Ensisheim. The following account accompanied this very singular mass when it was suspended, in the church:—"In the year of the Lord 1492, on Wednesday, which was Martimas, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EVE">eve</a>, the 7th of November, there happened a singular miracle: for, between eleven o'clock and noon there was a loud peal of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a>, and a prolonged confused noise, which was heard to a great distance, and a stone fell from the air, in the jurisdiction of Ensisheim, which weighed 250 pounds, and the confused noise was, moreover, much louder than here. There a child <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SAW">saw</a> it strike on a field situated in the upper jurisdiction, towards the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-RHINE">Rhine</a> and Inn, near to the district of Gisgard, which was sown with wheat; and did it no harm, except that it made a hole there; and then they conveyed it from that spot, and many pieces were broken from it, which the landvogt forbade. They therefore caused it to be placed in the church, with the intention of suspending it as a miracle, and many people came hither to see this stone." Again, Trithemius, in his Hirsangiansian Annals, employs <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> to this effect:—"In the same year, on the 7th day of November, in the village of Santigaw, near the townlet of Ensisheim, not far from <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>, a city of Germany, a stone, called a thunder-stone, of a prodigious size, for we know from eye-witnesses that it weighed 255 pounds, fell from the heavens. Its fall was so violent that it broke into two pieces. The most considerable is still exhibited at the door of the church of Ensisheim, suspended by an <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IRON">iron</a> chain, as a proof of the fact which we have mentioned, and to preserve it in the public recollection." We learn also from Paul Lang, "that there arose a furious storm on the 7th of November 1492, and that whilst the thunder roared, and the heavens appeared all on fire, a stone of enormous size fell near Ensisheim." It is worthy of observation that these chroniclers lived at the period which they assign to the descent of the stone, and that although their names are hastening to oblivion, Trithemius yielded to few of his contemporaries in labour and learning; whilst Lang, a German Benedictine, had travelled in search of historical monuments, arraigned the license of the Catholic clergy, and applauded the independence of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a> and Melancthon. In the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMMENTARY">Commentary</a> of Surius, a Carthusian monk of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLOGNE">Cologne</a>, mention is made of a shower of large stones which fell in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LOMBARDY">Lombardy</a> in 1510. These stones were harder than flint, and smelled of sulphur. The heaviest weighed 120 pounds. The same event is more particularly related by Cardan, in his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-WORK">work</a> entitled De Rerum Varietate (lib. xiv., c. 72). According to this author, near the River Adda, not far from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a>, and at five o'clock in the evening, about 1120 stones fell from the air, one of them weighing 120 pounds, and another 60 pounds. Many were presented to the French governor and his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPUTY">deputy</a>. In the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol14.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">Emperor</a> Jehan-schah, written in Persian by himself, and translated by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> Kirkpatrick, is an account of the stone that fell in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-LAHORE">Lahore</a> in 1620; and Ferishta has recorded, in the true oriental style, the conversion of "this son of thunder," as he calls it, into two scimitars, a dagger, and a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>, by order of the emperor. The emperor says,—Here I had this substance weighed in my presence. Its <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> was 160 tolas. I committed it to a skilful artizan, with orders to make of it a sabre, a knife, and a dagger. The workman reported that the substance was not malleable, but shivered into pieces under the hammer. Upon this I ordered it to be mixed with other iron. Conformably to my orders, three parts of the iron of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a> were mixed with one part of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMON">common</a> iron, and from the mixture were made two sabres, one knife, and one dagger." The celebrated Gassendi informs us, that on the 27th of November 1627, about ten o'clock in the morning, during a very clear sky, he saw a flaming stone, of the apparent diameter of 4 feet, fall on Mount Vaison, an eminence situated between the small <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of Perne and Guillaumes in Provence. This stone was surrounded by a luminous circle of different colours, nearly resembling the rainbow, and its fall was accompanied with a noise like the discharge of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>. It weighed 59 pounds, and its specific gravity was to that of common marble as fourteen to eleven. It was of a dark metallic colour, and extremely hard. From a curious book printed at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1672, and now become very scarce, entitled "Conversations tirées de l'Académie de M. l'Abbé Bourdelot contenant diverses Recherches et Observations Physiques, par le Sieur Legallais," we make the ensuing extract:—“A member presents a fragment of two stones which fell near <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-VERONA">Verona</a>, one of which weighed 300 and the other 200 pounds. These stones,” says he, “fell during the night, when the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> was perfectly mild and serene. They seemed to be all on fire, and came from above, but in a slanting <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, and with a tremendous noise. This prodigy terribly alarmed 300 or 400 eye-witnesses, who were at a loss what to think of it.” No philosopher of the present day doubts the descent of stony bodies from the atmosphere; and the testimony of innumerable witnesses of their fall, with phenomena nearly similar, places meteorites among the established facts of natural science. If several of the early notices of them are obscure, we have, in the end of the last and in the present century, many descriptions of their appearance, on their descent, by intelligent witnesses; so that scepticism on this subject can be no longer entertained. It is also very remarkable, that wherever they have fallen, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, in India, or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, their <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> is nearly identically the same, and agrees in composition with no known mineral. This has been established by the careful experiments of the Hon. Mr Howard, of Vaquelin, Laugier, Klaproth, and Berzelius, as well as by the investigations of Bourron and many other mineralogists. Their general composition may be stated as follows:—Silica, 40 per cent.; malleable iron, 25; <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol7.html#article-NICKEL">nickel</a>, from 6 to 8; with a small <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of iron pyrites, and variable proportions of alumina, lime, <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MAGNESIA">magnesia</a>, manganese; with traces of chrome, cobalt, and sulphur. In the present century many have fallen in France, Germany, India, and America; and in our own <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> one fell in <a class="xref" href="vol21.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a> in 1793, another in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GLOUCESTERSHIRE">Gloucestershire</a> in 1833, a third near Glasgow in 1804, and two in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> from 1810 to 1813. We shall now proceed to more detailed instances. We have now to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> our attention to a report of M. de Lalande, inserted in the Historical Almanac of Bresse for 1756. In the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of September 1753, about one o'clock afternoon, when the weather was very hot and very serene, without the least appearance of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a>, a very loud noise, like the discharge of two or three cannons, was heard within the circumference of six leagues, but was of very short <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>. This noise was loudest in the neighbourhood of Pont-de-Vesle; and at Liponnes, a village three leagues from the last-mentioned <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, it was even accompanied with a hissing like that of a cracker. On the same evening there were found at Liponnes and at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PIN">Pin</a> two blackish masses, of a form nearly circular, but very uneven, which had fallen on ploughed ground, and sunk by their own weight to the depth of half a foot below the surface. One of them weighed about twenty pounds; and a fragment of one of them, weighing eleven and a half pounds, was preserved in the cabinet of M. Varenne de Beest at Dijon. The basis of these masses resembled a greyish whinstone, and was very refractory; and some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FERRUGINOUS">ferruginous</a> particles were disseminated in grains, filaments, or minute masses, throughout the substance of the stone, especially in its fissures. On the 15th of September 1760, according to the Abbé Bachelay, about half-past four o'clock afternoon, there appeared near the Chateau de Chevabrie, in the neighbourhood of Luze, a small town of the province of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MAINE">Maine</a>, a stormy cloud, from which proceeded a loud peal of thunder, like the discharge of cannon, and followed by a noise which was mistaken by several people for the lowing of oxen. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> was heard over a space of about two leagues and a half, but unaccompanied by any perceptible <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>. The reapers in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PERIGUEUX">Perigueux</a>, about three leagues from Luze, on hearing the same noise, looked up, and saw an opaque body, which described a curve, and fell on soft turf upon the high <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-ROAD">road</a> from Mons, near which they were at work. They all quickly ran up to it, and found a sort of stone, nearly half of which was buried in the earth, and the whole so hot that it could not be touched. At first they ran away in a panic; but upon returning to the spot some time afterwards, they found the stone precisely in the same situation, and sufficiently cooled to admit of being handled and narrowly examined. It weighed <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> ounces and a half, and was of a triangular form. On the 20th of November 1768 a stone fell at Mauerkirchen, near the River Inn in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>, which weighed 38 pounds, and was of a triangular form, being about eight inches in thickness. Its fall was accompanied by a hissing noise. The next remarkable case that has been recorded occurred on the 20th of August 1789 at Barbotan, near Roquefort, in the Landes of Bordeaux. A much more remarkable phenomenon, however, of the same <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> occurred near <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AGEN">Agen</a> on the 24th of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1790. An inhabitant of St Sevère communicated the following particulars to M. Darcey the chemist, who was then resident at Paris:—“Our town's-people were yesterday very much alarmed. About a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>-past <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NINE">nine</a> o'clock in the evening there suddenly appeared in the atmosphere a fire-ball, dragging a long train, which diffused a very vivid <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> over the horizon. This meteor soon disappeared, and seemed to fall at one hundred paces from us. It was quickly followed by an explosion louder than that of a cannon or of thunder. Everybody dreaded being buried under the ruins of his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, which seemed to give way from the concussion. The same phenomenon was seen, and the report heard, in the neighbouring towns, as Mont de Marsan, Tartas, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAX">Dax</a>. The weather in other respects was very calm, without a breath of <a class="xref" href="../1810/vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> or a cloud, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MOON">moon</a> shone in all her brightness.” Those which fell on the houses produced a noise, not like that of stones, but rather of a substance which had not yet acquired compactness. M. Baudin mentions, that as M. Carris of Barbotan and he were walking in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of the Castle of Morines, about half-past nine o'clock in the evening of the 24th of July 1790, when the air was perfectly calm and the sky cloudless, they found themselves suddenly surrounded by a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PALE">pale</a> clear light, which obscured that of the moon, although the latter was nearly full. On looking up they observed, almost in their zenith, a fire-ball of a larger apparent diameter than that of the moon, dragging a tail which seemed to be five or six times longer than the diameter of its body, and which gradually tapered to a point; the latter ap- approaching to blood-<a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-RED">red</a>, though the rest of the meteor was of a pale <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-WHITE">white</a>. This luminous body proceeded with great velocity from south to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, and in two seconds split into portions of considerable size, like the fragments of a bursting <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOMB">bomb</a>. These fragments became extinguished in the air, and some of them, as they fell, assumed that deep red colour which had been observed at the point of the tail. Two or three minutes afterwards M. Baudin and his friend heard a dreadful explosion, like the simultaneous firing of several pieces of ordnance; but they were not sensible of any tremulous <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> under their feet, although the concussion of the atmosphere shook the windows in their frames, and threw down <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a> utensils from their shelves. When these gentlemen removed to the garden the noise still <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>, and appeared to be directly over their heads. Some time after it had ceased, they heard a hollow sound rolling in echoes for about 50 miles along the chain of the Pyrenees, and at the end of about four minutes gradually dying away in distance. At the same time a strong sulphurous odour was diffused in the atmosphere. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> which occurred between the disruption of the meteor and the loud report induced M. Baudin to conjecture that this fire-ball must have been at least 8 miles from the earth's surface, and that it fell about 4 miles from Mormes. "The latter part of my conjecture," says he, "was soon confirmed by an account which we received of a great many stones having fallen from the atmosphere at Juillac and in the neighbourhood of Barbotan." It appears, indeed, from the concurring testimony of intelligent persons worthy of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>, that the meteor really exploded at a little distance from Juillac, and that its fragments were found lying in an almost circular space of nearly 2 miles in diameter. Some of them weighed 18 or 20, and a few, it is alleged, even 50 pounds. M. de Carris procured one of 18 pounds, which he transmitted to the Academy of Sciences at Paris. That examined by M. Baudin was small, but heavy in proportion to its size, black on the outside, greyish within, and interspersed with many minute, shining, metallic particles. Our chronological <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of cases has now brought us to the fall of several meteorites near Sieña, the particulars of which, as reported by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BRISTOL">Bristol</a> and Sir William <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-HAMILTON">Hamilton</a>, are recorded in the first part of the Philosophical Transactions for the year 1795 (p. 163). The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a> of the Sieña meteor is the 16th of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1794. On the 13th of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a> in the following year, about three o'clock in the afternoon, another of these singular stones, weighing about 56 pounds, fell near the country-house of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Topham in Yorkshire.
